#8819. Research Shows This Is the Best Way to Balance Strength Training and Running

This guide helps you figure out how to squeeze strength workouts between all those miles.

There’s a reason why run coaches and personal trainers emphasize strength training in addition to running: Practicing both forms of exercise will allow you to build stronger muscles and increase your aerobic capacity at the same time. Combining strength training and a running schedule means you boost your fitness in multiple ways.

But sometimes, especially after a heavy leg day workout, your body can feel pretty tired and sore and seemingly not ready to take on miles. This isn’t just in your head. According to a review of 132 studies, it takes a full day or two more to recover from resistance training than it does a high-intensity run.

So if you’ve ever been tempted to skip the weights today in favor of a better run tomorrow, consider the advantages of strength training. Not only does it just feel good to move your muscles through full ranges of motion, especially after sitting all day, but it can also pay off in the long run for your run performance and overall health. In fact, several studies point to better running economy, as well as VO2 max and anaerobic threshold, when following a program that incorporates both endurance training and strength training.

Instead of ditching strength exercises to focus on mileage, the key is creating a strength training schedule that optimally fits into your run training. After all, strength training is supposed to help, not harm, your running. Here’s how to achieve that.

Get the strength plan that works for all runners! Race-Ready Strength, our new progressive 4-week training program, will get you in the best shape to reach your racing goals.

To get it right, you need to understand how your body reacts to moving heavy stuff. Picture pushing a hand truck 50 feet. Pretty easy. That’s running—your body is the hand truck and it moves its own weight rather effortlessly. Now slide the hand truck under a fridge and push it just five feet. A lot more difficult. That’s mechanical loading; it’s why 10 heavy squats feels so much more challenging than 1,000 foot strikes.

The reason strength training makes you faster is because it lowers the amount of energy required to hit a certain pace, explains Kenji Doma, Ph.D., a sports and exercise scientist at James Cook University in Queensland, Australia, and author of a 2014 study on strength training and running performance published in the European Journal of Sports Science.

Doma has also studied the effects of combining aerobic exercise and strength training on muscle hypertrophy and strength, as published in a Sports Medicine systematic review and meta-analysis in 2022. The researchers found that combining the two types of training doesn’t hinder strength and muscle-building gains, but can compromise explosive strength gains when performed in the same session—something to consider if that’s your goal.

What’s important to note is that when you lift weights, your brain alters its neural recruitment pattern, calling up the most fatigue-resistant muscle fibers so you exert less energy. That’s why you don’t want to skimp on strength training. Doma’s research offers guidance on how best to combine mile repeats and repetitions in the gym for a more well-rounded running and strength training schedule.

In the study that focused specifically on running performance, 15 runners of a wide range of ability and average weekly mileage did different strength-training sessions on three occasions. One workout was a high-intensity, total-body session, one was high intensity but for legs only, and one was a low-intensity, total-body workout.

Six hours after each workout, the runners did a treadmill test for 10 minutes at 70 percent of ventilatory threshold pace (easy), then 10 minutes at 90 percent of threshold pace (roughly close to half marathon pace), and then as long as possible at 110 percent of threshold pace. The runners also did the treadmill test at the outset of the study, to get a benchmark for how they would perform when fresh.

The high-intensity strength workouts significantly lessened the runners’ time to exhaustion at the end of the treadmill test. In the benchmark test, they’d lasted an average of close to five minutes at 110 percent of threshold pace. After each of the high-intensity strength sessions, time to exhaustion was almost a minute less, suggesting that the hard weight workouts six hours earlier had dramatically decreased the runners’ ability to sustain fast running.

Doma says his findings have practical implications for how runners should arrange their workouts.

First, he advises not to schedule a hard running workout later in the day of a weight session. “Running at maximal effort is impaired six hours [after] lower-extremity resistance training, and therefore trained to moderately-trained runners will need more than that to recover for running sessions set at high intensities,” he says.

Plus, running at maximal effort is still impaired 24 hours after lower-extremity resistance training, according to Doma. “Therefore, in the case of trained and moderately-trained runners undertaking high-intensity running sessions after lower-extremity resistance training, they may need more than one day to recover.”

Doma also found that running performance at lower intensities was unaffected by the weight workouts. “Runners could undertake strength training and running sessions on the same day six hours apart as long as the running session is set at submaximal intensities,” Doma says. In other words, if you have an easy, long run, or recovery run on the schedule, it’ll be fine to double up that day, as long as workouts are more than six hours apart.

If possible, Doma suggests arranging your schedule so that on days that you run and lift, running comes first. “I found that lower-extremity resistance training performed six hours prior to running sessions at moderate to high intensities cause carryover effects of fatigue the next day to a greater extent than the reverse sequence,” he says. “Therefore, if undertaking lower-extremity resistance training and running sessions on the same day, it is best to undertake a running session before a strength training session. For example, running in the morning before work and lower-extremity resistance training in the evening after work.”

In this scenario, it would make sense to have that morning run be one of your harder workouts of the week. Your workout the following day would then be an easy recovery run, which would be warranted even without the evening lifting, but is that much more called for on the basis of Doma’s research.

This sequence would also mesh with many coaches’ recommendation to have great discrepancy between your hard and easy days, so that you can better recover from your toughest workouts—instead of including hard elements of non-running training on your easy running days.

Scott is a veteran running, fitness, and health journalist who has held senior editorial positions at Runner’s World and Running Times. Much of his writing translates sport science research and elite best practices into practical guidance for everyday athletes. He is the author or coauthor of several running books, including Running Is My Therapy, Advanced Marathoning, and Meb for Mortals. Scott has also written about running for Slate, The Atlantic, the Washington Post, and other members of the sedentary media. His lifetime running odometer is past 110,000 miles, but he’s as much in love as ever.

#8818. Bicycling’s Gear of the Year 2027

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Great cycling gear doesn’t have to cost a fortune. These are the products our editors loved most this year.

There’s no shortage of new cycling gear promising to make your bike lighter, faster, or more comfortable. Over the past year, our editors have put those promises to the test on road and gravel rides, mountain bike trails, commutes, and in the workshop. For Gear of the Year, we’ve chosen the products that stood out most: the ones that solved a problem, made a ride more enjoyable, or delivered tangible performance that impressed us enough to recommend to you.

Our editors bring different perspectives to testing. Matt Phillips has tested bikes and gear for 30 years and has ridden more bikes than any other cycling journalist on the planet. Tara Seplavy has led product development at global bike brands, while Dan Chabanov has won national and elite titles in cyclocross and crit racing. Nearly all of us have worked in or managed bike shops.

Our picks reflect that range of experience and the different ways we ride. This year, we’ve organized them by price to make it easier to find something that fits your budget, whether you’re looking for a small upgrade or considering a bigger purchase. Whatever you choose, if it’s on this list, we think it will improve your ride.

Under $100 $100 to $300 $300 to $1,000 $1,000+

I get the skepticism about a product that seems to have figured out a problem that’s existed forever, but trust me, the Tyre Glider has made me completely rethink how I install tires. Instead of fighting the final few inches with my thumbs, you simply hook it under the bead and glide it around the rim. Until you use it, it just doesn’t make sense how simple and easy it is.

That mechanical advantage is especially useful with tight road tires and tubeless setups, where a conventional tire lever can feel precarious with carbon rims and spokes. It won’t replace a traditional lever for every job, but for the problem it’s designed to solve, it does it really well.

Last summer ended with me sporting a very prominent helmet vent hole tan line on my forehead. The reason was obvious: I avoided applying sunscreen there because every formula would sweat into my eyes. This summer I set out to find one that worked.

When I found Pelotan, I was skeptical of something marketed specifically to cyclists, but it works incredibly well. Although expensive, I found the 6-ounce bottle lasted me the entire season. It goes on light, evaporates quickly, smells nice, and most importantly doesn’t sting my eyes so I actually end up wearing it.

I often ride without gloves, so I’m picky about grips. After testing both the regular and fat versions of Ergon’s GDH Team, they’ve become my favorites for any bike built to get rowdy. The rubber is pleasantly soft and tacky, providing a secure hold with bare or gloved hands. Subtle fins under the fingers help keep my hands in place without forcing me to squeeze the bars hard.

Knipex makes some of the most enjoyable to use tools we have in the Bicycling workshop. The Pliers Wrench might look like an oddly shaped adjustable wrench, but its parallel jaws provide superior clamping force. It grips hardware securely without any slipping and marring.

These aren't bicycle-specific tools; they’re exceptionally good tools that happen to be incredibly useful around a bike. It comes in a range of sizes, but the 7 1/4-inch is the sweet spot: compact enough to live in a bike toolbox while still opening wide enough to handle most of the jobs I throw at it.

A front light is an easy addition to your road or gravel bike, but finding one that fits neatly on your cockpit can be tricky. Lezyne’s Road Drive 500 solves that problem with a slim, 75-gram body that tucks discreetly under a computer mount.

Despite its small size, the light offers a 500-lumen daytime flash and a 400-lumen mode for seeing the road or bike path after sunset. The replaceable battery lasts up to 55 hours in daytime flash mode or 4.5 hours in the 150-lumen enduro mode. Some computer mounts don’t let you adjust the beam's direction, but Lezyne includes a GoPro-style mount that lets you aim the light where you need it, at the expense of making the overall form factor a little less stealthy.

As a photographer and cyclist, I’m always looking for easier ways to carry cameras while riding. Peak Design’s Mobile Crossbody Multi Strap has become a useful way to keep small cameras and accessories secure and within reach.

Its mini quick-release mechanism lets me attach anchors to multiple devices and swap between them quickly. I’ve used it to carry a small gimbal camera while shooting the Philly Bike Race and as an added layer of security for cameras tucked into my pockets on rides. It’s also handy when traveling, letting me keep my phone or headphones tethered while making my way through an airport.

Spur Cycle’s R-Pro mirror gives road and gravel riders a simple way to see what’s happening behind them. Its alloy body and glass mirror have a high-end feel that looks at home even on a pricey carbon race bike, and it installs in just a few minutes.

I find it especially useful in heavy traffic, when a radar can be constantly pinging with notifications. A quick glance at the mirror helps me judge the distance to the vehicles behind me. It’s also handy on group rides to check that the person following me is still on my wheel. While the mirror doesn’t replace a radar, it never needs charging or pairing to a head unit.

I have found these Campagnolo 03 rotors to be categorically better than both SRAM and Shimano rotors while also being cheaper (a rare feat for a Campagnolo product).

The main issue I have with both SRAM and Shimano’s high-end road rotors is that after hard braking, they absorb enough heat to deform and briefly make noise. Riding the same roads after switching to Campagnolo rotors? No noise after hard braking. To me, this indicates the Campagnolo rotors manage braking heat better, which gives me more confidence in their performance; plus, silence is golden. At this point, I have replaced both Shimano and SRAM rotors with these Campagnolo ones and can recommend them highly as a better rotor alternative for any road bike groupset.

Back in 2025, I bumped into an old friend at Sea Otter. He was walking around with what might be the most curious saddle prototype I’ve ever seen. It looked like it was made from plastic and Styrofoam. It was also crazy light and, according to him, fully rideable.

Now, I finally have the production version. It’s still crazy light (146g on my scale). And those funky rails? An absolute joy to use. It’s such a simple solution: the saddle slides into the clamp instead of needing to partially take everything apart in some cases. But more importantly, as someone who has always tended to sit more forward, I love the wider nose on this saddle.

So far I’ve enjoyed about 500 miles on this saddle, and have been very, very pleasantly surprised. It has replaced the S-Works Power Evo saddle (which is quite popular and I also found very comfortable) on my road bike, but given how the Sixpack saddle is roughly a 1/3rd of the price, just as comfortable and 25 percent lighter, I feel no need to go back to the more expensive Specialized saddle.

Launched in 2025 as OEM equipment on Cervélo’s Áspero-5 gravel racer, Vittoria’s 700x42c version of its cotton-casing, all-season road tire is now available to the masses, and it’s excellent. The wider Corsa Pro Control features the cushion and grip of wider gravel rubber but rolls quickly, like a high-performance road tire. It’s the perfect upgrade for road riding on your gravel bike or building a go-fast all-road bike (provided you have enough clearance).

I’ve put roughly 1,000 miles on a pair of GP5000 TT TRs (set up tubeless) without a flat. That’s not something I can say about many high-performance tires, especially ones intended only for race days. I was actually a longtime Continental skeptic, but the GP5000 S TR started to change my mind, and the TT TR convinced me to finally change my tune. It combines competitive weight and low rolling resistance with a surprisingly long lifespan. If you want a fast race tire that can also handle training miles, the TT TR is worth a look.

In nearly 20 years of riding and racing, I avoided the urge to get custom insoles, even though I knew early on that my feet had some weird fit issues. This year, I finally gave in to my intrusive thoughts, and oh my god, I am not going back.

I truly didn’t think a custom insole would make as much of a difference as it did. But I’ve noticed all kinds of improvements, like my feet feeling much more stable and secure in the shoe without needing to ratchet down the closures. For the sake of experimentation, I even did a short ride with my previous comfortable (non-custom) insole setup, and I was shocked by how much discomfort I had gotten used to over the previous 20 years of riding. At this point, I would happily put custom insoles into a cheaper pair of shoes than ride stock insoles in a top-of-the-line shoe. I genuinely think the insole makes the bigger difference, and more riders should consider a pair for themselves.

At $190, Pearl Izumi’s Pi PRO/Black Mesh Jersey isn’t cheap, but it delivers the quality and performance I expect at that price. It’s a high-end racing jersey with understated looks, a combination that's hard to find in premium cycling kit.

The fit is cut for an aggressive position on the bike while maintaining excellent comfort and heat regulation. The paneled collar reduces pressure across the back of the neck, a common issue I’ve found with other aero-fit race jerseys. If you’re willing to pay a premium for a well-designed jersey but don’t want to look like a billboard, the Pi PRO/Black Mesh is a great option.

I am very stingy with my saddle recommendations because comfort is so uniquely personal to the rider. I know this because I ride a lot of different saddles, and I’ve discovered that only a very small minority are actually comfortable. But every so often I happen across a saddle that makes me say, “Oh, this one is special.” That’s the Ergon’s SRS Pro Carbon.

It’s plush without being squishy or saggy, offers even pressure distribution without feeling bulky, and is supportive without hot spots or pinch points. It’s also a rather good deal for a light (about 185 grams in an S/M size).

Typically, a European-made, carbon-railed saddle costs $300 or more, and that’s before you get into 3D-printed tops, so $220 seems almost reasonable.

I use a torque wrench almost every time I work on my bikes. Tightening parts to the correct torque helps prevent component failures, especially with carbon components, lightweight parts, or suspension linkages. Of the several torque wrenches in Bicycling’s workshop, I most often reach for Topeak’s Torq Stick Pro Digital.

The wrench adjusts from 1 to 20 Nm in one-tenth Nm increments. It beeps as you approach your selected torque and buzzes when you reach it. While it costs more than an analog wrench, I find it to be more precise and much easier to use, especially on parts that have torque ratings that include decimal points. Topeak’s set also includes common metric hex and Torx bits, an extender, an 8mm crowfoot for brake bleeds, and a small ratchet driver.

Heat training is a tool many of the world’s best bike racers use to prepare for hot summer races. The Core 2 Heat Sensor makes it easier to track and monitor that process, but I’ve found it useful even without fully optimizing my heat training.

The sensor monitors skin and core temperature and combines that information with heart-rate data to give you a heat-strain index. That makes it easier to gauge how your body is responding to the heat while riding. I use the sensor all summer to watch for spikes in my body temperature and take preventive measures before I overheat. With more summer events likely happening during periods of high heat, monitoring your body temperature more closely can be not just helpful, but tangibly beneficial.

The Q36.5 Dottore Pro jersey works across a wider range of temperatures than any other long-sleeve jersey I’ve tried. It holds enough heat to keep me comfortable on cool rides, but it also pulls moisture away from my body and feels cool enough for warmer days.

I’ve used it as a layer on a soaking-wet 50-degree ride, worn it on a 75-degree summer day, and ridden in it in plenty of conditions in between. On some of those rides, there were other pieces of clothing I would have changed, but I would have picked the same jersey every time. Its versatility means it can replace multiple layers, making it well worth the asking price.

The Varia RearVue 820 is Garmin’s first full update to its successful radar light in nearly six years. It delivers more information to compatible Garmin Edge head units, offers brighter light, supports USB-C charging, provides longer battery life, and extends detection range. On the road, the RearVue 820 feels like a noticeable step up from other radar units—notably, it consistently detects vehicles approaching from behind earlier than other devices.

Same-speed tracking was another revelation. Not having to constantly check whether the car that dropped off my screen was still following me or had turned into a driveway is something no other radar unit does reliably, and it's a big reason I would choose the 820 over other units. If you’re using a modern Garmin cycling computer that supports advanced tracking features, the Garmin Varia RearVue 820 is more than just an update to the RTL 515. It’s a big step forward in cycling radar technology.

But even if you’re not using the latest Edge device, my comparative testing showed the 820 was always the first radar to detect an approaching car, sometimes by several seconds. Sure, things like better battery life, a more convenient charging standard, and a brighter light are great. But when it comes to cycling radars, better, faster detection is king, and right now the RearVue 820 wears that crown.

The Apex Aeon bibs are stupid expensive, but great bibs are one of the few pieces of cycling equipment worth splurging on. These have become my favorite pair for long, hard, hot rides, maintaining their support and comfort from start to finish.

The straps and lowers are thick and feel almost overbuilt, a welcome change from cycling apparel that can feel wispy and fragile. The chamois is medium-thick and the firmest I can remember using, but it’s fantastically comfortable without feeling like a diaper. Like the rest of the bib, it shines brightest on longer rides. I’ve worn almost nothing else this summer, and whenever I ride in a different pair, I invariably wish I’d grabbed these instead.

It is no understatement to say SRAM is on a roll. Thanks to a combination of performance, features, and impeccable timing, its drivetrains are the benchmarks for mountain, gravel, and road riding at the moment. On the road, the newest Red (E1) stormed into the market with superbly comfortable hoods, brilliant brakes, and excellent shifting. One would be wise never to count Shimano out, but Red E1 announced to the world that it had forever altered the drivetrain status quo.

Other Bicycling editors and I have long argued that top-of-the-line drivetrains, especially in the electronic era, are never the smart buy. Give up a bit of weight, and you can get all the performance of a brand’s top-tier group for a lot less money. And that’s the case with SRAM’s Rival E1. It offers all the performance and improvements of Red E1, along with SRAM’s impressive ecosystem interoperability. The bonus buttons on the hoods are the only feature you might miss: Red and Force have them; Rival does not. Aside from those, Rival E1 offers the benchmark performance of Red E1 without the painful hit to the wallet.

In any given year, I ride between 20 and 30 different bikes (usually with a variety of wheels), and I will also likely test anywhere between five and ten standalone wheelsets. That is, I ride a lot of different road wheels every year, and these Rovals earned my Gear of the Year endorsement because I keep coming back to them.

One of the things I like most: I think Specialized has cracked the secret sauce with their carbon spokes. Every other carbon-spoked wheel I have tried has a much harsher ride than a traditional steel-spoke wheel. Both the Rapide Sprint and the Rapide CLX III feel more like traditional wheels, just with a bunch of weight lopped off. I keep coming back to the deeper Sprint version over the more all-around CLX III because I don’t really feel the roughly 90g difference, but I definitely notice the extra speed on flat and rolling terrain. It’s pretty wild that Specialized has managed to make a set of 60-ish mm deep wheels (63 mm and 58 mm deep, to be exact) this light while also making them feel so smooth.

#8817. The Best Power Racks of 2025: Our Top Picks for Strength Training

Our expert shares his experience, and an Olympic lifting titleholder shares advice on choosing the best option so you get stronger with this home gym staple.

Written by Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Stephen Sheehan, CPT Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

A power rack allows you to safely perform weightlifting exercises like barbell squats and bench presses, without a spotter, in your home gym. Add-on accessories like pull-up bars, dip stations, and resistance bands can help you get the most out of your power rack, giving you the tools for a versatile full-body workout.

Whether you have limited space or are looking for a budget-friendly power rack, there are options that may work for you. We compiled a list of the best power racks for your home gym with all the details you need to find the right equipment to take your fitness routine to the next level in 2024. Shane Sevcik—a USAW-1 (USA Weightlifting) certified coach, current USA Weightlifting Foundation board member, state record holder, and Masters Pan American and World title holder—also shares his insights into what to look for in power racks.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

The REP Fitness PR-1000 Power Rack has a four-post frame made from 14-gauge steel with laser-cut holes spaced two inches apart. There are two pull-up bars—one is 1.25 inches thick, and the other is two inches thick—so you can do accessory work such as pull-ups and grip exercises without using additional space or buying a separate piece of equipment. The pull-up bars are strategically placed on the rack, spanning the front and back posts, contributing to the overall stability. There are built-in weight storage pegs on the back base for additional sturdiness. You can customize the rack using multiple accessory options such as safety straps, a dip station, and more.

Tester Brandon Lunsford, C.P.T., CF-L1, used this rack to do exercises like squats, bench press, strict press, pull-ups, and more for almost two years. He describes it as an intermediate or beginner rack and noticed movement while un-racking 350 pounds. “The rack held the weight just fine, but there was some swaying after I removed the bar. I’d recommend it to a beginner or someone who doesn’t lift to that capacity because I was happy with it otherwise.”

We like that the PR-1000 comes with chrome-coated safeties extending past the rack, offering an additional place for a barbell. The numbered uprights allow you to adjust the safeties or J-hooks quickly and never have to worry about your bar being crooked. “The J-hooks were easy to move, and the hole spacing of one inch is adequate to get the bar lined up where you need it,” Lunsford says. “I can attest to the functionality of the safeties; they worked great for me when I failed a heavy bench over 250 pounds.”

The Titan Fitness T-3 Series Power Rack is a wall-mounted power rack that folds to a closed position, which only sticks out five inches from the wall. The bolt-down uprights and side bracings keep it stable, so you feel comfortable lifting weights to 1,100 pounds. Those who want to use the dual pull-up bars for dynamic movements such as kipping pull-ups or toes-to-bar benefit from the added stability the floor attachment provides. The rear pull-up bar is two inches thick, and the front pull-up bar is the industry standard of 1.25 inches thick.

This rack is made from 11-gauge steel and features two-inch by three-inch tubing. Typically, newer racks have three-inch by three-inch steel tubing, so attachments from other brands may not work. Lunsford says, “A rack is an essential piece of fitness equipment. What sets them apart is the build, value, and accessories. A full power rack of this style with a weight capacity of 1,100 pounds for around $400 is an excellent bang for the buck.”

Lunsford says the brand uses manufacturing processes to elevate the overall quality. “The holes are laser cut instead of punched, and the brand uses robot welders instead of guides operated by humans.” This technique allows for more efficiency, precision, and consistency in enhanced craftsmanship. The laser-cut holes are two inches apart, and the bench and clean pull zone have Westside hole spacing—holes in the upright that are closer together for more precise positioning.

Free shipping is available on all Titan products, and a one-year warranty covers manufacturing defects and issues that may arise while using the product. One callout we have is the rack does not come with safety arms, which range in price from $90 to $190, depending on which type you get. The rackable weight capacity is 1,100 pounds, but the included J-cups are rated up to 1,000 pounds, so if you want to move heavier weights, you’ll need to upgrade the J-cups.

Titan offers several accessories for purchase separately, including safety bars or straps, stabilizer feet, spotter arms, pin and pipe safety set, or an extension kit to upgrade to six uprights. Other customization options include choosing from a black, red, or blue rack color, two rack depths and heights, or adding a four-pack of weight plate holders.

At only 72 inches tall (six feet), the REP PR-1050 Short Power Rack is a solution for home gyms with low ceilings, such as garages or basements. This equipment has a sturdy yet compact footprint of 58 by 48 inches and supports up to 700 pounds.

While this power rack is short, it provides a solid range of features. It comes with dual pull-up bars (supporting up to 400 pounds), numbered upright holes spaced two inches apart, rear base weight horns, chrome-coated safeties, and plastic-lined J-cups. It’s also compatible with various add-on attachments, including cannonball grips for grip strength exercises and landmine attachments for exercises including landmine presses and rows.

The Fringe Sport Retractable Power Rack is an excellent option if your garage or home gym is tight on space because it is compact and easily stored. This convenient home power rack can be retracted and folded inward or outward for storage. When retracted, it only sticks out five inches from the wall. It has a compact base and can support up to 800 pounds.

The uprights are two-by-three-inch 11-gauge steel and feature Westside spacing in the bench zone. You can set the rack’s 1.25-inch diameter pull-up bar to multiple heights. It’s 91 inches tall, which may not be ideal for low ceilings.

The unit comes with J-hooks coated with ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMW), a strong, abrasion-resistant material, to protect your barbell. Fringe Sport provides an installation video to help guide you through the installation of this power rack. It includes four mounting brackets and six detent pins to lock the rack in position.

The Sunny Health & Fitness Power Zone Strength Rack Power Cage Squat Rack has a pulley system attachment for lat pulldowns and adjustable resistance you can load with weight plates up to the 352-pound limit. You can use the lat pulldown attachment for exercises like upright rows and curls. When you aren’t using the attachment, built-in safety hook latches provide easy storage for the top long or short lever bar.

This power rack has features to help you get a well-rounded workout. The adjustable angled pull-up bar has four positions, including wide and narrow grips. The J-hooks have 18 vertical height settings, and the spotter bars with safety latches help you squat with heavier weights. There are six resistance band pins, for additional resistance against the bar.

The Rogue Fitness R-3 Power Rack is the most compact option in Rogue’s R-Series and is an excellent option for a home garage gym. This power rack comes in two height options—90.4 inches or 84.4 inches—so it works in garages and home gyms with low ceilings.

This rack is made of heavy-duty 11-gauge steel with Westside spacing (a type of spacing that allows for granular control of bar placement, such as barbells and safety bars) through the bench in a one-inch pattern and two-inch spacing above and below the bench. The unit is compatible with various Rogue Infinity Series add-on attachments, such as the Rogue Matador, fully adjustable dip handles, or a bar hanger for barbell weight storage.

The unit has a 43-inch pull-up bar, infinity J-cups, pin/pipe safeties, and four band pegs. You can customize this rack by adding a bar, bench, or plates to your purchase on the Rogue Fitness website. This unit is versatile enough for various exercises, including low rows, pull-ups, chin-ups, squats, bench presses, powerlifting, CrossFit, and Olympic lifting.

The Fitness Reality Squat Rack Power Cage has an official weight capacity of 800 pounds. This unit can help anyone hit their goals, from beginners to elite powerlifters.

Like all good squat racks, the Fitness Reality Squat Rack Power Cage has solid steel safety arms rather than hollow tubes. It features two rear stability bars. Thanks to 19 adjustable height levels, you can use the unit for various exercises besides squats, including pull-ups, chin-ups, bench presses, and overhead presses. And it’s $299, the most affordable option on our list.

It has a multi-grip pull-up bar and two 23-inch safety bars with chrome locks. While it doesn’t come with J-hooks, dip bars, or plate storage attachments, one-inch holes allow you to use this equipment with standard-sized attachments.

A power rack—or power cage—has four uprights designed to serve as a base for powerlifting, Olympic lifting, and other strength training. They are commonly used with a barbell but may have optional attachments for non-barbell exercises using cables or body weight. A full power rack allows athletes to lift inside or outside the cage. Half racks have two uprights, so athletes must lift outside the rack because there is less depth.

Research links strength training, including weightlifting, to long-term health benefits like reducing disease.

A power rack provides equipment, like safety bars, to help you lift heavy weights safely without a spotter. Some power racks come with add-on attachments, such as pull-up bars and dip bars, to help you get a well-rounded workout. Additionally, most power racks are compatible with accessories you can buy for an extra price to customize your workout for your needs.

Exercisers use a power rack for strength training, Olympic lifting, and powerlifting. Additional attachments, such as a dip station or pull-up bar, allow you to use it for bodyweight exercises. Some have pulley systems for other resistance exercises.

Correctly using a power rack can successfully enhance strength training. “It’s all about consistency,” Sevcik says. “Make sure you have some kind of progressive overload built into your programming.”

Power racks provide a safe lifting experience, which is of utmost importance, especially if you plan on training alone. The safety straps, pins, or arms—also called safeties—are a critical safety feature. “One of my biggest pet peeves is when I see people who don’t know how to set the safety arms the right way and have the pins set way too low,” Sevcik says. “The purpose of those safety arms is to give you a safe way to bail out of a lift. Otherwise, you’re just using a power rack as a big immobile squat stand.”

So, what is the correct way to set up the safety arms? “To set them up for squats, put the unloaded bar on your back and squat down to the deepest position you can get yourself into,” Sevcik says. “The safety bars should be about an inch and a half or one notch lower than your bottom position, so if you ever fail on a squat, all you do is sit your butt down to the very bottom.”

Many come with safety arms, pins, or nylon straps, but some budget options may require purchasing them separately. If you’re new to using a power rack, we recommend asking a fitness professional for guidance on different exercises and safety.

Before purchasing, measure your space and look at the rack’s total footprint. While measuring the floor and comparing it to the base is essential, ceiling height is another crucial factor. You may need a shorter option if you use your rack in a basement or a room with low ceilings.

You can retract and store a folding power rack if you’re limited in space or need room for other activities. It’s a good idea to consider your height and weight when looking at the dimensions, especially if you plan to use the pull-up bar or other attachments. You may want to leave space on each side for accessories so you can attach them on the sides if necessary. We recommend you keep the space around the rack clear of obstructions, particularly in front, so you can safely complete your lifts or bailout.

Power racks come in a variety of styles, colors, and materials. Some construction and style factors to consider include:

The power racks on this list have capacities ranging from 700 pounds to 1,100 pounds. The lower and middle weight range will likely work for you if you are a beginner or intermediate exerciser. If you are an advanced athlete, you may want to opt for a power rack with a high weight capacity and heavy-duty steel. Attachments such as safety arms, J-hooks, or pull-up bars have varying weight limits. Always stay within the recommended weight range for your safety.

How much you’re willing to spend depends on your budget and training style. Many racks on this list include a basic setup, with the option to add accessories as needed, which cuts the cost. Other racks come fully loaded with accessories, so they are incredibly versatile. However, these options cost more, so it is crucial to consider the features and whether or not they are helpful for your workout style and goals. The racks on this list range from around $299 to $965, and many brands offer free shipping.

Power racks come in various styles and features. The following sections break down Sevcik’s power rack must-haves.

Sevcik says to look for thick, heavy-duty steel such as 11-gauge. “A rack made out of thicker steel creates more leverage on the uprights. Especially when you add those attachments.”

“I think a big must-have a lot of people overlook is to make sure your J-cups, or J-hooks, have some coating on them to preserve the knurling on your bar,” Sevcik says. “If you’re doing a bench press or deadlift, [knurling] is no big deal, but if you’re an Olympic weightlifter, that’s where my snatch grip is holding onto, and I want it to be as sharp and aggressive as possible.”

“I would make sure you have enough hole patterns to make a lot of adjustments. Sometimes, they’re too spaced out, for example, in two-inch increments instead of one,” Sevcik says. “I like to have the added adjustability, especially for those heavier weights.”

Sevcik says having the option to do pull-ups is a good idea. “They’re one of the most basic, fundamental movements. Plus, if you dedicate the square footage to put the rack in there, you’ll want to get as much utility as possible because you are sacrificing some real estate.”

“It’s important to have the option to add accessories,” Sevcik says. “You might not want a dip bar right now, but down the road, you may decide to incorporate more dips in the training program, and it sure is nice to have your power rack as your one central piece of equipment.”

Many power racks come with attachments, though certain brands require you to purchase add-on attachments separately. Some of the power racks on this list come with pull-up bars (chin-up bar), safeties, and J-cups included, while others do not. It’s important to read the details of what comes with your unit to know what additional purchases you’ll need to make to achieve your desired power rack workout.

We considered the following while choosing each product on this list:

We chose budget-friendly and high-end options suitable for any fitness level and listed several compact and folding options for those with limited space. We also spoke to Shane Sevcik, a USAW-certified coach and competitive athlete, about essential add-ons and safety features.

Research suggests 30 to 60 minutes a week of muscle-strengthening exercises can benefit your health. With the help of a power rack, you can achieve a wide range of strength training fitness moves without needing a spotter. A power rack can add convenience to your workout by enabling you to get a safe weightlifting workout anytime from the comfort of your home gym.

A full power rack has four to six uprights attached by cross members, creating a cage to lift in. A squat rack—also called a squat stand—is typically two uprights and weighs less than a power rack, making it more portable. Power racks are more versatile, with the option to add accessories, while squat racks usually do not.

If you choose a freestanding power rack, anchor it following the manufacturer’s instructions to ensure it’s safe and secure.

Generally, a freestanding power rack should be a few feet from the wall so you can perform exercises comfortably and safely. Always refer to the manufacturer’s guidelines and recommendations when setting up your rack.

Common gauges are 11-gauge and 12-gauge, with lower numbers providing thicker and stronger steel; however, these tend to be more pricey options. A thinner 14-gauge steel is slightly less sturdy but likely works well for a general home gym setup. We chose racks ranging from 11-gauge to 16-gauge to suit various budgets and fitness levels.

#8816. What Nike Shoe Matches Your Running Style?

Find your perfect pair no matter where the road (or trail, or treadmill) may take you with this buying guide.

Runners are a varied breed. Some crave the routine of a daily run and the endorphin boost it brings. Others may be training for an endurance event like a marathon or half marathon, with specific distance goals. You may be chasing a new PR, looking to hit the trails, or mixing running with other activities like lifting weights. So many different ways to run, so many shoes to choose from.

Luckily, there’s a Nike shoe to support your training goals, whether you run for fun or race competitively. Not sure which style fits your needs best? We’ve got you covered with the shopping guide below.

You can depend on your daily run—it’s what gives you energy and lifts your mood, no matter what else the day may bring. The Nike Pegasus line has offered that same dependability for more than four decades, and the technology just keeps getting better.

The reason why the Pegasus Plus 2 works for daily, all-purpose running is its technology: Superlight ZoomX foam in the heel pairs with an exposed Air Zoom unit in the forefoot to deliver comfort and energy return that powers up every mile. Up top, a sleek mesh material offers both support and flexibility without letting your foot overheat, while a revamped forefoot shape gives your toes a little more wiggle room. And the classic Waffle outsole design has an updated diagonal pattern with flex grooves for better traction and ground feel, so you’re more in tune with your terrain. Plus, those textured laces are less likely to come untied—so you’ve got one less thing to worry about when you’re heading out the door.

The Pegasus Plus 2 is also a good option to slip on for easy and slower recovery runs. Responsive and comfy without being super stacked, this shoe is the ultimate workhorse in your running closet.

For long runs and marathon training, you want max cushioning, like what’s found in Nike’s Vomero 18. Lightweight ZoomX foam stacked on top of responsive ReactX foam in the shoe’s midsole results in a plushy landing that has you feeling like you’re landing on a cloud with every step. Considering that the Vomero 18 is 13 percent more responsive than previous React technology (per the company’s own measurement), your legs feel less fatigued even as the miles add up.

An increased rocker design and pods placed strategically around the outsole allow for better push-off and smoother heel-to-toe transitions. The breathable engineered mesh material up top and plush padding in the tongue and lining help your feet stay cool and comfortable. This super cushy shoe that runs effortlessly is one of the reasons why RW shoe testers gush about it.

For those who like to customize their kicks, the shoe is part of the “Nike by You” line, allowing you to pick features like color and accents and even add your own text in the heel, tongue, and forefoot.

You’re not just a runner. You also rule the weight room, enjoy a good cardio class, and have been known to dabble in metabolic conditioning workouts. If you’re looking for an all-purpose training shoe, Nike’s versatile Free Metcon 7 fits whatever your workout ask. This sleekly designed cross-training shoe lets you have it all, from supporting multi-direction movements on the gym floor to dynamic cushioning when you want to hit the treadmill.

The shoe finds its multiuse purpose with a flexible design that features softer foam in the midsole and firmer foam in the heel for added stability. Plus, the full-length rubber outsole helps with traction on a variety of surfaces, including turf, concrete, and gym floors. You’ll also appreciate the webbed lacing and midfoot containment system designed to keep your foot firmly in place as you move around.

For those who want a mixed-terrain shoe that can hit the road and trail and also handle inclement weather like rain and snow, the Vomero 18 Gore-Tex is a great choice. These waterproof shoes are designed to take on puddles, pebbles, rocks, and roots without missing a beat.

The shoe has all the same stacked ZoomX and ReactX performance cushioning as the Vomero 18, plus a Gore-Tex waterproof liner to help your feet stay dry without getting too sweaty. The Storm-Tread outsole is specifically engineered for wet and slippery conditions, with an enhanced rubber compound for stronger grip and a thoughtful outsole pattern that keeps you grounded even on icy surfaces. Plus, the soft, protective mesh upper will keep your feet warm.

If you are looking for a shoe to race in, the long-awaited Alphafly 4 is an update to Nike’s popular carbon-plated shoe. It’s even lighter than its predecessor, the Alphafly 3, (approximately 6.6 ounces compared to 7.1 ounces respectively) and offers more energy return to help you chase your next PR.

That’s accomplished through its upgraded RF Air Zoom cushioning unit underfoot that uses vibration and frequency to create a smooth, comfortable ride, while the carbon fiber Flyplate gives you extra energy return to power through every mile. A slightly wider platform design compared to the Alphafly 3 also provides more stability so you can feel confident even on quick turns. And the wispy Atomknit 2.0 upper offers enough support to keep your foot firmly in place with as little added weight as possible.

Your shakeout run after a marathon or ultra should be about comfort at an easy pace. Think plenty of cushioning, a smooth, bouncy ride, and an unfussy upper. The Nike Vomero Premium ticks all those boxes, making it a good choice to slip on for post-marathon recovery runs.

Tired legs will appreciate a midsole that’s made up of ZoomX foam surrounding two energy-boosting Air Zoom units—one in the forefoot and one at the heel. The result is a light, comfortable ride with energy return that makes each step feel effortless and propels you easily along your route. You’ll want to wear this shoe for your daily runs for weeks after your 26.2-mile-and-beyond races.

Who doesn’t want to slip into something comfortable after a long run, or just a long day? The Nike ReactX Rejuven8 is just the thing, with a design that’s created to elicit all the aahs you can imagine. Thanks to React X technology in the upper and midsole, your feet will be surrounded in soft, responsive comfort. There’s extra room in the forefoot to allow your toes to rest and ventilation holes to allow your feet to breathe. Walking is easy and fluid because the sticky rubber outsole adds grip to the ground below you; therefore, no additional balancing act to get from one place to another. The result: A recovery shoe you’ll never want to take off.

We all love getting gifts, but shopping for shoes can be tricky when you’re not the one who will be wearing them. A little advanced knowledge can make a big difference in ensuring your present is truly appreciated. Here are some buying tips:

Check what they already run in. If you can, look at the label inside a pair of running shoes they like, or ask someone who knows. Note the model, size, and width—running-shoe sizing may differ from their dress-shoe size—as well as any preferences, such as cushioning or toe-box room.

Check the return policy. See if the store has any specific limits on returns and exchanges, and if you can get a gift receipt so your giftee has the option to exchange the shoe for a different size.

Keep fit in mind. Remember that footwear largely depends on individual fit, with some shoes running bigger or smaller than the given size. When possible, avoid final sales (where the shoe is not eligible for returns) just in case there’s a fit issue.

The Nike running shoes best suited for long runs and marathon training are the Nike Vomero 18. You want to make sure your shoe offers both stability and support to reduce injury risk and protect your joints. Many distance runners today prefer shoes with maximalist midsoles, which feature a large stack of foam to cushion against impact, as well as energy return rocker designs for faster push-off and landings. These are all things the Nike Vomero 18 delivers on.

When it comes to race-day itself, especially for half-marathons and full-marathons, many runners seeking a time goal prefer performance shoes like Nike’s Alphafly 4, which have a thin carbon plate for strong energy return and maximum speed.

When looking for a recovery-run shoe, you want one that feels comfortable and provides plenty of support and a smooth, stable ride without being overly technical. The Nike Vomero Premium is the best Nike running shoe for easy recovery runs because it’s a shoe that delivers full-length cushioning and a roomy fit so your feet stay happy.

To choose the right size and width for Nike running shoes, go to a store that specializes in running shoes and try a few pairs on. Most running stores will let you jog around the floor (and some even let you jog around the block) so you have a sense of what works best. Running shoes should feel roomy but not so much that your feet move around a lot. You should be able to fit about a thumbnail’s width between your longest toe and the front of the shoe. There also shouldn’t be any pressure on your pinky toe, and only a little bit of pressure on your big toe.

If you’re experiencing side pinching, bulging or spilling over, or flat arches, a wide shoe may be for you. These Nike models are available in wide widths: Downshifter 14, Pegasus 42, Revolution 8, Structure 26, Vomero Plus and Vomero 18.

#8815. 6 Core-Strengthening Exercises to Spice Up Your Routine

Grab one dumbbell and challenge your core with these moves.

The core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics. But your torso muscles—which include your abs, back, glutes, and hip flexors—play a crucial role in cycling that goes way beyond looks.

Research shows just how important core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine. One 2019 study, published in PLoS One, found that an eight-week core training program improved balance and core endurance (which you need to maintain posture through long miles) in the 21 college athletes who participated. Another research review, published in Frontiers in Physiology in 2022, says core training should have a place in all athletes’ training programs.

The authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability. The authors also write that these core strength benefits help prevent “energy leaks,” therefore leading to better performance.

To help you gain these benefits of a strong midsection, you need a solid workout to add to your routine. Thankfully, Noam Tamir, C.S.C.S., founder and CEO of TS Fitness in New York City, created this dumbbell core-strengthening workout.

In addition to the research that proves the benefits of core strength for athletes, the moves Tamir chose for this workout make an ideal mix for those looking to improve performance. Not only will the moves improve your stability in an upright posture, allowing you to ride and breathe more efficiently, but they also target the core from multiple angles, hitting every muscle of the torso.

Even better: While these moves resemble familiar core exercises, each one has a creative spin. This means they not only challenge your body in fun new ways, but also engage your brain.

How to use this list: Do each exercise below, in order, for the reps listed. Repeat for 3-4 rounds. Rest as needed between exercises and rounds.

Tamir demonstrates the exercises in the video above so you can learn proper form. You will need one light to medium dumbbell for this workout. An exercise mat is optional.

Why it works: The half-kneeling halo exercise focuses on trunk stability. “It works the core at 360 degrees because the dumbbell is moving around the body while you’re maintaining an upright position,” Tamir says. You do the same thing on a ride—hold a strong posture and upright body position while your arms and legs move.

How to do it: Start kneeling, right knee on ground, and left foot planted in front, both knees bent 90 degrees. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chin. Keeping torso and lower body steady, circle dumbbell clockwise around head. Elbows stay close to head. Return to chin. Repeat in other direction. Do 8-10 reps in each direction. Switch leg stance each round.

Why it works: Target the obliques with this rotational move. You’ll also hit the rectus abdominis (those six-pack looking abs) and work on coordination of the upper and lower body, Tamir explains.

How to do it: Start seated on floor. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chest. Lean back slightly, and lift legs off floor, hips and knees bent about 45 degrees. Bring dumbbell to outside of left hip by rotating torso to right and extend left leg straight out, foot lowering close to floor. Keep shoulders down and back. Next, bend left knee and extend right leg out, lowering foot close to floor and lift dumbbell up and over to the right, rotating torso to the right. Bring weight back down to outside of left hip, as you extend right leg out and pull left knee back in. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Why it works: This explosive movement focuses on the hips. “The core is not limited to just the abdominal muscles,” Tamir says. “You also need the whole body to create power, strength, and endurance.” This exercise gets more muscles in on the action, while the hinge motion helps to improve riding, especially during acceleration, he adds.

How to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart, dumbbell in right hand down by side. Hinge at hips, by sending butt straight back, dumbbell reaching behind you. Keep back flat and core engaged. Using glutes, drive feet into floor and extend hips. Let the power of your glutes send dumbbell forward and up to shoulder height. Engage core, like you’re hitting a standing plank position at the top. Let the momentum of the dumbbell guide you back into a hinge position. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps.

Why it works: This anti-rotation exercise works the deep core muscles, including the transverse abdominis that wraps around your midsection, and the multifidus, the posterior core muscles that protect your spine, Tamir explains. “It also helps to stabilize the pelvis to reduce risk of injury,” he adds, and aids in strong posture by working the back.

How to do it: Start in a plank position, left hand on a dumbbell, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Feet should be slightly wider than hips. Pull left elbow straight up, dumbbell reaching to ribcage. Lower back down. Repeat. Keep hips as steady as possible. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Why it works: The pullover crunch focuses mainly on the rectus abdominus (the muscles on the front of the torso) which helps to stabilize the spine and, in turn, maintain good form, Tamir says.

How to do it: Lie faceup, holding a dumbbell vertically with both hands overhead, dumbbell behind you, arms extended. Bend knees, feet planted on floor. Pull dumbbell overhead and crunch up, lifting head, neck, and shoulders off floor. At the same time, lift feet off floor, driving knees toward arms. Slowly lower back down, dumbbell hovering off floor behind you, and feet hovering off floor in front of you. Repeat. Do 12-15 reps.

Why it works: This is a great move for stabilizing the spine, while teaching abdominal bracing, Tamir says. The weight on one side also forces the core to resist rotation, which you need for efficiency on the road.

How to do it: Lie face up. Hold dumbbell in right hand over shoulder, arm straight. Extend left arm overhead, biceps by ear. Lift head, neck, shoulders, and legs a few inches off floor. Use legs to rock back and floor, maintaining the hollow body position. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat with dumbbell in left hand.

Mallory Creveling is an ACE-certified personal trainer and RRCA-certified run coach, who also holds certifications in kettlebell training, sports performance, and more. She has more than 15 years of experience covering fitness, health, and nutrition for a wide range of publications, and nearly 10 years of experience as a trainer and fitness instructor. Mallory stays on top of her continuing education in fitness, as well as the latest science in wellness. She has worked with some of the best experts in their medical fields, and regularly interviews researchers, trainers, athletes, and more to find the best advice for readers looking to improve their performance and well-being.
