#8746. What to Do About These High Interest Rates

Whoa, have you seen what just happened to interest rates!?

Suddenly, after at least fourteen years of our financial world being mostly the same, somebody flipped over the table and now things are quite different.

Interest rates, which have been gliding along at close to zero since before the Dawn of Mustachianism in 2011, have suddenly shot back up to 20-year highs.

Which brings up a few questions about whether we need to worry, or do anything about this new development.

These questions are on everybody’s mind these days, and I’ve been ruminating on them myself. But while I’ve seen a lot of play-by-play stories about each little interest rate increase in the financial newspapers, none of them seem to get into the important part, which is,

“Yeah, interest rates are way up, but what should I do about it?”

Why Is This Happening, and What Got Us Here?

Interest rates are like a giant gas pedal that revs the engine of our economy, with the polished black dress shoe of Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell pressed upon it.

For most of the past two decades, Jerome’s team and their predecessors have kept the pedal to the metal, firing a highly combustible stream of easy money into the system in the form of near-zero rates. This made mortgages more affordable, so everyone stretched to buy houses, which drove demand for existing homes and new construction alike.

It also had a similar effect on business investment: borrowed money and venture capital was cheap, so lots of entrepreneurs borrowed lots of money and started new companies. These companies then rented offices and built factories and hired employees – who circled back to buy more houses, cars, fridges, iPhones, and all the other luxurious amenities of modern life.

This was a great party and it led to lots of good things, because we had two decades of prosperity, growth, raising our children, inventing new things and all the other good stuff that happens in a successful rich country economy.

Until it went too far and we ended up with too much money chasing too few goods – especially houses. That led to a trend of unacceptably fast Inflation, which we already covered in a recent article.

So eventually, Jay-P noticed this and eased his foot back off of the Easy Money Gas Pedal. And of course when interest rates get jacked up, almost everything else in the economy slows down.

And that’s what is happening right now: mortgages are suddenly way more expensive, so people are putting off their plans to buy houses. Companies find that borrowing money is costly, so they are scaling back their plans to build new factories, and cutting back on their hiring. Facebook laid off 10,000 people and Amazon shed 27,000.

We even had a miniature banking crisis where some significant mid-sized banks folded and gave the financial world fears that a much bigger set of dominoes would fall.

All of these things sound kinda bad, and if you make the mistake of checking the news, you’ll see there is a big dumb battle raging as usual on every media outlet. Leftists, Right-wingers, and anarchists all have a different take on it:

The one thing all sides seem to agree on is that we are “experiencing hard economic times” and that “the country is headed in the wrong way”.

Which, ironically, is completely wrong as well – our unemployment rate has dropped to 50-year lows and the economy is at the absolute best it has ever been, a surprise to even the most grounded economists.

The reality? We’re just putting the lid back onto the ice cream carton until the economy can digest all the sugar it just wolfed down. This is normal, it happens every decade or two and it’s no big deal.

Okay, but should I take my money out of the stock market because it’s going to crash?

This answer never changes, so you’ll see it every time we talk about stock investing: Holy Shit NO!!!

The stock market always goes up in the long run, although with plenty of unpredictable bumps along the way. Since you can’t predict those bumps until after they happen, there is no point in trying to dance in and out of it.

But since we do have the benefit of hindsight, there are a few things that have changed slightly: From its peak at the beginning of 2022 until right now (August 2023 as I write this), the overall US market is down about 10%. Or to view it another way, it is roughly flat since June 2021, so we’ve seen two years with no gains aside from total dividends of about 3%.

Since the future is always the same, unknowable thing, this means I am about 10% more excited about buying my monthly slice of index funds today than I was at those peak prices.

Should I start putting money into savings accounts instead because they are paying 4.5%?

This is a slightly trickier question, because in theory we should invest in a logical, unbiased way into the thing with the highest expected return over time.

When interest rates were under 1%, this was an easy decision: stocks will always return far more than 1% over time – consider the fact that the annual dividend payments alone are 1.5%!

But there has to be some interest rate at which you’d be willing to stop buying stocks and prefer to just stash it into the stable, rewarding environment of a money market fund or long-term bonds or something else similar. Right now, if a reputable bank offered me, say, 12% I would probably just start loading up.

But remember that the stock market is also currently running a 10% off sale. When the market eventually reawakens and starts setting new highs (which it will someday), any shares I buy right now will be worth 10% more. And then will continue going up from there. Which quickly becomes an even bigger number than 12%.

In other words, the cheaper the stocks get, the more excited we should be about buying them rather than chasing high interest rates.

As you can see, there is no easy answer here, but I have taken a middle ground:

For most of us, the biggest thing that interest rates affect is our decisions around buying and selling houses. Financing a home with a mortgage is suddenly way more expensive, any potential rental house investments are suddenly far less profitable, and keeping our old house with a locked-in 3% mortgage is suddenly far more tempting.

Consider these shocking changes just over the past two years as typical rates have gone from about 3% to 7.5%.

Assuming a buyer comes up with the average 10% down payment:

This all sounds kind of bleak, but unfortunately it’s the way things are supposed to work – the tough medicine of higher interest rates is supposed to make the following things happen:

The net effect of all this is that prices should stop going up, and ideally fall back down in many areas.

This is a tricky one because the real “value” of a house depends entirely on supply and demand. The right price is whatever somebody is willing to pay for it. However, there are a few fundamentals which influence this price over the long run because they determine the supply of housing.

The first item (construction cost) is pretty interesting because it is subject to the magic of technological progress. Just as TVs and computers get cheaper over time, house components get cheaper too as things like computerized manufacturing and global trade make us more efficient.

I remember paying $600 for a fancy-at-the-time undermount sink and $400 for a faucet for my first kitchen remodel in the year 2001. Today, you can get a nicer sink on Amazon for about $250 and the faucet is a flat hundred. Similarly, nailguns and cordless tools and easy-to-install PEX plumbing make the process of building faster and easier than ever.

On the other hand, the last item (bullshit restrictions) has been very inflationary in recent times. I’ve noticed that every year another layer of red tape and complicated codes and onerous zoning and approval processes gets layered into the local book of rules, and as a result I just gave up on building new houses because it wasn’t worth the hassle. Other builders with more patience will continue to plow through the murk, but they will have less competition, fewer permits will be granted, and thus the shortage of housing will continue to grow, which raises prices on average.

Thankfully, every city is different and some have chosen to make it easier to build new houses rather than more difficult. Even better, places like Tempe Arizona are allowing good housing to be built around people rather than cars, which is even more affordable to construct.

But overall, since overall US house prices adjusted for inflation are just about at an all-time high, I think there’s a chance that they might ease back down another 25% (to 2020 levels). But who knows: my guess could prove totally wrong, or the “fall” could just come in the form of flat prices for a decade that don’t keep up with inflation, meaning that they just feel 25% cheaper relative to our higher future salaries.

The funny part about our current “high” interest rates is that they are not actually high at all. They’re right around average.So they might not go down at all for a long time.

Remember that graph at the beginning of this article? I deliberately cropped it to show only the years since 2009 – the long recent period of low interest rates. But if you zoom out to cover the last seventy years instead, you can see that we’re still in a very normal range.

But a better answer is this one: Interest rates will go down whenever Jerome Powell or one of his successors determines that our economy is slowing down too much and needs another hit from the gas pedal. In other words, whenever we start to slip into a genuine recession.

In order to do that however, we need to see low inflation, growing unemployment, and other signs of an economy that is finally cooling down. And right now, those things keep not showing up in the weekly economic data.

You can get one reasonable prediction of the future of interest rates by looking at something called the US Treasury Yield Curve. It typically looks like this:

What the graph is telling you is that as a lender you get a bigger reward in exchange for locking up your money for a longer time period. And way back in 2018, the people who make these loans expected that interest rates would average about 3.0 percent over the next 30 years.

Today, we have a very strange opposite yield curve:

If you want to lend money for a year or less, you’ll be rewarded with a juicy 5.4 percent interest rate. But for two years, the rate drops to 4.92%. And then ten-year bond pays only 4.05 percent.

This situation is weird, and it’s called an inverted yield curve. And what it means is that the buyers of bonds currently believe that interest rates will almost certainly drop in the future – starting a little over a year from now.

And if you recall our earlier discussion about why interest rates drop, this means that investors are forecasting an economic slowdown in the fairly near future. And their intuition in this department has been pretty good: an inverted yield curve like this has only happened 11 times in the past 75 years, and in ten of those cases it accurately predicted a recession.

So the short answer is: nobody really knows, but just for fun I’ll make a guess. Then if I’m wrong in public, you can come back and make fun of this in the comments.

I think we’ll probably see interest rates start to drop within 18-24 months, and the event may be accompanied by some sort of recession as well.

I like to read and write about all this stuff because I’m still a finance nerd at heart. But when it comes down to it, interest rates don’t really affect long-retired people like many of us MMM readers, because we are mostly done with borrowing. I like the simplicity of owning just one house and one car, mortgage-free.

With the current overheated housing market here in Colorado, I’m not tempted to even look at other properties, but someday that may change. And the great thing about having actual savings rather than just a high income that lets you qualify for a loan, is that you can be ready to pounce on a good deal on short notice.

Maybe the entire housing market will go on sale as we saw in the early 2010s, or perhaps just one perfect property in the mountains will come up at the right time. The point is that when you have enough cash to buy the thing you want, the interest rates that other people are charging don’t matter. It’s a nice position of strength instead of stress. And you can still decide to take out a mortgage if you do find the rates are worthwhile for your own goals.

So to tie a bow on this whole lesson: keep your lifestyle lean and happy and don’t lose too much sweat over today’s interest rates or house prices. They will probably both come down over time, but those things aren’t in your control. Much more important are your own choices about earning, saving, healthy living and where you choose to live.

With these big sails of your life properly in place and pulling you ahead, the smaller issues of interest rates and whatever else they write about in the financial news will gradually shrink down to become just ripples on the surface of the lake.

In the comments: what have you been thinking about interest rates recently? Have they changed your decisions, increased, or perhaps even decreased your stress levels around money and housing?

Mr. Money Mustache September 5, 2023, 2:56 pm

I’m usually in favor of at least 20%, because when you work out the effective interest rate increase that PMI is hitting you with, it usually works out to a very good return on that extra 10%.

For example, imagine a 500k house, and you are debating between a 50k or 100k downpayment (10 or 20%). And let’s say the interest rate is down at 5%.

If the PMI premium is a typical 0.8% of the loan value $450k, you’d be paying an extra $3600 per year in PMI premiums. Just for the privilege of not putting down the extra $50k.

That’s 7% of the potential extra downpayment that gets eaten up every year!

Or to put it another way, if you put in the second $50k, you are earning 5% in foregone loan interest PLUS 7% in saved PMI premiums. 12% in total, which is the best return around.

It’s a similar return when deciding between a 15 vs 30 year mortgage (the 15 year mortgage provides the extra risk free return). The return decreases the longer one keeps the mortgage, but for most people who move / re-finance within 7 years or so, it’s well worth it.

My brother got a mortgage from Navy Federal Credit Union with no PMI. So those deals are out there. This is not a VA loan, just standard mortgage. I’m thinking other credit unions might offer the same.

A good option at the moment for military people looking to purchase homes is a VA assumption loan. Essentially you “assume” the VA loan of another person instead of getting a new loan at today’s rates. The downside is that the purchase takes much longer, and since interest rates have been going down for decades, it hasn’t made sense to do an assumption loan for decades, so most people aren’t familiar with the process. We’re about 3 months into the process, and it’s looking like end-to-end it is going to take 5-6 months, but we’re assuming a 2.25% interest rate instead of today’s ~7%. You also can’t choose how much your down payment is. You have to have enough cash on hand to pay off whatever the difference is between the purchase price and what the seller has left on the mortgage.

My mortgage is 2.5% – P&I is $886/mo. Last year, we had about 28 years left and the interest was slightly higher than the principal payment each month – about $450/mo. or so in interest. Did a lump sum payment and cut off about 15 years of payments – now almost all my payment goes to the principal. The interest each month is now only about $230/mo.

In this sense, the savings in interest each month is about equal to what I’d be earning if I’d kept the lump sum in a money market. I’ve also got peace of mind because A. if I didn’t make another extra payment, I’ll still have a paid-for house in about 13 years, and B. since the money is already spent on the mortgage, it removes the temptation to find something else to use it on.

So the short answer to your comment is: yes, the front-loaded nature of the mortgage does factor into the equation. From an interest savings perspective, it’s definitely more profitable to pay the mortgage down during the first half of the amortization versus the last half.

As I understand it, the front-loaded nature of interest on a mortgage is just a reflection (the mirror image, maybe) of compound interest. So an extra principal payment in year 1 of a 30 year fixed-rate mortgage has a greater impact than one in year 25 because it has longer to compound, not because it gives a greater rate of return.

If you make an extra payment of $100 this year, next year your balance will be lower by $102.85. And in 27 years your balance will be lower by $100*1.0285^27=$213.56.

But if instead you put $100 in your high-yield savings account, next year you will have $105. So you really will approach the payoff amount faster that way (as long as the interest rate you’re earning remains higher).

You understand it correctly! You don’t pay more or less interest as a percentage of your loan by paying it off early or by paying it for 30 years – when you make extra payments early, you simply borrowed the total amount of money for less time. Naturally you pay less aggregate interest if you pay the loan off early, because you borrowed the total sum for less time. If your mortgage is 5%, for example, the total interest you pay as a percentage of what you borrowed will be 5% regardless of whether you pay off the loan in year 1 or year 30. Amortized payments confuse people into thinking that they’re paying more interest in the beginning than the end – no, you’re paying the percentage of whatever is outstanding. The amortization just allows one to have the same payment over the life of the loan, rather than a huge payment now and a itty bitty payment later. So it appears that you are paying more in interest, but it’s just that the interest that is owed is a greater percentage of the payment amount in the beginning because you owe more money.

In any case, you are totally correct that in a static situation paying yourself $100 into a 5% bank account instead of paying $100 extra to a 2.75% mortgage will earn you the delta (5-2.75 =2.25%) real annual return, compounded. Of course there’s no guarantee the savings return remains at 5%, whereas the interest rate on the fixed mortgage is guaranteed to be 2.75%.

Yeah, all good points – I didn’t mean to sound like a “just build more sprawl” type of person.

But I think that cities SHOULD open up the floodgates for infill redevelopment – stuff like the old parking lots and abandoned shopping malls that currently take up most of the space in central cities including mine.

But to stop the self-perpetuating problem of crowding and car traffic, make sure you have modern, people-friendly rules in place (which are also builder friendly because we’d rather build more houses rather than wasting land on car parking).

– eliminate “minimum parking” requirements – shrink roads and eliminate free taxpayer-paid car parking and make all the asphalt self-funding – add super safe and pleasant bike and pedestrian accomm0dation instead, which is more than 90% cheaper to build.

“Infill redevelopment” – I didn’t know there was a proper term for this but YES, that’s exactly what I’ve been saying for years. So much moaning & groaning over the “lack of affordable housing” – and yet, on the flip side, equal moaning & groaning over “strip mall ghost towns” and blighted areas of empty commercial properties. Instead of hacking up and parceling off more farmland and prairie to build overpriced McMansions with postage stamp-sized yards, why not develop what’s already there into housing? There are already all the roads, highways, byways, and parking lots you could ever need. Most also have some sort of parks or green space nearby, unkempt tho they may be, plus schools and access to public transportation. It seems like a no-brainer to me: instead of destroying more of what’s green and unsullied, why not rehab the bounty of concrete & steel & asphalt just sitting empty & unused?

I don’t pretend to understand all the reasons behind it, but I suspect it has more to do with a very few making a very large amount of money, than it does with anything truly prohibitive or “bad for humans” in trying to re-develop urban wastelands into habitable neighborhoods.

From what I’ve heard, commercial-to-residential conversions can be pretty complex, which is why you don’t see that many. The biggest challenges from what I hear are plumbing (offices/storefronts aren’t designed to have bathrooms/kitchens everywhere) and lack of windows (only on the outside, so interior spaces can’t be used as separate apartments). Not impossible, but often the retrofitting can wind up running more than just bulldozing the whole thing and starting from scratch. Starting with a parking lot might be easier.

Some developers are figuring out this puzzle, so hopefully the situation improves. There’s certainly plenty of unused commercial property to repurpose.

Bottom line is that it’s cheaper (for the developer) to build on fresh land in 95% of the cases. Redevelopment is far more expensive than new development. The costs for new development are often outsourced (new roads, new schools, new utilities, etc) whereas the developer is going to foot the bill on redevelopment (with some exceptions where a state/fed offers incentives for blighted areas, industrial waste sites, etc).

Attempting to control overpopulation is an unequivocally bad idea. A horrible scenario is going to play out in China in about a decade due to their one child policy. Most of the first world is heading for a situation of very problematic demographics (too many old people, not enough young). The United States has more or less avoided it, but let’s not manufacture the problem for ourselves in 30 years.

There is plenty of water even in a place like phoenix if it was priced and regulated appropriately, and we would have more than enough space in existing city boundaries if we didn’t subsidize parking and transportation in the worst ways possible. Changing those pricing and regulation schemes are the angles we need to look at, but we definitely need more units of housing.

I am based in Germany and snagged a historically low interest rate of .87% on my mortgage. The difference is that it is fixed for 10 years so this business of prediction is indeed quite critical to my short and mid term financial planning.

I have had the mindset of paying off the place as rapidly as possible just as a bit of a hedge on the long term uncertainty of life. I figure, worst case scenario with a paid off home I can ride off into the sunset. However, I like my job and see myself in my field at least another 20 years (I am 33). Hence, I have a bit of a challenge as interest rate predictions would seem to drive my behavior greatly: Option 1 – pay off a super low return mortgage to hedge a long term increasing rate Option 2 – pay off the minimum on my mortgage and invest the remainder because the delta is so massive due to the historic rate I snagged Option 3 – some hybrid of the two

There’s the option of an accelerated pay-off of my mortgage every year so I have until December to decide as I save throughout the year, but it is always interesting times as I do find I need to develop an opinion on the whole mortgage situation.

Option 2 makes the most sense to me. If you want to be conservative you can always invest the additional funds in some type of interest bearing account — in the US that would be something like FDIC insured CDs currently at over 5%, not sure what the German equivalent might be. Then, after 10 years you can use everything saved in the conservative interest bearing accounts and apply it to the mortgage all at once. You’ll have benefitted from the difference in interest rates.

Yes, the delta is massive, so take advantage of it if you have the discipline to not spend the money elsewhere!

If you’re in REITs, beware of anything involving commercial property right now, including bigger multifamily housing. Look at the Return on Assets the REIT (or any company) generates. Is this greater than or less than the interest they’ll have to pay to refinance their debts?

If they are earning less on their assets than it costs to finance the assets, expect losses or dividend cuts as they deleverage. E.g. they are borrowing at 6% to hold assets yielding 3%.

Lots of REITs with negative cash flows are in an unsustainable position. It would make sense for them to start shedding assets that no longer earn their cost of capital instead of burning cash while hoping for rates to fall. But when everyone does that…

Another misconception unrelated to your comment that is worth noting is that if the Fed cuts rates that the 10yr and mortgages will come down.  They will come down some but that is related to the option adjusted spread on the mortgage (don’t worry about what that part means, that’s maybe a 0.5%-0.75% swing factor).  Mortgages price off of longer dated treasury rates (~10yr treasury or blend of 5 and 10yr) and these are already baking in a series of cuts beginning in 2024.  So the cuts would need to be more significant than people expect to move mortgage rates significantly.  In other words, if the Fed cuts short term rates in an orderly fashion to 3.5% mortgages might not move all (aside from that option adjusted spread) and the yield curve might just look normal again.

#8744. Elizabeth Van Winkle Shares How Resilience Can Help Make the Military Better

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Ask someone who serves in the military or in a civilian leadership role within the government why they are doing what they do, and there’s a good chance you will hear an answer that references the “mission.”

While the specific mission varies by role, a common thread unites them: being part of something bigger than themselves in service to the greater good of America. Feelings of patriotism, pride, and purpose are powerful motivators. But on the toughest days, many of these same leaders carry themselves forward with a fourth ‘P’: pressure.

Dr. Elizabeth ‘Elise’ Van Winkle understands each of those motivators, and she knows firsthand how heavy that fourth one can become. During a pivotal chapter in her government career, that pressure took a severe toll on her health. Now when she speaks about her career, she offers advice for anyone who may be in a similar position. Regardless of the mission in question, your health will matter.

Van Winkle acknowledged that fitness wasn’t a priority when she was younger, but that changed when she went to college and majored in psychology and English.

“That was probably my foray into fitness and health, the psychological side,” she said. “That is an important part of fitness to me.”

Van Winkle’s original focus was to enter a career in criminology and trauma, and she started that pursuit in the Boston, Massachusetts public school system for behavioral and psychiatric issues. Seeing children dealing with adverse issues and life situations was a valuable learning experience for her.

“The kids taught me a lot about resilience and heartache, perseverance, rage, and emotional darkness.”

Once she became a mother, Van Winkle opted to return to school to get her Ph.D. in research psychology, with a focus on neuropsychology. During that time, she had her second child and landed an intern position with the Department of Defense.

“My plan was to do research and data analytics on health and resilience, stay a year, and then move into work at NIH or do something in neuropsychology.”

Sometimes the best-laid plans can go awry, and Van Winkle’s career would have a meteoric rise that she did not see coming. She stayed in the DoD and worked her way up to a Senior Executive Service (SES) level throughout the next several years. Then came the 2016 election. A combination of being in the right place at the right time and the incoming changes with the Trump administration meant Van Winkle was elevated from a one-star SES to a three-star SES equivalent within a couple of weeks. Then shortly after, she was named the Acting Assistant Secretary for Readiness.

“That propelled me into a level of political leadership that I had never really been in.”

It also led to a massive increase in responsibility. The self-described “data geek” went from leading a team of 25 people with a budget of $4 million to now leading upwards of 900 civilians, military, and contractors with a budget of $1 billion. Almost immediately, an executive order gave her team 45 days to develop a readiness recovery framework that measured the readiness of the entire Joint Force and what would be needed to recover that readiness as well as appropriation lines.

Van Winkle added, “Anybody in the Department knows that when someone says 45 days, they really mean 30 because it has to go through coordination.”

Van Winkle’s trajectory may have felt like a whirlwind, but she accepted what became her own mission. She committed every waking hour that she could towards her new role and responsibilities. That also meant putting other things on the backburner like time with her kids and her own personal needs. As a result, she became sick but was undeterred. Knowing her team would not leave until she did, Van Winkle even closed up her office so her staff would leave, then snuck back on her own to continue her work.

Finally, her team put a meeting on her calendar that led her to the Pentagon Health Clinic. The physician informed Van Winkle she had three different infections and asked her to consider going to the hospital, but Van Winkle knew there were scheduled advisor meetings and a commitment at the White House in her future. So, the physician gave her antibiotics and said something that Van Winkle said haunted her.

“She said, ‘I’ve heard it before. I imagine it’s the mission.’”

Van Winkle admitted seeing every flag along the way but opted to drive right through them for the sake of her own mission. She eventually recovered, was able to resume her duties, and a permanent assistant secretary was named later on, but Van Winkle learned a lesson that she shares openly today. Regardless of what the mission is or what challenges face you, you must make your health a priority in order to succeed. Her personal experience combined with what she learned in college and throughout her career has given her a more comprehensive perspective on what optimal health and fitness really looks like.

“I now truly see fitness as crossing the elements of physical, psychological, and spiritual.”

Today, Van Winkle serves as the Industry Executive for Federal Government at Oracle, helping translate complex military needs into technology solutions that support the Joint Force.

“My job is really to help Oracle understand that government perspective, the Department of War perspective, and really translate what can be some fairly complex elements within the federal government back to the technology venture at Oracle.”

Alongside her corporate role, she frequently speaks to military audiences about leadership and resilience: a message rooted in her Pentagon experience. Her core principle is that individual health directly dictates collective unit readiness. Van Winkle also shares her knowledge and experience from her time in the Pentagon and about resilience when she speaks. As she learned through her own experience, each person’s health and resilience matters because it impacts the readiness of the larger group.

“Every member of the unit must be performing at 100 percent for the unit as a whole to perform at 100 percent.”

As important as that is, Van Winkle noted that communication and transparency about a problem is just as important because if someone in the unit is under 100 percent and does not share that with leadership, it could lead to bigger issues for the entire unit later on.

“I think leaders often presume that members understand this, but what I would hear from military members is a focus on mission above and beyond all else. And that sometimes meant that they would step over those red flags in order to maintain this facade and that everything is okay.”

She concluded, “Ignoring the problem is just setting a timer. They may be able to hold it together for a while but not forever.”

Many members of the military have shared that they don’t bring up their personal problem because they don’t want to be the reason that the readiness of the unit is compromised. In Van Winkle’s opinion, the moment the problem is ignored, readiness is already compromised.

“If a leader knows someone is struggling or someone is injured or someone is going through a crisis, they can do something about it before it becomes a full-blown issue that impacts the unit and the mission. If the leader does not know about it, you are then creating a blind spot.”

Those in commander and leadership positions should also see addressing those problems and resilience as investments into readiness because programs focused on resilience can save time and energy for the sake of the mission.

“If you wait for it to become a readiness problem, you really lose before you even begin. So preventing these things is an incredible return on investment.”

Aside from advances in technology, the military’s emphasis on readiness and well-being of the service members in recent years is going to benefit many future recruits who decide to join the Joint Force. Van Winkle advises that there are other things leaders can do to make sure those who wear the nation’s uniform can be better both physically and psychologically and therefore, more capable of maximizing readiness.

“Look closely at yourself, and think of it like a maintenance check like you do for a weapons system,” she explained. “As humans, we tend to preserve stability over instability and we strive towards homeostasis, but this often means that we don’t see what’s in front of us, particularly if it doesn’t align with how we see ourselves.”

Van Winkle also noted that life can take unexpected turns whether you are ready for them or not, and being resilient means being able to adjust when needed as quickly as possible.

“Life is masterful at creating instability, and we are constantly adjusting to the experiences that we have. If done right, it can make us stronger and more resilient.”

Finally, she suggested not being afraid to have the tough conversations that come with service, readiness, or life. The willingness to speak about it not only helps the service member. It can help the leader as well, which can lead to service members focusing more on patriotism, pride, and purpose while being better prepared for the pressure.

“It does an incredible amount to maintain morale and cohesion in the unit, and it really does prevent those bigger problems.”

M&F Senior Military Editor Rob Wilkins contributed to this Fit to Serve article.

The ultimate domestic travel rewards benefit for families and couples

Imagine this: you book a flight for yourself, and your spouse — or your best friend, or your mom — flies with you for the cost of taxes alone. Not a discount. Not a sale. Completely. Free. For up to two full calendar years. That's the Southwest Companion Pass, and it is, without question, the single most powerful perk in all of domestic travel rewards. The ChooseFI community has a saying: if you only ever pursue one travel rewards strategy in your life, make it this one. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A round-trip Southwest flight from Denver to Cancún might run $400 per person. A family of four flying during spring break? You're looking at $1,600 cash. But with the Companion Pass, you pay for two tickets and the other two fly nearly free (taxes and fees only) — cutting your out-of-pocket cost in half, every single flight, for nearly two years. Run the numbers over a year of typical family travel and you're looking at **$2,000 to $8,000 in total value** from a single benefit. The CPP (cents per point) range here — **1.5 to 5.9 cents per point** — is what makes this genuinely remarkable. Southwest's Rapid Rewards program values points at roughly 1.4 cents toward any flight. But the Companion Pass doesn't just redeem points efficiently; it *doubles the value of every redemption you make while it's active*. That's the pricing inefficiency the loyalty system has quietly built in, and the FI community is uniquely positioned to exploit it. Think about what 135,000 points normally buys: roughly $1,890 worth of Southwest flights. Solid, but not earth-shattering. Now attach the Companion Pass, and those same points — redeemed strategically over two years — effectively unlock $3,780 or more in flight value for your household. No blackout dates. No seat restrictions. No change fees. Just book, fly, repeat. This isn't a first-class lounge or a lie-flat bed over the Pacific. It's something arguably more valuable for the FI-minded family: **sustainable, repeatable, nearly free domestic travel** that works with your actual life.

The Companion Pass isn't a points redemption — it's a status benefit. That distinction is everything, and it's the insight that separates people who get this from people who miss it entirely.

Here's how it works: Southwest grants the Companion Pass when you earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. Once you hit that threshold, you designate one person as your companion, and that person flies with you on every flight — paid or points — for the remainder of that calendar year plus the entire following calendar year.

The key word is "earn." Points transferred in from partners count. Credit card signup bonuses count. Shopping portal purchases count. Almost every way you accumulate points counts toward the 135,000 threshold — except points purchased directly from Southwest.

The pricing inefficiency here is a calendar arbitrage opportunity. If you earn the Companion Pass on January 2nd, you get it for the rest of that year and all of the next year — nearly two full calendar years of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it on November 15th, you get roughly 13 months. The strategy is to time your credit card signup bonuses to post in January, maximizing your benefit window.

Most ChooseFI members build their 135,000 points through a combination of strategies:

Chase Ultimate Rewards → Southwest Rapid Rewards (1:1, Instant) Chase transfers to Southwest at a 1:1 ratio and the transfer is instant — points appear in your Rapid Rewards account within minutes. This makes Chase points (earned on cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Ink Business cards) the most efficient fuel for this strategy.

Marriott Bonvoy → Southwest Rapid Rewards (3:1, 1-5 days) Marriott transfers at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Southwest point), and transfers take 1-5 days. This is a less efficient path — use it only if you have a surplus of Marriott points and no better option.

The most reliable path to 135,000 points is stacking Southwest credit card signup bonuses. Southwest's consumer and business cards frequently offer bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points each. A couple who each opens one card, or one person who opens both a personal and business card, can often hit the threshold with signup bonuses alone — before spending a dollar on the portal.

Since Southwest charges no fuel surcharges on award flights and points never expire, there's no penalty for building this balance over several months. The Rapid Rewards program is revenue-based with dynamic pricing, meaning points cover the full fare including taxes — no hidden redemption fees to erode your value.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account and your Southwest Rapid Rewards account and tally your existing points. You need 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points earned in a single calendar year to trigger the Companion Pass. Note: points already sitting in your Rapid Rewards account from prior years don't count — you need to earn 135,000 in the target calendar year.

The optimal window is October through December of the prior year. Apply for Southwest credit cards (personal and/or business) so that your signup bonuses post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Verify with Southwest's current card offers — signup bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points are common. A couple can each apply for a card; a solo pursuer can apply for both a personal and a business card if they have qualifying self-employment income.

Call Chase or Southwest after your first statement closes to confirm when points will post. Timing is everything.

Once your signup bonuses post, calculate how many points you still need. If you're short:

Southwest will notify you by email once you've crossed 135,000 qualifying points. Log into your Rapid Rewards account at southwest.com and navigate to "My Account" → "Companion Pass" to confirm the benefit is active.

You can designate — and change — your companion up to three times per calendar year. Name your most frequent travel partner first. Go to southwest.com, log in, and find the Companion Pass section to add their name and contact information.

Searching is simple: go to southwest.com and search any route. Toggle between "$ Dollars" and "Rapid Rewards Points" to see your cost. When you book with points and your companion is designated, Southwest will automatically prompt you to add your companion to the same flight. Your companion pays taxes only — typically $5.60 each way for domestic flights.

Pro tip: Southwest opens its booking window 330 days in advance. For peak travel like spring break or holiday weeks, set a calendar reminder and book the day the window opens.

The Companion Pass works because Southwest treats it as a status benefit rather than a points redemption. Most airline companion programs require you to burn miles for the second ticket or limit usage to specific fare classes. Southwest flips this model: once you earn the pass, your companion flies on every single flight you take — paid or award — for the remainder of the qualifying year plus the entire following calendar year. The only cost is taxes. Because Southwest has no blackout dates, no fuel surcharges, and no change fees, the pass amplifies in value with every trip you take. The January-earning calendar arbitrage is the key optimization that turns a good benefit into an extraordinary one.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's make this real. It's March, and your family of four wants to spend a week in Orlando this July — theme parks, pool time, the works.

A quick search on southwest.com shows round-trip flights from Chicago Midway to Orlando for $320 per person. For four tickets, that's $1,280 cash. Standard family travel math: painful but doable.

You have the Companion Pass active, earned back in January. You book two tickets: yours at 22,000 Rapid Rewards points (worth ~$308 at 1.4 cents per point), and your spouse's ticket at $5.60 in taxes as your designated companion. Your two kids? You use 44,000 more points for their tickets. Total out-of-pocket: 66,000 points + $11.20 in taxes.

Let's value those 66,000 points at their Chase transfer cost — you transferred them 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards, where they were worth roughly $825 in travel via the portal. But by pairing them with the Companion Pass, your spouse flies nearly free, effectively doubling your points' purchasing power on this trip.

Cash price: $1,280. Your cost: 66,000 points + $11.20. That's a CPP of roughly 1.9 cents per point on the base redemption — but accounting for your companion flying nearly free, the effective CPP on the entire trip rockets to 3.8 cents per point. Well within the 1.5–5.9 cent range where this sweet spot lives.

And here's what makes Southwest specifically wonderful for families: no change fees. Book in March, change in June when your kid's baseball tournament schedule shifts, rebook without penalty. No one in the FI community is paying $200-per-person change fees.

The experience itself? Economy class on Southwest, open seating, snacks, and friendly crew. It's not lie-flat business class to Tokyo — but that's not the point. The point is your family of four flies to Florida for a week, and the flights barely register on your annual budget. That's FI-level travel.

Time your credit card applications so signup bonuses post in January of your target year. A bonus that posts January 5th gives you until December 31st of the following year to use the Companion Pass — nearly 24 months of 2-for-1 flights. This single timing decision can mean the difference between 13 months and 23 months of value.

The Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal (rapidrewardsshopping.com) awards points on purchases at hundreds of retailers. Even after you've earned the Companion Pass, continuing to earn Rapid Rewards points means more flights at lower point costs. Treat it like a cashback portal and check it before any online purchase.

Southwest opens availability 330 days in advance. For Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and summer weekends in popular markets, set a calendar reminder and book the exact morning the window opens. Southwest doesn't have blackout dates, but high-demand flights sell out in Wanna Get Away fare class — the cheapest points tier — quickly.

You can change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. If your life situation changes — a different travel partner, a new relationship, a child aging into a separate ticket — use this flexibility. Just don't burn all three changes frivolously.

Purchased points do not count toward the 135,000 qualifying threshold for the Companion Pass. Don't make this mistake when you're close to the threshold — transfer from Chase instead.

Some people try to earn the Companion Pass in November or December. You'll get it for only a few weeks before the calendar resets. The math simply doesn't work. January earning is the only strategy worth pursuing.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards Performance Business Credit Card (or similar business cards) have separate signup bonuses that stack with personal card bonuses. If you have any self-employment income — freelancing, a side hustle, a rental property — you likely qualify. This is often the fastest path to 135,000 points for a single applicant.

The Southwest Companion Pass was practically invented for the FI-minded family. If you have a consistent travel partner — a spouse, a partner, a parent you visit annually — and you fly domestically more than two or three times a year, this benefit will transform your travel budget.

Minimum points to get started: You need to earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. In practice, this means you either need access to Southwest credit card signup bonuses (which requires good to excellent credit, typically 700+) or a substantial existing balance of Chase Ultimate Rewards points to transfer at 1:1.

How it fits the FI strategy: The Companion Pass is a force multiplier. Every dollar you would have spent on a second ticket stays in your investment accounts instead. Over a two-year Companion Pass window, a couple who takes six domestic trips per year could easily bank $2,000-$4,000 in travel savings — real money that compounds.

Who this is NOT for: Solo travelers get zero benefit from the Companion Pass. International travelers who primarily fly non-Southwest routes won't find much use here. And if you're averse to economy class or require a specific airline's premium cabin, this redemption isn't your path.

The Southwest Companion Pass earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is almost entirely about the *earning*, not the booking. Once you have the Companion Pass, booking is literally the simplest award experience in travel rewards: search southwest.com, find your flight, click "Add Companion." There are no partner airlines to navigate, no availability calendars to decode, no call centers to endure. It's a 5/5 on ease of booking for a reason. The moderate rating comes from **three earning challenges**: **1. The credit requirement.** Southwest credit cards require good to excellent credit. If you're early in your credit-building journey, this strategy may need to wait 12-18 months while you strengthen your profile. **2. The timing discipline.** Earning the pass is straightforward, but earning it in January takes planning. You need to apply for cards 2-3 months in advance and coordinate signup bonus posting dates — something most people have never had to think about. **3. The 135,000-point threshold.** This is a real number. It requires intentional credit card strategy, not casual spending. For a single applicant without a business card, it may require supplementing with Chase transfers or portal activity. **How to overcome these challenges:** - Start planning in **October or November** for a January earn target - Check whether you qualify for a Southwest business card — it dramatically simplifies reaching the threshold - Use the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal year-round to passively accumulate qualifying points If you've successfully applied for a travel rewards credit card before and you have a consistent travel partner, you can absolutely do this. The ChooseFI community has helped hundreds of families earn the Companion Pass — and not one of them regretted the effort.

Open a personal and/or business Southwest credit card so that signup bonuses of 50,000 to 75,000 points each will post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Call to confirm when points will post after your first statement closes.

Once signup bonuses post, calculate your gap. Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards at 1:1 (instant) to fill any shortfall. Use the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal for additional earning on everyday purchases.

After Southwest confirms your Companion Pass, log in to southwest.com and designate your travel partner. Book flights as normal — Southwest will prompt you to add your companion for taxes only ($5.60 each way domestic).

Set calendar reminders for Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and summer travel. Southwest opens its booking window 330 days in advance. Book the morning the window opens to lock in Wanna Get Away fares at the lowest point costs.

The Companion Pass is valid for the remainder of the calendar year in which you earn it plus the entire following calendar year. If you earn it on January 2nd, you get nearly 24 months of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it in November, you get roughly 14 months. This is why timing your earning to January is the critical optimization.

Yes. Signup bonuses, spending on Southwest cards, points transferred from Chase Ultimate Rewards, and points earned through the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal all count as qualifying points. The only points that do not count are those purchased directly from Southwest.

Yes. The Companion Pass works on both cash-purchased flights and flights booked with Rapid Rewards points. Your companion pays only taxes — typically $5.60 each way for domestic flights — regardless of how you booked the ticket.

Southwest allows you to change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. Log into your Rapid Rewards account on southwest.com and update the companion information in the Companion Pass section. Plan strategically since you only get three changes per year.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Southwest Companion Pass is the single most powerful domestic travel rewards benefit available to FI-minded families and couples. At a cost of 135,000 qualifying points — achievable through credit card signup bonuses and Chase transfers — you unlock nearly two full years of 2-for-1 flights on every Southwest route with no blackout dates and no change fees. A family of four taking six domestic trips per year can realistically save $2,000 to $4,000 annually, money that goes straight back into your investment accounts. Time your earning to January, stack your signup bonuses, and designate your most frequent travel partner. This is the redemption that makes domestic travel a rounding error in your FI budget.

It’s 50 years since the original movie captured our hearts and fighting spirit in 1976, but the movie’s motivating message; that we can all push ourselves to be more than we thought we could, is still as relevant today as it ever was. With more than 40,000 runners expected to descend in Philadelphia, each of the three Rocky Run categories have sold out.

The first official Rocky Run began in 2014 with heavyweight beginnings, attracting 7,000 runners, but it has gone from strength to strength since. And, while organizers had expected around 30,000 competitors to descend in Philly this year, the final number will clock in at an incredible 40,000.

Those who are ready and set for November 14, 2026, have a choice of three categories, catering to different abilities, so that anyone can “Go For it.”

The half marathon actually combines the 5K and 10-mile runs, meeting the 13.1-mile requirement, and besides channeling your inner Rocky Balboa and going the distance, there are cool medals to be won. The 5K finisher medal celebrates 50 years of Rocky, while the 10-mile finisher medal depicts The Italian Stallion’s triumphant celebration at the top of the famous steps leading up to the Philadelphia Museum of Art. The 13.1-mile finishers is a large, heavyweight design that has “50” emblazoned on one side, while the other side has a vintage image of Rocky in training.

In addition to the Rocky Run, Philadelphia continues to show its love for the most famous fictional boxer in history. The city held its first “Rocky Day,” on December 3, 2023. No doubt, the inspirational story of one man going the distance continues to resonate around the world.

“Once again it’s a magical time of the year, The Rocky Run,” said Stallone in a recent social media post to promote the activities on November 14. Of course, Sly has been heavily active during Rocky’s 50th celebrations. He released his appropriately titled autobiography, “The Steps” and even brought back the man behind Rocky’s signature soundtrack, Bill Conti, for a live concert in New York to go along with a screening of the film. And for those, who still can’t get enough of Sylvester Stallone’s creation, the story of how a struggling actor defied the odds to become the star of one of cinema’s most successful franchises is also set to hit theaters, with “I Play Rocky” starring Anthony Ippolito as the struggling boxer given a once in a lifetime shot, and Stephan James playing Apollo Creed.

As to whether Sly will make an appearance at this record-breaking Rocky Run, fans are certainly hoping that Philadelphia’s favorite son will tread his old stomping ground once again.

#8736. Robert Strauss Has the Full-Body F45 Workout to Stay Fit over 40

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

As the General Manager of WWE’s NXT brand, a pro wrestling coach, and the owner of eight gyms across Florida, Robert Strauss understands the importance of rapid workouts to stay ripped. To that end, the man known to millions of WWE fans as “Robert Stone,” says that F45 workouts are perfect for staying fighting fit, and he proved it with a dedicated demonstration for M&F.

The F45 concept sees gym goers from all over the world following the same daily workout. “Everybody does the same workout every day, and you’re never going to do the same workout twice,” says Strauss. “It’s a 45-minute workout that includes your warmup, your workout, and your cooldown.”

Indeed, F45 workouts tackle fitness from all angles. There are focused cardio days, strength days, and hybrid days to keep each session stimulating. And, there’s often a choice of two different exercises as you move through the circuit. “So, you really can get a full body workout in, any day that you come into an F45, and you’re always going to leave drenched in sweat, I promise you that,” adds the NXT GM.

F45 sessions begin as soon as the clock activates and include short demonstrations followed by a guided warmup with dynamic stretching, to prepare yourself for the pump ahead. Then, after the main session is done, there’s a cooldown period before you tackle the rest of the day, feeling ready to bodyslam the world.

Greeting us at his Baldwin Park, FL, location, Strauss, who is the father of twin boys, explained that F45 has provided structure so that he can keep up with the next generation at both at home and in NXT. He completed the following session between duties, proving that he hasn’t missed a beat.

(In this class, there were 4 minutes for setup)

Execute each exercise for 45 seconds.Rest and transition to the next exercise for 15 seconds.

High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) sessions such as this one can easily burn more than 500 calories in 45 minutes, depending on the effort put in, and you’ll supercharge your fat burning power with Excess Post-Exercise Oxygen Consumption (EPOC) for the rest of the day.

You won’t need to walk around a vast gym space to hit all of the muscle groups either, because you’ll be completing each station while staying pretty much on the spot. This particular workout offered back and core strengthening exercises like crunches and rows, upper body testers like presses and extensions, and movements that also build the lower body with sumo stances and lying leg raises.

“One of the most inspiring things about NXT is that most of the trainees there are half my age,” says Strauss of his motivation to maintain muscle. “They are all phenomenal athletes that come from all over the world, and they are in the greatest shape. So, seeing them inspires me to continue my fitness journey. Also, I’m a twin dad to 10-year-olds, and I want to inspire them the way NXT Superstars inspire me. I want to inspire my kids so that they see their daddy is fit, and they want to be fit. It’s an important part of life for your mental and physical well-being,”

You can catch Strauss in his role as General Manager Robert Stone, stamping his authority on NXT, every Tuesday night on the CW Network in the U.S. and streaming internationally on Netflix.

#8730. At 43, Robert Strauss Continues Training to Be the ‘Dad Bod Destroyer’

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Whether you know Robert Strauss for his work as “Robbie E” in TNA or more recently, “Robert Stone” as WWE’s General Manager of NXT, there’s no questioning this exciting performer’s work ethic. Fortunately, as the father of twin boys, and owner of several gyms in Florida, Stone is showing no signs of slowing down. And, at age 43, the “Dad Bod Destroyer” tells M&F how he’s evolved in order to hang with the next generation, both on screen and at home.

Formerly a physical education teacher, Robert Strauss made his pro wrestling debut in the year 2000 and soon worked preliminary matches for WWE until he signed a major deal with Total Nonstop Action in 2010, gaining fame as the charismatic “Robbie E.”  It was during his time in TNA that Strauss won a multitude of titles, including the promotion’s TV and X Division gold.

He also lifted the tag team belts on two occasions alongside Jessie Godderz, and in that team, known as “The BroMans,” the duo even received support from seven-time Mr Olympia, Phil Heath. Of course, Strauss is no stranger to Muscle & Fitness. In 2017, he became a popular contributor with his “Dad Bod Destroyer” workouts, detailing how he stayed in fighting shape while balancing life with his twin sons Cash and Carter, who were just months old as that point. In 2026, Strauss is still making a name for himself in the pro wrestling business, by keeping a tight leash on the young superstars of NXT, but while his current role involves a desk rather than a squared circle, Strauss is always ready for action.

As Robert Stone, the world traveled grappler has maintained his fitness and physique by evolving, to stay consistent. For example, as a young lion, he was able to throw around weights with the same reckless abandon that he showed to many a hapless foe inside the ring. But at 43, and juggling his now 10-year-old twins with a hectic role as NXT GM, coach at WWE’s Performance Center, and broadcast commentator to boot, Strauss has a busier schedule than ever despite the fact that he does not currently compete. Fortunately, the performer has combined his passion with his profession and also owns eight gyms across Florida — that’s five F45 and three FS8 studios—so he’s never stuck for a timely way to stay toned.

Because F45 workouts last no more than 45 minutes, Strauss is able to get great value from his sweat equity. “You’re able to get it all in,” he tells M&F, noting that following an efficient plan has cut down his workout time without sacrificing quality. “Sometimes there are days where I don’t have an hour and a half. I don’t have two hours to get in everything, if I want to stretch out, if I want to warm my body up,” adds Strauss, appreciating the fact that F45 sessions are already planned out and ready to go. “At 43, I do need to regularly warm my body up. So, the 45 minutes is clutch, to be able to just come in and leave, and everything be done.”

For mobility, Strauss shares that FS8 workouts focus on a lighter style of resistance training for improving mobility and maintaining longevity, while still building strength. That’s because FS8 sessions combine Pilates and yoga, with a major emphasis on the core as well as controlled, meaningful movements.

Because of his commitment to crushing each workout, Strauss still looks like he could step between the ropes at any moment, and he maintains a low level of bodyfat to stay ripped, but as a mature athlete, he prefers a sustainable approach to nutrition rather than the latest fads, and this means embracing the balance. “The thing is, I really know my body,” he explains. “Mentally, I want to enjoy things sometimes. I’m not always eating a strict, clean diet. I want to have a good time with my wife or my twins. If they want to get ice cream on the weekend, I’m going to get it too, if I want it.”

The clever coach says that allowing himself to indulge also provides him with the motivation to eat cleaner for the rest of the week. “It adds fuel to the fire for my next workout,” says Strauss. Still, this athlete is keen to avoid eating too late in the evenings and particularly avoids starchy carbs and processed sugars before he hits the hay.

Strauss refuses to rule out the possibility that Robert Stone could one day return him to the ring. He certainly would not be the oldest grappler on the roster if he did. Randy Orton and The Miz are 46, CM Punk is 48, and Rey Mysterio is 51. WWE fans also know that Stauss’s colleague and SmackDown General Manager, Nick Aldis, who is 39, returned for a one-off match against Gunther at SummerSlam 2026.

“If someone pushed me past the point where I need to step in the ring again, I don’t need a week to get ready,” says the authority of NXT. “I don’t need three months to get ready… I can be ready in an hour.”

#8726. The Peptide Door Is Cracking Open, Even If The Risks Aren’t Going Away

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Recently, an interesting thing happened. An athlete could read the World Anti-Doping Agency’s prohibited list and conclude that using certain peptides was a good way to lose a medal and win a ban. Then he could read a new federal announcement about those same compounds and conclude that Washington was opening the door to them. Same molecule. Two government-adjacent messages that seem to be saying two entirely different things. This could lead to quite a headache if you don’t bother reading the fine print.

On Oct. 30, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) published a draft interim policy involving six experimental peptides: BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, epitalon, and Semax. The idea is to use enforcement discretion while regulators decide whether these substances belong on the list of ingredients that certain licensed pharmacies and physicians can use in compounding. In plain English, HHS says it does not intend to pursue enforcement against qualifying compounders who follow a set of conditions. That is not the same thing as approving six new drugs.

Compounding is when a licensed professional prepares a medication for an individual patient rather than dispensing a mass-produced, approved product. The proposed policy calls for patient-specific prescriptions, traceable ingredients, quality documentation, reporting of serious adverse events, and other safeguards. It’s a long way from some internet chemist shipping you a vial labeled “research use only” with a complimentary discount code from a guy who benches four plates on Instagram.

I can see the argument for this. People are buying these things anyway. If a person is determined to use an experimental peptide, there’s an obvious appeal to getting it through a licensed professional instead of trusting an anonymous supplier whose laboratory might be a shack in a Chinese suburb. HHS says the policy is intended to steer people away from risky, unregulated sources. Fair enough. But a cleaner supply chain is not the same as a molecule that has been proven to work.

That’s the part the peptide evangelists tend to skip. BPC-157 has a reputation for repairing practically everything except a a broken heart. TB-500 gets talked about like it comes with replacement tendons in the box. But the clinical evidence supporting these sweeping claims in humans is thin. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) scientists raised concerns about the lack of convincing clinical data and about product safety.

An advisory committee nevertheless supported broader compounding access for six substances. Disagreement among experts is not proof that either side has discovered a miracle. But, the empirical data is unavoidably overwhelming. It’s a clear case of not believing the dyno numbers – the car feels faster. Such reports have dialed up to the point where the usual culprits smell dollar signs. However thin the clinical data, its being drowned out by an ever growing cadre of gym bros who swear it works, the list is prestigious too. Now all of a sudden the government tosses a glimmer of light down the hallway?  Out of nowhere? Isn’t it usually the government that’s slamming the door shut?

Note that the draft doesn’t authorize supplement companies to dump these compounds into pre-workouts and doesn’t establish that a product is safe or effective. The federal notice is open for public comment, and the policy can be revisited if safety or quality problems emerge. There are also state-level rules to contend with. Anyone announcing that peptides have been “FDA approved” has either misunderstood the document or is counting on you not reading it.

Now comes the part where competitive athletes have to pay close attention: BPC-157 and TB-500 remain prohibited under the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) rules used by many tested sports. A change in how federal regulators view compounding peptides does not rewrite the WADA rulebook. A prescription is not automatically permission to compete with a substance in your system.

The U.S. Anti-Doping Agency (USADA) has already sanctioned athletes over these compounds. Proof that the obstacle is here to stay.  What the outlaws will have to contend with is that while there are banned peptides that can already be detected directly in an athlete’s urine or blood, others present a much tougher analytical problem. And a ban doesn’t require WADA to have a practical routine test for the substance before they ban it. So, that right there is the loophole. And trust me when I tell you, it’s going to be exploited. Why? Because peptides work.

I’m all for serious research. I’m also for admitting when thousands of testimonials cannot all be wrong. If the new policy leads to better manufacturing controls and useful clinical data, good. If it merely replaces the sketchy online vial with a more expensive sketchy vial wearing a white coat, we haven’t accomplished much. There’s an important difference between making something easier to obtain and proving it’s worth obtaining. And if you compete in a tested sport, there’s a third question: whether using it costs you your career. Don’t confuse the three. And remember, if an athlete is prone to cheating, chances are he will cheat. And with what will he use to cheat? The stuff that works. Peptides are just now showing up in force and its a force to be reconned with.

On Episode 310 of The Menace Podcast, host Dennis James was joined by Milos Sarcev, Chris Cormier, and special guest Terrence Ruffin, and the conversation moved towards the 2027 Mr. Olympia final. The man they call “Ruff Diesel” talked to the panel about the progress he needs to make, to finally win a title at the Olympia.

Ruffin, an iconic Men’s Physique competitor has appeared in nine Olympia finals, and qualified for his tenth by securing victories at the Mexico and Slovakia Pro events in October. Ruffin was at ninth place at the ‘O’ in 2016 and 2018 but found a career high placing of second in 2020 and 2021. He came fifth in 2026, so what does he need to work on, in order to progress in 2027?

“Do you believe in your heart that you can still win the Olympia,” asked host Dennis James. “100%” came the quick response from Ruffin, who explained that despite his vast experience, he is still very excited about that prospect. Ruff Diesel then provided a glimpse into the adjustments he may need to make, if he is to dominate bodybuilding’s biggest stage.

“My biggest issue is, I always end up doing too much,” he explained. “I told myself, this year, I’m going to say no to a lot more stuff.” Ruffin shared that his constant travel and business interests could be spreading him too thin. “But I’m trying to not do so much,” he relented.

“But you’ve started a new business too,” challenged The Menace. “You’re prepping for the Olympia and you’re opening up a gym. I mean, come on.”

Ruffin agreed that he takes on a lot. “I’m even (going to) have a meeting with the gym tomorrow, about handing off a couple of things,” he said. “Just to make sure I can focus like I need to.”

Ruffin says that he has learned to appreciate that getting to the pinnacle of bodybuilding requires his complete attention. “I’m giving up a part of the business at the gym, so I don’t have to do, like, the day to day,” he explained. The competitor now intends to keep his diary clearer by turning down events and reducing his travel. “I’m just all in, on just the gym training, and all of that.”

With a renewed focus on the prize, Milos Sarcev pushed further on what progress Ruffin will need to make with his physique, in order to win. “Conditioning, or size?” asked The Mind. “Both,” answered Ruffin, with a smile.

To see this conversation in full on The Menace Podcast, where the panel also discussed the latest bodybuilding gossip, news, and results, check it out on the Muscle & Fitness YouTube channel.
