#8718. The Arizona Experiment!

The thing that drew me to early retirement is freedom, and that’s still the best part of it.

Back in 2005, the primary reason for this freedom-seeking was being able to devote my best hours to being a Dad – I had a feeling my career in tech would be too demanding to sustain once the full-time job of raising children kicked in.

Eighteen years later, wow has that guess ever turned out to be right. Early retirement has proved to be the most amazing, worthwhile adventure and it’s still just getting started. It was an astonishing thirteen years ago that I wrote to you about Little MM starting kindergarten, and now he’s done with high school.

It has given me the space to enjoy so many new experiences, working hard and playing hard sometimes, but also slowing things way down when necessary, to deal with and grow through some real hardships.

But now, with that child-raising phase finally almost done, I’m cashing in a few of those Freedom Chips for a particularly big change: moving to a warm sunny place for the winter to try out a new life in the walkable, bikeable, car-free community you’ve probably heard me raving about in the past: Culdesac Tempe.

So on the first of December I’ll be packing up the essential clothes, tools and gadgets, and throwing my very best mountain bike onto the Model Y to make the epic road trip across the mountains. Just in time to escape the incoming Colorado winter. And my son will be joining me for the trip!

Looking for updates? I have added a separate tracker page here.

We’ve booked ourselves a spacious two bedroom apartment there, for four full months. Little MM will be roughly alternating his months between Arizona and Colorado so he can still have time with both parents, while I’ll be there the whole time.

A big part of the fun is that this will force me to invent a whole new life for myself, away from the easy comforts of the big community and plentiful construction sites that keep me so busy here.  It will be both a big change and a significant challenge, which is exactly what all of us need on a regular basis to keep life full of meaning and joy.

The exact details are still in the works, and I’d love to hear your ideas and feedback (see the “get in touch” note below. But here’s what I’ve got so far:

Okay, you’re onto me. If I’m going to go to the trouble of typing shit into the computer and sharing it with you, there’s usually a purpose behind it other than just journaling my own personal life, and this another one of those cases.

First of all, there are the first-layer selfish goals: I want to have the best winter ever, meet a bunch of smart new people, and I also want Culdesac to be a huge success so they will build more neighborhoods like this around the country and set an example that permanently improves the way US cities build and expand themselves in the future.

But even if you don’t care about all that, I also want to use this as a little statement about trying deliberate life changes.

By throwing myself into a new community which aligns so nicely with my own values, I hope to serve as a reminder that maybe you might want to try the same thing. Or just try anything new.

In a comfortable, prosperous country like ours, some of the built in tendencies of Human nature tend to work against us, saying,

“Hey – I’ve noticed we have plenty of food and reasonable shelter and that’s good enough. So let’s just double down on the Netflix, comfort foods, and occasional luxury purchases and that will keep us safe.”

Instead, I want you to set your life treadmill to just a bit of a steeper, healthier incline setting.

That means questioning the status quo and doing your best to keep at least one little experiment on the go in the background. Maybe that means forcing yourself to move to a better place, or taking steps towards getting a new job that gives you a better work-life balance.

The biggest move I ever made was leaving family and friends and my old job behind to move to the US, alone, at age 24. Looking back, I’m shocked I had the courage (and the organizational skills) to pull that off back then. I’ve become older and a bit slower, and so comfortable that it’s hard to imagine doing something so bold now.

But even today 24 years later, I thank my past self every single day for doing it. My present life is an incredibly different and better thing because of that past bit of courage.

The spirit of positive experimentation might also mean starting to challenge your body more regularly – giving it harder work and exposing it to a wider swath of temperatures and movements. Or joining new Meetup groups to expand your circle of friends and experiences.

It doesn’t really matter exactly what you do, as long as you point your feet in what feels like a good direction and just start moving. Create some purposeful change, which will surely feel a bit difficult, simply because change is hard. And hard things are good.

Future Arizona Neighbors: I’ll see you in four weeks!

Further reading: I’ve been reading books, doing life experiments, and writing about the value of strategic hardship for a while now. But the latest is a book called Dopamine Nation by the talented psychiatrist/author named Dr. Anna Lembke.

To summarize: your brain creates a baseline for happiness based on the HARDEST thing you do, and then compares everything else to that. So if you do hard things, life in general seems fantastic because of this perspective. If you eliminate all hardship, suddenly even the pleasures of life seem bland, and you live a spoiled and unmotivated life.

Interested in stopping by for your own Mini Culdesac Experiment? They have a few short-term rentals available at rather reasonable rates (less than nearby hotels) – check em out at book.culdesac.com

I’m bringing the car just as a convenient electric moving truck to carry two people and four months of living supplies. Once I get there, I’ll find a safe place to park it offsite and live the full car-free lifestyle of Culdesac, much like I do when I’m here at home. I typically only use cars to carry really heavy stuff or for trips to other cities and states, but it’s even easier to accomplish this in Tempe with its location right on the light rail and with their onsite bike, scooter and even car sharing lots.

My place in Colorado is currently set up as a two bedroom house on the main floor, plus an apartment with a separate entrance on the walkout lower level. When I’m at home, I use the whole thing as one home – the apartment just makes a great place to host a fairly constant stream of visiting friends. But for the winter I’m hoping to rent out one of these spaces to a friend or trusted acquaintance who will take good care of everything, while I leave the other section free for the occasional visits I’ll be paying to this area over the winter. Aside from keeping an eye on the place, it will be a great way to practice the age-old Mustachian technique of making money while taking vacations!

As it stands, I have no plans beyond this point. I’ll head back to Colorado for my home base, but with this being a new phase of life I’ll be layering on new adventures. Aside from the two mountain properties that I’ve been helping to build out, I may end up with an MMM Mountain Retreat of my own someday. Conclusion: ongoing thoughts on the Culdesac experiment are here: https://mrmoneymustache.com/culdesac/

Looking forward to hearing about your time in AZ!

Awesome! Moving to a new place is the perfect way to get a new perspective on things. Enjoy culdesac. I worked with Ryan a while back. They’re doing great stuff. I’m hoping this sort of thing catches on in other places across the country.

Love This! Welcome to the Valley MMM. Winter is most definitely prime time around here. Looking forward to connecting again at a future meet-up!

Not suggesting every day, but it might be interesting once or twice. And, don’t miss the Superstition Mountains at least once. In the spring it has beautiful wild flowers. Best of luck.

Cool! Hope you can use your blog to popularize the Culdesac experiment and get more people thinking about car-free communities.

I have a question: You’re going to be in Arizona during the winter months. That’s the nicest time of year to live in the desert. During the summer, it must get brutally hot. Do you think that will be a disincentive for people to move to Culdesac, knowing they won’t be able to rely on the comfort of air-conditioned cars?

Humans are pretty adaptable, but there are limits to what we can acclimate to. I enjoy walking, but even I would have second thoughts about leaving the house to go for a stroll if it was 120 degrees outside. And climate change is only going to make the heat worse. I’d have concerns about living somewhere that routinely gets that hot if walking or biking were the only ways of getting around.

Mr. Money Mustache November 2, 2023, 7:39 pm

Yeah, Phoenix summers are definitely not for everyone! Although Culdesac is designed specifically to make it easier to bear, with the desert-friendly white buildings with close spacing and plenty of shade structures.

When it comes to the heat, a car is the LAST thing I want to be getting into! Those glass domed furnaces get up to 200 degrees within minutes every time you park them in a climate like that. I’d greatly prefer to be in a neighborhood where I can walk in a shaded alley, and perhaps shift my schedule a bit during the summer months so I take a Siesta for the hottest part of the day and enjoy a bit more of the evening hours in exchange.

The other thing to note is that somehow, five million people DO choose to call Phoenix home and the population is still growing rapidly. A big part of this is that the human body can adapt to a much wider range of temperatures than we realize. Both my Phoenix friends (115F summers) and my Ottawa family (-30F winters) say, it’s not that bad” even though both of those temperatures would sound unbearable to, say, a Hawaiian.

Our son lived in Tempe for 10 years and mostly rode his bike to work at the local community college in Mesa.In the HOTTEST summer months,he was able to grab a bus to the campus.Never needed a car.We learn to adapt to the hot hot summers, we switch up when we do stuff, we go slower, you do NOT hike locally, you go up NORTH for that.. overall,I love it here in t he desert and don’t miss winter,snow,driving in ice, etc. Creative folks like MM will do great!! Lack of humidity makes a big deference in how the heat affects you . 100 degrees is like 75 degrees in Florida . I can stay all day outside in shade when the temp is at 110 . Just need to drink a lot of water.

I was in the Phoenix area a few weeks ago. It is amazing how quickly you adapt. Temperatures where I live are in the 50ties to 60ties, it was above 100 in Phoenix. During the day in the sun, it is really hot (it’s more than 120 in the sun in mid October!). In the shade it actually felt comfortable. At night at 85 I put on a jacket, because it felt chilly.

Florida on the other hand… I was there in February one year: It felt rather cold, but I got a sun burn. Late summer the humidity is killing me.

That is SO awesome, MMM! I made the move to southern California in 1996, and I have NEVER regretted it. I grew up in Wisconsin, and although I love the scenery there, it’s just way too cold 8 months out of the year.

Your blog reminded me of the book “Four Thousand Weeks,” by Oliver Burkeman. It’s an amazing book on how looking at “time” differently (to me, more realistically), can change how you experience your life.

As I’ve gotten older, I’ve noticed that the constant “do, do, do” of our culture and our personal mindsets allows for very little time to really consider what is important to us, but also how recognizing that we can’t do it all, have it all, and get it all done, allows for us to really think about what we do want to do, have and get done in our lifespans (which average about 4,000 weeks).

So excited to hear that you’re giving Tempe a whirl! I lived there for 2 years and I loved it. You can go a really long way on the off street bike paths, just make sure to bring water and drink it a lot. I used to love riding to the Botanical Garden/Zoo/Hole In The Rock from there. There are also multiple mountains you can ride to and hike. Echo Canyon trail is my favorite hiking trail in the world, and it’s a reasonable bike from Tempe. South Mountain has a lot longer trails to hike on too (College Ave has a bike/ped bridge over the highway so it’s easy to get to). The greenway trail up past McKellips Lake is also just a wonderful ride. There used to be a farmers market type thing on it. I wonder if it’s still there? Also, be sure to go the AZ International Marketplace, the most Mustachian grocery store I’ve ever been to (they once sold me a whole head of garlic for $0.10).

Don’t forget to travel to nearby towns/cities too while you’re down there. Saguaro National Park in Tucson is amazing. Sedona is home to some of the most beautiful views in the country, but the town itself is kind of a miserable strip mall. I would suggest going to Prescott AZ first, because it’s almost as beautiful naturally and far nicer as a town, with a great walkable downtown. Flagstaff is another fun stop on the way to the Grand Canyon.

You probably don’t need this blog post I wrote a long time ago about how to live in Tempe without a car, but maybe others will find it useful. I don’t know the details of culdesac, but much of what you say is fair in general. Our development system is quite broken as it depends on risk-adverse, profit-seeking developers to build out a communities’ land use vision, which may or may not be supportive of car-lite living in itself. It has resulted in sprawl and “luxury” everything sameness and widespread auto dependence. I agree ideally there would be lots of employment in the development, but I would argue that dense, transit accessible housing is the greater need in our system. Less regulation is often the answer here (e.g., removing parking minimums, increasing residential zoning density), but in your example, clearly some way of ensuring that the development follows through on its promises it made for approval is needed. On the flip side, any housing built, even if it is for AirBnbs is creating housing and likely converting other short term to long term rentals due to competition. Any dense housing in an area that isn’t car dependent is a win in my book, and culdesac’s ideals seem about as good as a developer of a single parcel can do to prove a concept and get the ball rolling. I hope they are vey successful and make lots of money to prove the concept elsewhere, which can translate into lower price points, mixed use, 15 minute cities, etc.

I’ve often wondered about the problem of renting when one doesn’t have a “job”. I am going to be selling my house this spring (after 40 years), and am planning to rent moving forward. I just assumed that providing a landlord with documented income information via tax returns would be enough to prove one’s income stream. The irony is that ever since I retired, I make more money per annum that I ever did while working, due to lucky investments along the way that generate income. Once the house is cashed in, the residual income from the invested funds will generate more monthly income than most renters earn through employment. So the “you can’t rent without a job” really makes no sense at all. Unless the landlord or property management company are total morons.

I know this is a few days late, but if you see it, there is also qualifying based on assets. I’m not working and my hubby is doing a fun but shittily paid Americorps job, so we couldn’t qualify on income. Fortunately, the agent asked about assets and we qualified that way.

When we previously lived in Alexandria, they also wouldn’t let you pay upfront. Didn’t make sense to me, but that was the policy. You also might have better luck with an individual landlord than a property company. I had a friend who paid for 2 whole years in advance in Philly a few years ago.

I recently read that book after hearing the author interviewed by both Joe Rogan and Andrew Huberman. It gave me a new perspective on motivation and “happiness”, and closed the loop on these ideas as so practically described by MMM. Satisfaction, contentment, and motivation come to us by way of the “struggle” and the the effort of dealing with and facing challenging situations of all sorts – physical, emotional, and mental. Feeding our desires constantly – eating, entertainment, alcohol, drugs, shopping, etc. – only serve to make us less and less happy and more and more depressed. Eliminating our cravings and desires, while pursuing intentional hardships to keep us fit, sharp, and strong, ultimates results in a more satisfying state of mind and a fulfilling sense of wellbeing. It all comes together with the MMM philosophy of living a simple, frugal, productive, and healthy lifestyle.

While you’re in Arizona, you may want to check out Arcosanti, about half way between Phoenix and Sedona. It’s the original attempt at a prototype arcology, the 1960s urban planning model defined by Paolo Soleri and later popularized in Sim City and many science fiction novels. He focussed on combining dense urban living, environmental conservation, and place-based architecture. Arcosanti is itself beautiful, and it’s fascinating to see how the ideas that germinated there have slowly been manifesting in places like Culdesac.

Hmm, yeah that is indeed a bit too personal for this comments section (I do my best not to mix my relationship life with the MMM Internet life – except for that one necessary mention that we amicably parted ways in 2018).

But I do like to share a general message, because divorce is such a common thing yet it is widely associated with shame and blame: it is OKAY if it’s right for you. It’s not a failure or a negative, selfish choice. And more people need to get over the fear of making changes like that in their lives, once they have done their best to think it through. And more people need to be nice about it as they go through the process.

I think I’m a long-term-couple person at the core, so I happily look forward to settling down in that way in my own future. But as with any relationship, both people need to be compatible and appreciative with each other. And as an outrageous optimist, I believe there ARE plenty of wonderful people out there for everyone!

Anyway, obviously the desert has lots of beautiful hikes and bike rides. But do yourself a favour (note the “u” in favour LoL) and go check out The Desert Botanical Gardens. It’s one of the absolute gems in The Valley. It can sometimes have lots of tourists there … particularly us Canucks. But it’s for good reason. It is spectacular. And they have lots of cool events there too. We take all our visitors there. And if you’re so inclined, the library offers free passes to DBG and lots of other local attractions too.

(1) The Musical Instrument Museum is pretty huge and unique

(2) The drive out to Tortilla Flats is really beautiful. It literally is an old stage coach trail that was turned into a twisty 2 lane highway.  And you can go boating or kayaking in Canyon lake, which is pretty sweet.

(3) Sedona is obviously one of the most gorgeous places in the US and a reasonably short drive. If you’re going to go to the Grand Canyon from Sedona (or even if you’re just going to Flagstaff), there’s this fabulous older highway called 89A that takes you to Flagstaff. It’s so much more fun than taking the freeway.

(4) There are oodles and oodles of free Disc Golf courses (my new obsession and the price is right)

(5) South Mountain has a thing called “Silent Sunday” where they close the mountain to cars. So you can ride your bike up (obviously challenging) but then down (woo hoo!)

(6) There’s a cool thing downtown called “First Friday Art Walk” every month. Google it.

(7) Most importantly, my favourite place to ride my bike is in the Northern part of The McDowell Sonoran Preserve. Specifically, I like the trail called “The Long Way Around”. It’s just the right length (around 25 km). The ground is very beginner friendly. In fact, I have a hybrid, not a mountain bike and it does fine. But the trail still has lots of ups and downs and twists and turns, so it’s a blast. So much so, that the first time I rode there, I was giggling like a kid, even though I’m 55. It’s as easy or hard as you want it to be, based on how fast you go. And also it’s one of the nicest parks in the area.

(8) Taliesin West is super cool. Particularly if you get a good guide. It was Frank Lloyd Wright’s personal project. His winter home. So he was free to do whatever crazy things he could dream up, without having to account to a client. The handyman in you will love it!

I could go on, but that’s off the top of my head.

One last note. If you wear something Canadian; like for example, I wear a CBC logo on my hat or my partner wears something from the Leafs … a zillion snowbird Canadians will approach you and ask what part of Canada you’re from.

Anyway, here’s to a great time in Arizona.

Hey MMM, my wife’s been following you for a long time and told me you were moving out to Tempe. I grew up there, and still meet up with friends I’ve known in the area since elementary school. Tempe’s a great college town- Go Sun Devils!

I live in east Mesa now, close to Usery Mountain National Park and the Superstition Mountains. I’m a retired teacher, solar guy, and artist. I do a lot of hiking and biking in the area, as well as SUP and kayaking. If you and your son would like a tour guide/hiking/biking/river partner, be sure and get in touch.

#8717. Joe Baena Gave Fans a Glimpse of His Bodybuilding Debut

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Joe Baena may be the son of Arnold Schwarzenegger, but he is certainly forging his own path in the competitive bodybuilding business. The 29-year-old recently made his debut at the INBA PNBA World Cup in El Segundo, CA, reaching an impressive fifth place on the natural stage. And, for anyone who is aspiring to compete in the future, Baena chronicled his first pro outing for an insightful glimpse.

“Each photo has a great story of what it is like to be a competitor at a bodybuilding show,” posted Baena for his 895,000 Instagram followers, providing all the backstage goings on during the World Cup on November 7.

Earlier this year, the young upstart dominated in the Men’s Physique category of the NPC Classic Physique and Open, during his amateur debut, and then went to earn his pro card at the INBA Iron Gladiator event a week later on April 4.

Sharing his feelings as he arrived for the World Cup, Baena said, “Tan on, nerves high, and just trying to mentally prepare for the day ahead. Excited to see the carbs doing their work and that the abs are still there after two meals.”

Sharing an image of the changing room, Baena explained that before each competitor gets under the spotlight, they like to watch the other athletes first. “Seeing the guys in the other classes is always very exciting,” he wrote. “As you can see new things in their posing routines and styles. Everyone brings their individual personalities to the stage.”

Half an hour before his own routine, Baena began to carb up. “About 20 to 30 minutes before stepping on the stage, I’m getting my last light carbs in to fill up the muscles and look as pumped as possible,” he shared. “A couple rice cakes and a little honey drizzle does just the trick.”

Then comes “The Pump Up” to get the blood flowing into the muscles. “There’s no gym or equipment provided for most bodybuilding competitions, so you have to bring your own resistance bands or get some help from another competitor backstage,” explained Baena. “The camaraderie was amazing and everyone was just so excited to be there.”

For this detailed prepper, being specific about which muscles to pump is highly important. “You gotta make sure you pump up the right muscles, especially the ones that are lacking or need the most volume to present,” he shared. “For me, I know my arms aren’t the biggest, so I always put a little extra effort into pumping up the biceps and triceps.”

“The first thing when you step out on stage is you all lineup and basically square up next to each other,” said the competitor. “Presenting yourself in the best way possible is important along with standing out from the other competitors. After you’ve all lined up and done the mandatory poses it’s time for the pose down! You all get as close to the judges as possible and flex off together. Standing next to each other, hitting all your favorite poses and trying to present yourself as the largest, most ripped and best-looking competitor out there. Occasionally going pose for pose or just doing your own thing, you want to attract the judge’s attention as much as possible.”

The posing routine is the “last but definitely not least” aspect of the competition, wrote Baena. “The posing routine is my favorite part of the whole process. The artistry aspect of bodybuilding is what I think makes the sport so great. Building your body up to be statue-like and choreographing a routine that emulates and shows the aesthetic and beauty of the body.”

Having flexed for all that he was worth at the World Cup, Baena explained that with 11 competitors in his category, “It was extremely nerve-racking, standing there waiting for my name to get called out. My goal going into the show was to get into the top five so when I heard my name get called at fifth place it was a huge relief. I achieved what I signed out for and could finally think forward about getting a burger. Of course, the dream is to win the show and be the number one overall, but it all comes in due time and with the right amount of work. This was only my first pro show, and I couldn’t be more proud of myself. This is my first year competing with my first show being the end of March, the second show been the week after, and this being only my third show. A lot of the guys I competed with have been competing for many years now, so it is great motivation to be able to stand up and stack up next to them.”

Finally, Baena indulges in a well-earned meal. But what did he eat? “The Apple Pan,” he revealed. “Definitely one of the best burgers in LA. Had to celebrate at the Apple Pan for my first meal post competition. I ordered two burgers and two slices of pie. Somehow, even after eating all that I still had room for more.”

Glowing after “The Champion’s Pie,” Baena said, “I’m a huge pie lover and having been on prep during many weddings, my birthday, and other celebrations (where) I had to skip on many desserts, this pie tasted incredible, but I will say achieving a goal you set out for is a lot sweeter than any cheat meal.”

And that’s just as well, because soon begins the prep for Baena’s next competition.

The S&P 500 is an index that tracks the 500 largest publicly traded companies in the United States, weighted by market capitalization. It includes Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia, Alphabet (Google), Meta, Berkshire Hathaway, and approximately 493 other companies that collectively represent about 80% of the total U.S. stock market value.

The index is maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices, which periodically adds and removes companies based on criteria including market cap (must exceed ~$18 billion), profitability, liquidity, and domicile. When a company is added to the S&P 500, every index fund tracking it automatically buys shares — and vice versa when companies are removed.

An S&P 500 index fund is a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund (ETF) that holds all 500 stocks in the same proportions as the index. Instead of picking individual stocks, you buy one fund and instantly own a piece of every major U.S. company. The fund mechanically replicates the index — no stock picking, no market timing, no overpaid fund managers.

The data is overwhelming. Over any 15-year period, approximately 92% of actively managed large-cap funds underperform the S&P 500 after fees, according to the SPIVA scorecard. Over 20 years, that number exceeds 95%. The reasons are simple: active fund managers charge 0.50% to 1.50% in annual fees, they generate taxable trading activity, and they cannot consistently pick winners.

Warren Buffett bet $1 million that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a selection of hedge funds over 10 years. He won decisively — the index fund returned 125.8% vs 36.0% for the hedge fund basket. As Buffett has said: "By periodically investing in an index fund, the know-nothing investor can actually outperform most investment professionals."

The top S&P 500 index funds deliver nearly identical performance because they all track the same index. The differences come down to expense ratio, minimum investment, fund structure (ETF vs mutual fund), and tax efficiency. Here is a detailed comparison of the five most popular options.

The most popular S&P 500 ETF and the default recommendation for most FI seekers. At 0.03% expense ratio, a $500,000 investment costs just $150 per year in fees. VOO is tax-efficient due to the ETF structure and Vanguard's patented heartbeat trade process, which minimizes capital gains distributions. Fractional shares are available at most brokerages.

The lowest-cost S&P 500 fund available at 0.015% — half the cost of VOO. No minimum investment requirement makes it ideal for beginners. As a mutual fund, you can set up automatic investments in exact dollar amounts (e.g., $500/month). FXAIX is an excellent choice if your brokerage is Fidelity.

BlackRock's S&P 500 ETF with a 0.03% expense ratio, matching VOO. Functionally identical performance. Slightly different creation/redemption mechanics than VOO but the practical difference for individual investors is negligible. A strong alternative if you prefer iShares or trade through a brokerage that offers commission-free iShares ETFs.

The oldest and most heavily traded S&P 500 ETF, launched in 1993. SPY is the most liquid ETF in the world, making it the preferred choice for active traders. However, its 0.0945% expense ratio is over three times higher than VOO or IVV. For long-term FI investors, VOO or IVV are better choices. SPY's structure as a unit investment trust also makes it slightly less tax-efficient than VOO.

Schwab's mutual fund offering at 0.02% expense ratio with no minimum investment. Like FXAIX, the mutual fund structure allows automatic dollar-amount investing. An excellent choice for Schwab customers building automated investment plans.

Investing in an S&P 500 fund takes less than 15 minutes:

For retirement accounts (401k, IRA), look for the S&P 500 index fund option within your plan. It may have a different name (e.g., "Large Cap Index Fund" or "Institutional S&P 500") but will track the same index.

The total stock market index (tracked by VTI/VTSAX/FSKAX) holds approximately 3,600 stocks compared to the S&P 500's 500. The additional 3,100 stocks are mid-cap and small-cap companies. Here is how they compare:

Historically, the performance difference between the two is minimal — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year in either direction. The S&P 500 has outperformed in periods when large-cap growth stocks dominate. The total market has outperformed when small and mid-cap stocks lead. Over 20+ year periods, the returns converge closely.

The FI community's honest answer: it does not matter much which you choose. Investing $25,500 per year in VOO or VTI will produce nearly identical outcomes over 20 years. Consistency and contribution amount matter far more than the choice between S&P 500 and total market.

S&P 500 index funds typically yield 1.2% to 1.6% in annual dividends. In a tax-advantaged account (401k, IRA, Roth), dividends compound tax-free. In a taxable account, qualified dividends from S&P 500 funds are taxed at the favorable long-term capital gains rate (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income).

ETFs (VOO, IVV) are generally more tax-efficient than mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) in taxable accounts because ETFs rarely distribute capital gains. Vanguard's mutual funds are an exception — their patented ETF share class structure gives Vanguard mutual funds ETF-like tax efficiency. For taxable brokerage accounts, VOO or VFIAX (Vanguard's mutual fund version) are the most tax-efficient choices.

The most common mistake with S&P 500 index funds is waiting for the "right time" to invest. Research from Vanguard shows that investing a lump sum immediately outperforms dollar-cost averaging about two-thirds of the time, because markets go up more often than they go down. Missing just the 10 best trading days over a 20-year period can cut your returns nearly in half. If you have money to invest, the data overwhelmingly says to invest it now — not next week, not after the next pullback, not when it "feels right."

Open an account at Vanguard (for VOO/VFIAX), Fidelity (for FXAIX), or Schwab (for SWPPX). All three offer commission-free trading on their own index funds, excellent customer service, and robust retirement account options. You can also buy any of these funds at most brokerages.

ETFs (VOO, IVV) trade like stocks at real-time prices and are more tax-efficient in taxable accounts. Mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) allow automatic dollar-amount investing and are better for set-it-and-forget-it contribution schedules. For retirement accounts, either works equally well.

Transfer cash to your brokerage account and buy your chosen fund. Start with whatever you have — there is no minimum too small. FXAIX and SWPPX have $0 minimums, and VOO can be purchased in fractional shares at most brokerages for as little as $1.

Automate monthly or per-paycheck contributions. This removes emotion from the process and ensures consistent dollar-cost averaging. Most brokerages let you schedule recurring purchases of mutual funds. For ETFs, some brokerages offer automatic ETF purchases as well.

If you hold other asset classes (bonds, international), rebalance once per year to maintain your target allocation. Otherwise, do nothing — do not check daily prices, do not sell during downturns, and do not chase performance. The S&P 500 has recovered from every crash in history. Time in the market beats timing the market.

Fidelity 500 Index Fund (FXAIX) has the lowest expense ratio at 0.015%. Schwab S&P 500 Index Fund (SWPPX) is next at 0.02%. VOO and IVV tie at 0.03%. All four are excellent — the fee difference between FXAIX (0.015%) and VOO (0.03%) on a $500,000 portfolio is just $75 per year. Choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage.

VOO is better for long-term investors. It charges 0.03% vs SPY's 0.0945%, saving you about $325 per year on a $500,000 portfolio. VOO is also more tax-efficient due to its ETF share class structure. SPY's advantage is liquidity for active trading, which long-term index investors do not need. For buy-and-hold FI investing, VOO is the clear winner.

Either is an excellent choice. The S&P 500 covers approximately 80% of the U.S. stock market by value. A total market fund adds mid-cap and small-cap stocks for fuller diversification. Over long periods, performance is nearly identical — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year. The FI community consensus is that the best fund is the one you will consistently invest in without overthinking the decision.

As little as $1. FXAIX and SWPPX have zero minimum investments. VOO and IVV can be purchased as fractional shares at most brokerages. There is no minimum too small — starting with $50 or $100 per month and increasing contributions as your income grows is exactly how most people on the FI path begin.

The S&P 500 has returned approximately 10.3% per year on average since 1957 (including dividends). Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7.0% per year. These are long-term averages — individual years range from -38% (2008) to +38% (1995). The key is staying invested through the down years to capture the recovery gains that follow.

S&P 500 index funds carry market risk — they can lose significant value in the short term (the index dropped 34% in early 2020 and 38% in 2008). However, the S&P 500 has recovered from every decline in its history and has never lost money over any 20-year period. For investors with a 10+ year time horizon, the risk of not investing (missing out on 10% average annual returns) is far greater than the risk of temporary market declines.

S&P 500 index funds are the single most important building block for long-term wealth. With expense ratios as low as 0.015%, you keep virtually all of your returns while owning a piece of the 500 largest U.S. companies. VOO, FXAIX, IVV, and SWPPX all deliver near-identical performance — choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage and automate your contributions. The FI community has proven through thousands of real-world examples that consistent investing in a low-cost S&P 500 index fund, held for decades without panic selling, is the most reliable path to building wealth and reaching financial independence.

#8711. Why the Jefferson Curl Can Be Valuable for Some Lifters

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Repeated or prolonged spinal flexion can increase stress on the tissues around the spine. The Jefferson curl targets spinal flexion by improving spinal control and strengthening positions you might find yourself in and out of the gym.

It’s considered an obscure exercise. If you’ve never heard of or seen it, you might think it’s the latest move for giving your biceps a pump. But the Jefferson curl is far from an arm-day exercise.

The Jefferson curl ia actually lower-back move—one that contradicts almost everything known about lower-back health. To perform it, you hold a weight in front of you and slowly lower it toward the floor while flexing your spine. In other words, you round your back under load and keep bending.

End-range spinal flexion is a key reason many trainers hesitate to add the Jefferson curl to their clients’ workouts. But for the right lifter, it can mean better control, greater flexion tolerance, and improved mobility. However, if it isn’t a good fit, it can increase your injury risk.

So, should you include it in your program?

According to two strength experts, the answer is, it depends.

The Jefferson curl is a controlled exercise where you deliberately flex the spine one segment at a time while holding a light weight. From the neck down, slowly round your back through the upper, middle, and lower back as you reach toward the floor.

The goal is not to see how far you can flex, but to control spinal flexion through a range you can own while placing the entire posterior-chain tissues under tension.

Sets and reps: According to Physical Therapist Bo Babenko, start with 3 to 5 repetitions at a time, using only 15 to 20 pounds as a stretch. Emphasize taking 2 to 3 deep breaths at the bottom, with an elongated exhale to stretch the tissues involved.

Placement: After your main strength work or during a mobility session.

The Jefferson curl challenges (arguably) one of strength training’s biggest blind spots: the idea that the spine should always stay rigid. Outside of a neutral spine while lifting, your spine is designed to move. You flex to tie your shoes, pick things up, sit, reach, climb, and perform plenty of athletic movements. Avoiding spinal flexion doesn’t prepare you for those demands.

That is where the Jefferson Curl can help. When performed well, it lets you train spinal flexion rather than encountering it when fatigued or in a variable environment. The point is not to teach you to round your back during a max deadlift. The point is to recognize that spinal stiffness and spinal movement are both movement skills.

But spinal flexion is dose-dependent. Too much of anything, even water, will hurt you.

That is why this lift deserves neither a blanket ban nor a free pass.

There are some rewards with the risk, and here they are.

One of its biggest benefits is that it asks you to move the spine one segment at a time, rather than treating your entire spine as a single rigid block. That controlled flexion and extension can improve body awareness and give you more options for how you move.

The Jefferson curl also places the hamstrings, spinal erectors, and other posterior tissues under tension through a longer ROM than many strength exercises. “I believe the Jefferson curl certainly has a place,” explains Babenko. “To decompress the spine and stretch out the posterior chain.”

Most flexibility work is passive, but the Jefferson curl takes a different approach by loading the range you are trying to improve. That means the hamstrings and trunk are not just becoming more flexible; they are learning to produce and control force in that range.

If your hamstrings are tight, your spinal control disappears, or you start chasing depth without control, you’ll find out quickly. That makes the exercise useful for both mobility assessment and training.

Repeated or prolonged spinal flexion can increase creep in passive tissues such as ligaments and discs, raising the risk of lower back injury. Critics view it as an unnecessary risk. Their argument is simple: if you can improve mobility without loading end-range spinal flexion, why take the chance?

Any lifter worth their salt knows to keep their back neutral during deadlifts, squats, and rows. “Most lifters need to generate, transfer, and resist substantial forces while maintaining core stiffness and controlling spinal motion,” explains strength coach Matt Wenning. “These exercises can develop these qualities without requiring loaded end-range spinal flexion.”

Loading flexion can blur the line between a controlled mobility drill and poor technique during heavy lifting.

It’s not meant as a strength test, but some people will always try to see how much weight they can do. “I had a patient show up with back pain,” says Babenko. “She was trying to build up well over 150 pounds on the Jefferson curl, and, well, she hurt her lower back.”

Too much load increases the risk. Instead of slow, controlled segmental flexion, you get a loaded collapse with little benefit.

Hamstring stretching, hip-hinge drills, and RDLs can all enhance hamstring mobility without taking the spine through deliberate loaded flexion. That makes the Jefferson Curl optional.

There is no direct research on the Jefferson curl itself—a point backed up by Wenning.

“Direct evidence that Jefferson curls improve athletic performance, prevent low-back injuries, or outperform established strength and mobility interventions is insufficient.”

But most research focuses on spinal flexion, segmental spinal movement, flexibility training, and how spinal tissues behave under repeated or prolonged flexion.

A 2023 study comparing spinal flexion and extension exercises with more trunk movement found improvements in spinal flexibility, including finger-to-floor distance. This supports one of the Jefferson curl’s main purposes: learning to move through spinal flexion gradually rather than treating the spine as a single rigid unit.

One study found that 20 minutes of full lumbar flexion altered passive tissue contributions and increased demand on the spinal extensors afterward, meaning the extensors had to work harder after sustained flexion.

That study focused on sustained or repeated flexion exposures, not a few slow Jefferson curls. A set of five deliberate reps is not the same dose as sitting or hanging in deep flexion for 20 minutes.

No current research says spinal flexion is dangerous. “The spine can certainly flex, and spinal flexion itself is not inherently dangerous,” says Wenning

You know the pros and cons, but that doesn’t determine whether the Jefferson curl is a good fit. But this does.

The Jefferson curl sits in the moderate- high risk, moderate-reward category. The risk comes from loaded spinal flexion. That does not mean flexion is dangerous, but it does mean the dose matters. Too much load, range, fatigue, or volume can turn this mobility drill into unnecessary stress on the spine’s passive tissues.

“Jefferson curls offer limited advantages for most lifters,” says Wenning. “Particularly when more established exercises can address the same training goals with greater specificity and more controllable loading.”

The reward is that the Jefferson curl can train something most strength programs avoid: controlled spinal flexion. It can improve segmental spinal control, reveal mobility restrictions, and load the posterior chain through a long range of motion. For healthy lifters who tolerate flexion well, it can be useful.

The biggest factor in the risk-to-reward equation is intent. If you treat the Jefferson curl like a max-strength lift, the risk climbs fast. If you treat it like a light, slow, carefully progressed mobility-strength drill, the equation changes.

The reward isn’t massive, and the risk isn’t trivial, which is why this exercise belongs in the “use with a reason” category rather than the “everyone should do it” one.

The Jefferson curl isn’t one-size-fits-all, and people have opinions on both sides of the spectrum. Critics see a rounded spine and assume danger. Supporters sometimes swing too far the other way and act like controlled flexion makes the spine bulletproof.

Many exercises have a larger margin for error, like biceps curls, while others have a smaller margin, like the Jefferson curl. That means you should approach this exercise with caution.

But for the right lifter, used with light loads and a slow progression, it can be one way to train a position most strength programs avoid altogether. Spinal flexion sometimes happens, so it helps to be prepared.

The problem isn’t always spinal flexion; it’s treating flexion without respect.

He still surfs. He still trains jiujitsu and Muay Thai. And the actor still lifts and still enjoys putting himself in situations that demand something from him physically.

What has changed at 40 is the way he prepares for all of it.

There was a time when Eastwood could train hard, wake up sore, and trust that his body would bounce back. Now, he is far more interested in staying mobile, pain-free, and ready for whatever he wants to do outside the gym.

Over the last five years, Eastwood says that shift has become increasingly intentional.

“Recovery is probably the biggest difference,” Eastwood told M&F. “I think I’d probably put it number one. I listen to my body more and take more care in my recovery than I ever did in my 20s or 30s.”

This doesn’t mean that he’s less serious about training, it just means Eastwood’s objective has evolved. Looking like a capable athlete has given way to a much more important goal: staying physically capable.

“Obviously I want to be strong, but I also want to be really flexible and limber and be able to react to whatever the world throws at you, where you’re not going to pull something or you’re not going to hurt yourself.”

Eastwood ,who’s latest film, Lucky Strike, is now streaming on Hulu, used to organize his gym work around the familiar bodybuilding split—chest, back, and different muscle groups on different days.

Now he prefers training that puts his entire body to work.

“I think [now I’m] just a little bit more focused on holistic workouts,” Eastwood said. “I’m far more focused now on my core, just because of body pain and how your body feels, and all the things that feel better, which kind of stem out from your core.”

When he isn’t working on a film, Eastwood says he typically lifts three or four times per week, splitting those sessions between gym and home workouts. He also tries to fit in Muay Thai or jiujitsu. Yoga has become a constant.

Eastwood says there isn’t a day that passes where he doesn’t do some version of it, often half an hour in the morning and another later in the day.

When he is filming, the expectations change.

A 6 a.m. call time might require a 5 a.m. gym session. Long production days can already be physically taxing, so those workouts become less about progress. It’s an evolution in the thinking that every training session needs to prove something. Eastwood still trains hard, but there isn’t much value now in forcing his body through movements that no longer feel worth the risk.

“You’re spending a lot of time on your feet, and it’s typically physical,” Eastwood said. “So you’re kind of just doing a little more maintenance when you’re working. You’re not getting the gains that you might get if you’re not working.”

The gym has never been the only testing grounds for Eastwood.

Surfing, martial arts, and hiking are still a part of his life, and each demands something slightly different from his body.

It’s a large part why strength alone no longer satisfies him.

“If I want to continue to do jiujitsu, and I want to do Muay Thai, and I want to continue to surf, I’ve got to take care of my body,” Eastwood says. “Which means strength, flexibility, and mobility. I’ve got to kind of do all these things, or my body is going to get trashed doing these sports.”

Those activities also provide him with feedback that a mirror will miss. A stiff body doesn’t perform well on a surfboard. Poor mobility isn’t less obvious when someone is trying to control you on a mat. Carrying unnecessary soreness into either activity can turn something meant to be enjoyable into a problem quickly.

Eastwood hasn’t lost his appetite for these passions that come with risk. However, age has made him more selective about which risks within those passions are worth taking.

That means foregoing chasing a massive surf or testing himself on the mat against whoever wants to go the hardest. When he was younger, these thoughts might have not even entered into his thinking.

Now, it’s more thoughtful. He still wants the challenge, to compete with himself, and to feel capable. These activities are just no longer a barometer for his toughness.

Ask him what physical quality matters more now than it did at 25, and the answer is an understandable one.

“Flexibility,” Eastwood says. “Flexibility and just not being in pain. If you can take care of your body where you’re not in pain all the time, that’s really valuable.”

One of the biggest shifts for Eastwood is the attention to recovery.

Yoga, sauna sessions, and Epsom salt baths have all been part of his routine for years, but sleep has become especially important as both his training and work demands have changed.

“Just getting a good night’s sleep, I value it so much more now,” Eastwood says.

10 to 15-hour set days require focus, energy, and often physical effort. Arriving not fully rested often produces immediate consequences.

“I can’t do the job that I do well and focus if I haven’t had a great night’s sleep,” he said.

His approach to nutrition is also uncomplicated. Eastwood says he follows a Mediterranean-style diet built around whole foods, including fish, red meat, grains, and plenty of vegetables. He also refuses to turn an occasional bag of chips or dessert into a moral crisis.

“I don’t make it some hard and fast rule that you have to do,” he says. “I just think those just get a little too rigid.”

His preference for simplicity also played a role in why Eastwood became a co-owner of North Performance.

Eastwood says longtime friend Mike Lucas shared the frustration of trying to travel while managing individual supplements. Both men wanted something easier to maintain without pretending a supplement could replace the fundamentals.

“You still have to work out. You have to get good sleep and have good recovery,” he says. “Having good supplements is just going to help those things. The basics are the basics. They don’t change regardless.”

When he is filming, Eastwood says North is part of his morning routine, but the rest of his priorities remain the same.

He still has to eat well. He still has to move. If the day is packed and there are only 25 minutes for himself, he’ll find somewhere to fit in exercise, yoga, or mobility work. Everything beyond that is what he calls “extra credit.”

It’s a simplicity that defines fitness at 40 for him.

Looking strong doesn’t mean anything if his back is aching or his body is too tight to do the things all of his training was meant to prepare him for.

The goal going into the next decade is simple: keep enough strength to be useful, maintain mobility to move well, and have enough durability to keep saying yes to the things he enjoys.

“I think fit is more how you feel and less aesthetic,” Eastwood said. “[Looking good] is great, but if you’re in pain because you’re not doing it correctly, then who gives a shit about what you look like?”

#8705. Science Finds that Dairy May Not Lead to Excess Fat as First Thought

For a long time, the public were cautioned against regular dairy food consumption, but a recent study from the University of Toronto, published by the Journal of Nutrition, appears to show that frequently delving into eggs, milk, and cheeses, could actually benefit your health and won’t make you fat. Here’s why.

In the ‘70s, a war on saturated fat consumption encouraged us to avoid products like whole milk, butter, and cheese because of the high levels that they contain. Then wellness culture in the new millennium further derailed the case for diary, citing inflammation, acne, and disrupted hormones on this food stuff. Of course, some people are lactose intolerant, and have problems processing dairy food, but the Toronto study has challenged the campaign against dairy, with some surprisingly edible results.

74 overweight adults undertook a 12-week study and were randomly assigned to one of three groups:

All the groups were counseled on healthy eating, so that they could manage their food intake. At the completion of the trial, the team took measurements including body weight, composition, cholesterol, blood markers, and metabolic health.

In both of the regular high fat dairy eating groups, the participants experienced improvements in their blood pressure while consuming a greater amount of protein, calcium, and vitamin D than the first group. Importantly, neither their waistlines nor BMI suffered. “Those that had three servings of dairy didn’t have adverse levels of blood cholesterol or lipids or evidence of insulin resistance,” explained Gerald Harvey Anderson, who was the lead author and works in the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Toronto.”

With full-fat dairy containing more saturated fat than reduced fat products, how could this be? The experts believe that dairy’s combination of fats and protein is what makes it a positive food. “With dairy products, it’s got two proteins, casein and whey, that are bound together with fat and with nutrients mixed in,” said Anderson. The “Dairy Matrix Hypothesis” suggests that the physical structure of dairy determines how the body processes its nutrient profile.

Of course, ice cream, milkshakes, and other treats that contain a ton saturated fat as well as massive amounts of sugar is a different story, but the Toronto study said its results with natural dairy products showed that  “Neither treatment nor time affected waist circumference, fat and fat-free mass, resting metabolic rate, fasting blood cholesterol, and urine creatinine.” The team concluded that “Frequent and daily consumption of full-fat dairy as part of a healthy diet is consistent with CFG (Canada’s Food Guide).”

This news also adds to another promising benefit of dairy, that was reported earlier this year. The American Academy of Neurology showed that those who regularly ate high fat cheese presented a 13% lower risk of dementia overall, and a 29% risk of vascular dementia. Cream was also associated with a 16% lower risk of all-type dementias.

The Toronto study found dairy to be a significant source of magnesium and potassium to boot. “The results align with the conclusion of an expert group that there is no evidence to support the avoidance of high-fat dairy in diets,” it said.

#8701. How to Correctly Add Forward and Reverse Lunges into Your Legday Workouts

When it comes to strengthening your legs, building muscles in your lower body, and improving all-round balance, lunges are a great move to lean into, but what is the difference between the forward and backward lunge? In a recent Instagram post, IFBB Pro, endurance athlete, and transformation coach Petar Klancir demonstrated the details.

Take a step in the right direction with these unique lunges.

“What is the difference?” asked The Croatian Colossus, who has built an Instagram base of more than one million followers thanks to his informative training videos. In essence, both of these variations are compound movements, so they tax multiple muscle groups at the same time. Whether you lunge forward or backward, you’ll be working the quads, hamstrings, calves and core. You will also flex the hips either way. But what does change is the emphasis placed on each muscle, and how they build your legs in different ways, as Klancir showed.

“Front step lunges target the quads more, due to the mechanics of the exercise,” explained Klancir. “The emphasis is on stepping forward, which requires the quads to control the impact of the foot’s landing. And there is a high degree of flexion.”

The quads take the majority of the load with forward lunges, because the mechanics that Klancir mentioned, require the quads to negotiate the lowering, and then lift your center of mass and return you to the starting position.

Tip: To avoid knee stress, be sure not to step out too far forward on the lunge. At the bottom of the lunge, your knee should only just be ahead of your chin.

“Back step lunges target the glutes and hamstrings,” said Klancir. “Due to emphasized hip-hinge movement.”

Reverse lunges are often considered easier to execute, because the front foot remains flat on the floor, providing a greater foundation and less requirement for core balance. They are also less stressful on the knee, because the load is shifted by the hamstrings and glutes to a greater extent than the quads.

Tip: Keep the front foot stable by keeping knee over ankle at all times.

For a complete leg blaster, your can try both movements by focusing on form. Then, once you are comfortable with your foot placings, you can build in some additional hypertrophy by adding a pair of dumbbells to the overall load.

Sam Retford, who is known to millions of Outlander: Blood of my Blood fans as Dougal MacKenzie, looks very comfortable on a show that requires him to navigate the unpredictable Scottish terrain, and there’s a good reason why. Not only does Retford love the great outdoors, but he’s also vastly experienced in a variety of skills. From riding a horse to cave diving, or rucking to offroad bike racing, this actor is as able as they come. So, staying still for just a second, Retford tells M&F why Outlander is such a personal and professional high, and how his favorite pastimes informed the role and his physique.

Now living in Glasgow, Retford’s love of adventure was passed down through blood. “My mum was a proper ranch cowgirl,” says Retford, who was born in Australia. “She has ridden horses all around the world, so she taught me to ride.” The star says that he loves nothing more than to get a bunch of pals together and go exploring, and has recently biked in The Himalayas, crossed the rivers of Amazonia, and cave dived around the United Kingdom. When the news came down that Retford would take up the role of Dougal MacKenzie and battle it out in 18th century Scotland, he was understandably all-in.

While most actors stay within the confines of a gym to ready for their roles, Retford added to his indoor workouts by acclimatizing to his new filming environment. As War Chieftain Dougal MacKenzie, Retford wanted to get a feel for the rugged highland landscape. “I wanted this guy to be physically capable,” he tells M&F, noting that he practiced rucking up and down the hills with a weighted backpack. “Even going and sleeping in the heather. I really wanted to build a physique capable of doing these long winter treks, but remain flexible enough to be agile in battle, to be strong enough to carry heavy loads—so everything had to be functional.”

The type of physique required to hunt and survive in the wilds of Scotland would not require a six-pack or be akin to an underwear model, so Retford wanted to build his character with authenticity. “I wanted him to have a big strong back and strong legs,” says the actor. “Okay, he can, lift but can he swing a sword around as well?”

Sam Retford earned a second-degree black belt in Taekwondo in his youth and understands the importance of exercise for agility and injury prevention. He also likes to swing the Indian Mace Bells for balance. But in the gym, his workouts include plyometric moves that require explosive power, such as box jumps. When lifting weights, the star focuses on time under tension and replicating proper form while squatting or making an overhead press.

The star also introduced instability into his lifting elements, for example with elevated platforms or unilateral movements in order to prepare him for the uneven ground outside. Still, the actor says that ultimately, the best way to prepare for his sprinting and fighting scenes was to run in the woods and climb trees. “Just moving about on set and staying warm,” he recalls.

Fans of Outlander: Blood of My Blood will have noticed that the physicality has leveled up in Season 2. For example, Dougal MacKenzie becomes embroiled in a serious battle in Episode 5 and must be rescued from being trapped underwater in Episode 6. Fortunately, the enthusiastic adventurer is more than comfortable with holding his breath. In Episode 2, Dougal also found himself in a fistfight with Brian Fraser (played by Jamie Roy).

Retford wants people to know, however, that progress is individual, takes time, and is not as easy as some social media accounts would like you to believe. He is also keen to point out that it takes a team of stunt coordinators, special effects wizards, lighting, and audio technicians to make any actor appear at their best. “You’ll notice I do quite a lot of shield work and headbutting, as opposed to sword fighting,” he explains. “That’s because I’m a lefty, and my right-handed combat is not very good. So, I have to keep the sword well and truly sheathed for a lot of it, to not cut anyone’s fingers off!”

Blood of My Blood no doubt the dream job for this thrill seeker. “Just to be out there in the cold, in the thick of it, running around, swinging swords. I mean, it’s a beautiful type of physicality, and it’s an amazing thing to call your job. So, I try never to complain. I’m always grateful.”

With Retford more than open to battling through a third season of Outlander: Blood of My Blood, the talented performer is also producing an upcoming documentary in Uganda and also has an eye on traveling to Mexico. “The key is to just say yes to crazy things,” he beams.

Season 2 of Outlander: Blood of My Blood premieres can be streamed via Starz.

When an American joins any branch of the United States military, they repeat an Oath of Enlistment to make the commitment official.

I do solemnly swear that I will support and defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic; that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the same; and that I will obey the orders of the President of the United States and the orders of the officers appointed over me, according to regulations and the Uniform Code of Military Justice. So help me God.

On November 12, 2026, 64 men and women ventured to the Rayburn Office Building of the U.S. Capitol to take that oath and enter the Air Force and Space Force Delayed Entry Program. This swearing-in was the climactic moment of the second annual National Signing Day, an event hosted by the Air Force’s 317th Recruiting Squadron.

The concept of this event came from retired Air Force Master Sergeant and M&F Senior Military Editor Rob Wilkins, who said the idea was inspired by watching his son’s announcement for where he was going to play college football.

Wilkins explained, “I was watching this take place and thought to myself, ‘We should be doing something like this for the military.’”

Wilkins’ idea became a reality thanks to several people he worked with, including Congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska, Air Force Senior Master Sergeant Matt London, and others within the 317th. It made what was already a significant moment in the lives of these future service members even more memorable for them and their families who accompanied them.

Staff Sergeant Maddalyn Secrist was one of the recruiters on-hand for the event and was very involved with making the 2026 event a success. Secrist shared that having this on Capitol Hill took something local to the DMV area and gave it a sense of national awareness.

“It gives it more of a public view and gives these Airmen and Guardians the recognition that they need.”

Prior to their swearing-in, each person’s name was announced as they went to the table to sign on the dotted line and have their photo taken, reminiscent of the high school athletes who announce where they will play in college. Each new recruit was cheered by family, friends, and fellow American citizens as well as members of the Trump Administration like Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Military Community and Family Policy Stephen B. Simmons and recently appointed Executive Director of the President’s Council on Sports, Fitness, and Nutrition, Jacob Phillips.

Among those new recruits was Kevin McAllister, who was one of the older members of the group. At 35 years old and with a family tradition of service, McAllister knew that being physically prepared was a must, which is why he committed to longer runs and more intense training in preparation for the day. He also had to mentally dedicate himself to the process and suggests others who may be considering service do the same.

“I had to find the right mindset. There was a lot of running and calisthenics, but it taught me how to use different muscles,” he said. Even though he was fully prepared to take the oath, being in the Capitol definitely added a level of gravitas to the day.

“We are surrounded by the place where laws are made. The history of the United States is here. Just getting to add this to my family legacy makes me look at the flag differently.”

Bacon addressed the group and offered words of gratitude and encouragement that could be traced back to his own 30-year military career before entering the House of Representatives. He also shared wisdom that could be beneficial to people from all walks of life, whether they are in the military or not.

“Be the best at the job you’re going to get,” Bacon advised. “Learn that job inside and out so your boss can go, ‘I can trust that person.’”

There is no official word on future Signing Day events, but Secrist hopes that recruiters can use highlights or social media posts from this day to inspire their own applicants and create a similar experience to showcase why being a part of the Joint Force is so special.

Secrist said, “We think other recruiters can see this event and get inspired to do something like this in their own squadrons.”

To learn more about the Air Force or Space Force, go to airforce.com or spaceforce.mil.
