#8657. Unused Bank Accounts Go to the State – Move Money Yourself Once a Year

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

An unused bank account can lose money to inactivity fees, and after three to five years without activity from you, the bank must turn the balance over to your state as unclaimed property. Make a deposit or withdrawal yourself at least once a year, or move the money to an account you use and close the old account.

The accounts at risk are the ones you rarely think about, like a savings account from your first job, a second checking account, or a child’s account no one checks.

An account can earn interest every month and still count as inactive, because banks and state law look for activity you start, such as a deposit, a withdrawal, or contact with the bank. Some states also count a login, and some don’t count a recurring transfer you set up, so make the deposit or withdrawal yourself.

Until the money goes to the state, the bank can also charge a recurring inactivity fee if your account agreement allows it, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency notes. Say a $1,200 savings account from your first job earns no interest and charges $5 a month after a year without activity. In a state that waits three years, $120 in fees comes out before the bank sends the remaining $1,080 to the state. In one that waits five, the fees reach $240 and the state gets $960.

The state holds that money for you until you claim it. To find an old account that may already be there, search every state you’ve lived in.

An account you don’t need is better closed. Move its balance to the account you use, then close the old account, so the bank can’t charge it a fee or send it to the state.

For an account you keep, update your address with the bank. Before the money goes to the state, the bank usually has to try to reach you, and some banks mail that notice to the last address they have. Then look up in the account’s fee schedule how long it can go without activity before an inactivity fee starts.

Set a calendar reminder to make a deposit or withdrawal yourself before that point and at least once a year, even $5 moved to your main account.

#8656. You’re Not Rich — And Neither Am I

Warren Buffett has spent decades telling anyone who’ll listen that he lives simply. Same house in Omaha he bought in 1958 for $31,500. No mansion, no car collection, nothing flashy.

He eats at McDonald’s, drinks Coke by the case and has said more than once that a person could live like him on a fraction of his fortune and lose nothing that actually matters.

A physician two decades into a cardiology career already has a six-bedroom house on two acres with a three-car garage. Something that would put Buffett’s Omaha home to shame.

But Buffett flies private. On his personal jet. Which he owns. (He also owns the company that made his plane just FYI).

That cardiologist couldn’t touch a private jet with a ten-foot pole. Not on a $600,000 salary carrying a jumbo mortgage, two kids in private school and a home equity line he opened for the kitchen renovation.

Buffett could write a check for that physician’s entire house and still have money left for the furniture.

My point is, quantifying wealth is not a black and white endeavor. McMansions don’t lead to private jets. And “modest” lifestyles don’t rule them out.

It’s a strange world we live in. One where most people are blindly chasing perception rather than what actually matters.

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

Also read: Why Most Doctors Retire With Too Much Money (And What to Do About It)

The Federal Reserve’s Survey of Consumer Finances states that the median American household net worth is $192,084. The average is more than 5x that at $1.06 million due to a relatively small number of extremely wealthy households that pull the average up.

Physicians, as a group, are ahead of that median and the gap keeps widening.

Medscape’s 2026 Physician Wealth & Debt Report found that 24% of physicians now report a family net worth of $5 million or more — largely thanks to stock market gains and rising home values.

However, the same report makes it clear this wealth isn’t evenly spread. The physicians in the $5 million group are mostly in procedure-based specialties which have the highest earning ceilings to begin with.

Plenty of physicians in lower-paying specialties spend most of a career well short of that mark despite carrying the same title, the same debt load at the start, and the same years of deferred income during training.

All physicians start with some sort of student debt — small or big — regardless of specialty. The median medical school debt for the class of 2025 is $215,000, not counting undergraduate loans.

Or any non-education debt, credit cards and car loans that tend to accumulate during residency for that matter.

A newly minted attending earning six figures can still have a negative net worth. It takes years to pay down debt and bring it up to zero.

Years more to enter the black. Those early years are the reason for the gap between a $5-million-net-worth radiologist and a physician twenty years into practice who still hasn’t crossed seven figures.

Let’s talk about two doctors who have the same degree and the same starting debt but two very different philosophies on spending money.

For this example we’ll play into the most common stereotypes doctors have faced — and fought hard to shed — for years.

Dr. Flashy “invests” in a new Range Rover every three years. He’s got a lake house two hours outside the city, a boat he uses maybe four weekends a summer — if the weather cooperates.

And surprisingly to some, he’s not broke. He makes real money and a part of his lifestyle is funded from that same income.

Almost every single one of these major purchases generates its own follow-on bill which continues to recur exponentially.

The Range Rover’s routine maintenance costs more than a lot of people’s monthly car payment. The lake house needs a new roof eventually, landscaping every season, comes with a property tax bill that rises every time the county reassesses and someone to physically check on it every time a storm rolls through three states away.

The boat comes with marina fees, winterizing and a marine mechanic who bills by the hour. Buying something nice is the equivalent of signing up for a subscription with an indefinite term and a rising rate.

This is called the hedonic treadmill. Once someone upgrades something in their life, the old version stops being satisfying, permanently. And the new version only delivers that same satisfaction for as long as the novelty lasts.

Eventually the purchase itself becomes pointless. It was the feeling of upgrading that felt good but that feeling fades fast enough that the next upgrade becomes necessary just to get back to the baseline.

Luxury goods are sneakily good at triggering this because so much of what they deliver is the status attached to the price tag. Any functional improvement or value they bring is usually beside the point.

Dr. Flashy’s income may be large. He might even be a neurosurgeon earning $829,161. But at some point his lifestyle needs additional funding to keep up. That’s when he turns to financing.

Eventually, the bank becomes something he is increasingly dependent on.

To be clear, I’m not speculating on his character. Forbes reports that the highest-income American households, those above the 90th percentile, carry the largest average credit card balances of any income group (over $11,000 on average) despite being the group least likely to carry a balance at all.

So data shows us that the people who look the most financially comfortable are disproportionately dependent on revolving debt to stay there. Not all high earners are predisposed to open lines of credit, but when they do, they tend to rack up more of it because the lifestyle they’re financing costs more to maintain than anyone else’s.

The thing is, money is finite even with a large income. Spending more of it means you need more just to sustain the spending at its current level. And that treadmill doesn’t slow down as the years go by.

Dr. Net-Worth has the same income as Dr. Flashy. Same specialty, even, same call schedule, same patient panel.

But Dr. Net-Worth drives a Honda he’s had since fellowship. It’s got a cracked bumper he keeps meaning to fix. He lives in a house that’s nice but completely unremarkable from the street — not something you’ll see featured in Architectural Digest.

Still, his investment accounts feature a sum that would make your eyes water. No one except him and his accountant know what it is.

We have come to perceive net worth as some concrete evaluation of a person’s wealth. But it really isn’t. In fact, the more zeroes it has, the less real it is.

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

I mean, this year we saw Elon Musk become (briefly) the first ever trillionaire. But does that mean he’s got a Scrooge McDuck vault full of gold coins stacked to the ceiling?  Well, he might — but he won’t have an actual trillion in there to dive into and swim around in.

That number is mostly the market’s opinion of his equity stakes on a given day. An opinion that can — and does — swing by tens of billions of dollars before lunch and back again by dinner. All without a single dollar changing hands or a single decision on his part.

Dr. Net-Worth’s number works the same way just on a smaller scale. Most of it lives in a house he’s still making payments on every month, a retirement account he can’t touch before a certain age lest he trigger a penalty, and an ever-growing brokerage account he could never imagine drawing from.

All of it is his. Yet, he doesn’t use a dollar of it beyond the mortgage payment and the grocery bill. He’s rich! Technically. Psychologically, it might as well be someone else’s money.

You can’t fault him for being this way. Sometimes it’s just temperament. Plenty of high earners are simply frugal by nature, genuinely uninterested in the lake house and actually happier to keep the Honda running for another hundred thousand miles. Nothing wrong with that. At least Dr. Net-Worth doesn’t need rescuing from the life he has chosen.

But sometimes the hesitation to spend stems from fear. Constant worry that the money could vanish overnight, that one bad market year or one malpractice suit could erase everything you’ve built.

That spending on anything beyond the bare essentials is an invitation for disaster to strike. Dr. Net-Worth worked his butt off to build a financial fortress that classifies him as financially free. Yet the day may never come when he actually gets to taste that freedom.

Dr. Flashy is one bad year/one slow season at the practice/one unexpected repair bill on the boat away from a very uncomfortable conversation with a lender.

Dr. Net-Worth has already won the game by any objective measure but refuses to enjoy it.

Financial planner Derek Hagen says that money that isn’t pointed at anything in particular just accumulates, and accumulation without a purpose behind it isn’t freedom. Dr. Net-Worth has plenty of money with no real purpose for it.

Dr.  Flashy has an answer: status and visible proof that he has “made it”. But his answer costs more to maintain with every passing year, never quite delivering the sense of arrival he’s chasing.

There’s no handbook that outlines exactly where the divide between enjoying the money and hoarding it is. And anyone who claims there is one wants to sell you something.

You, the physician reading this, are probably nothing like Dr. Flashy or Dr. Net-Worth. And asking which one is better or worse isn’t the point either.

Your money, no matter how it is accumulated or spent on, deserves to be used to fund a life you chose on purpose. Not one assembled by accident out of habit, fear or…what the neighbors might notice.

Buffett kept the house and bought the plane because both of those choices added up to a life he actually wanted. That is rich (of course being worth $144.6 billion doesn’t hurt).

Everything else is just perception in a strange world that will never stop raising the bar.

Good, thoughtful article, Thanks! I have to agree about the ongoing obligations that the treadmill gets us into. I have to identify with Dr Net-Worth, but rather than having no purpose, I would say that one real, tangible benefit he has is security. Knowing he or his spouse can incur some life altering accident or illness and not affect the well being of the rest of the family. As an example my mother in law has dementia and has been in memory care for a decade. Her current bill is 200k per year. She and her husband planned very well and regardless of how long she lives she will be taken care of. The kids have not needed to contribute at all. My household has planned in a similar way. I know I will never need to be supported by my kids.

Thank you for separating a headline net worth figure from a life actually funded by it. The contrast between Dr Flashy and Dr Net-Worth is useful precisely because neither extreme answers the question of what the money is for. I found the follow-on costs point especially practical: a purchase is rarely a one-off price, and marina fees, maintenance and rising property taxes can quietly turn a status purchase into a continuing obligation. On the other side, treating a net worth statement as a market snapshot, rather than spendable security, helps explain why accumulating without a purpose can still feel anxious. A more useful middle path might be to define, in advance, what ‘enough’ looks like in cash-flow terms — housing, time, work flexibility and family priorities — and then judge each upgrade against that, rather than against another physician’s lifestyle or another year’s market valuation.

Of course, $5 million in a West or East Coast city means something entirely different than $5 million in a medium sized town in the Midwest or South. By way of information, if anyone is interested in how their assets compare relative to the U.S. net worth figures (by age, education or region).

Also, in another 6-8 weeks, the Federal Reserve Bank will issue the results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finance (SCF), which presents its own set of (updated) net worth and income figures.

The lingering question is – how do you determine the net present value of future social security payments or a pension, if eligible for one? Do you include that in a net worth statement or not?

The takeaway I have this article is to be neither a hoarder nor a ‘flashy’. Be comfortable in your spending style. And, in spite of the stress of the medical profession, it is good to practice gratitude for the opportunities to serve and have a roof over our heads.

Btw, I think the US government is going to face financial headwinds over the next 10 years. Social security and Medicare are going to run out of money (2032, 2033). In 2027, a large number of long-term bonds are going to mature and need re-financing. The real details can be found on the web, but you have to go digging for them. Carpe Diem.

Thanks for reading, and for adding so much to the discussion.

You’re right about geography. Five million in Manhattan or the Bay Area buys a smaller house and a longer commute than the same number buys in Omaha, which might explain why Buffett never bothered leaving. (Your link to the net worth comparison looks like it got eaten by the comment system, by the way. Feel free to repost it.)

On Social Security and pensions: I leave them off the net worth statement. You can’t sell them or borrow against them, and most of their value dies with you, so folding them in puffs up a number that’s already mostly opinion. Where they earn their keep is the retirement income plan. A pension paying $40,000 a year does roughly the work of a $1 million portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate, which means the nest egg you need to build shrinks accordingly. I’d count them in that spreadsheet and keep them out of the other one.

On the trust funds, one detail tends to get lost in the headlines. When the reserves run dry in the early 2030s, benefits don’t drop to zero. Under current projections, incoming payroll taxes would still cover something like three quarters to four fifths of scheduled payments. Painful, sure, but a haircut is a very different problem than a guillotine. For younger docs, penciling in about 75% of your statement estimate seems like reasonable caution without veering into doom.

And I’m with you on gratitude. Most of this job’s stress comes with a roof, meaningful work and the chance to retire on our own terms, which is more than a lot of people ever get to complain about.

Carpe diem right back at you. -Jorge Sanchez, MD

#8655. Small Local Scholarships Draw Far Fewer Applicants than National Ones – Apply to Several

Apply for small local scholarships through your high school counselor, community groups, local employers, and your college’s departments. Each is open only to students from one area or group, so far fewer people compete than for a national award. A few hours on these applications can pay more than one long national essay.

The Coca-Cola Scholars Program gives $20,000 each to 150 high school seniors a year, and it picked its 2026 class from more than 107,000 applications.

A local award is open only to students from one county or school, or to the children of one company’s workers. Far fewer people compete for it than for a national one. The Scholarship Foundation of Santa Barbara serves a single California county. For the 2026-27 school year, it received 3,481 applications and gave more than $8.4 million to 2,288 students. Santa Barbara’s awards work out to about $2,400 for every application it received, against about $28 per application at Coca-Cola.

Small checks add up, too. Say a senior wins four awards of $500 to $2,000 from her credit union, a Rotary club, her mother’s employer, and her high school’s booster club, for $4,500 toward her first year.

Write one core essay about a goal or a setback you handled, then rework its opening and closing for each prompt. Keep every deadline, prompt, and recommender in one spreadsheet, and ask teachers for recommendation letters at least three weeks before your first deadline.

Tell your college’s aid office about every award, since outside scholarships can shrink the aid the college gives you. The College Board notes that some colleges cut their own grants and others cut your loans, so ask which one your college cuts first. And skip any service that charges a fee to find scholarships for you, since the Federal Trade Commission warns that some hand over nothing at all once you’ve paid.

Ask your high school counselor or your college’s aid office for a list of local awards this week, then apply to every one you’re eligible for.

#8654. Hyatt Category 4 Free Night Certificate — Card Perk Sweet Spot

Savings rate, FI number, and the path to freedom.

Withdrawal plans, Roth ladders, and early access.

Index funds, asset allocation, and real estate.

Roth conversions, capital gains, and FI tax planning.

Career growth, side hustles, and entrepreneurship.

Beliefs, purpose, and financial psychology.

Exercise, nutrition, and mental wellness.

The simplest high-value card perk in travel rewards — no points math required

Picture this: you walk into a stunning hotel lobby — maybe it's the Hyatt Regency Kyoto, maybe it's the Andaz Maui at Wailea, maybe it's a chic Hyatt Centric in the heart of a city you've always wanted to explore. You hand over your World of Hyatt card at check-in, and the night is on the house. Not because you're a high roller. Not because you spent $50,000 on a credit card. Because you crossed a spending threshold you were hitting anyway, and Hyatt rewarded you with a free night certificate that covers any Category 1–4 property in the entire portfolio. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about travel rewards done right: identifying the moments where a credit card benefit perfectly intersects with your normal life, and extracting maximum value with minimum complexity. ## The Math That Makes This a No-Brainer Here's the value proposition in plain numbers. Category 4 Hyatt properties — places like the Thompson Nashville, the Hyatt Regency Maui, or the Andaz San Diego — regularly command **$200 to $400 per night** in cash. On peak dates, holiday weekends, or in premium markets, that number climbs even higher. Your free night certificate covers any of these properties at no additional points cost. None. Zero. This isn't a discount. It's a full, unrestricted free night at properties that charge real-world luxury rates. Why does this represent a genuine pricing inefficiency? Because Hyatt's Category 1–4 certificates are earned through a flat spending threshold — $15,000 on the World of Hyatt Credit Card in a calendar year — and can be redeemed at properties whose nightly rates vary enormously. A Category 4 certificate costs the same to earn whether you use it at a $150 roadside property or a $400 resort. The system rewards you for targeting the high end of the range every single time. For a household already putting everyday spending on a rewards card, $15,000 across a full calendar year is often an achievable benchmark. Groceries, utilities, insurance premiums, quarterly tax payments — it adds up faster than you think. And when it does, Hyatt drops a certificate in your account that can deliver **$300–$400 in hotel value** without spending a single additional point. In the World of Hyatt program — consistently rated the **best hotel loyalty program for value per point** — this certificate is one of the most quietly powerful perks on any hotel card in the market.

The core mechanism here isn't a transfer partnership exploit or a routing rule loophole. It's simpler and more durable than that: Hyatt's Category system creates a ceiling, not a floor. When you earn a Category 1–4 free night certificate, you're not locked into a $150-a-night budget motel. You're handed a key that opens any door in that range — and some of those doors lead to genuinely spectacular properties.

Hyatt operates on a fixed award chart, ranging from 3,500 points for a Category 1 night all the way up to 45,000 points for a Category 8 night. Unlike programs that use dynamic pricing (where award costs swing with cash demand), Hyatt's chart is static. A Category 4 property costs the same 15,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in February or New Year's Eve.

Your free night certificate functions exactly like those 15,000 points — but you earned it through card spending, not through a points balance. This means the certificate has a defined and predictable value: whatever a Category 4 property charges in cash on the night you use it is exactly what you're getting for free.

The pricing inefficiency exists because Hyatt assigns categories based on average nightly rates across the year — but peak-season rates at desirable Category 4 properties can blow well past that average. A Hyatt Regency in a major city might be Category 4 because its average annual rate qualifies, but on a conference weekend or holiday weekend, that same room might cost $350–$400. Your certificate captures that peak-season value without any upcharge.

While this sweet spot is certificate-based (no points required), World of Hyatt integrates beautifully with two major transferable currency programs:

This matters for your broader strategy. If you want to stack a certificate with a separate points redemption — say, booking multiple nights where the first is covered by the certificate and subsequent nights use transferred points — you have two strong, flexible on-ramps into the Hyatt ecosystem. Chase Ultimate Rewards is the workhorse of the FI community's travel rewards stack, and having Hyatt as an instant 1:1 partner makes it one of the most actionable transfer relationships in the game.

Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award redemptions — a meaningful distinction compared to some airline programs where surcharges can swallow most of your savings. Your certificate redemption is clean: one certificate, one free night, no surprise fees at checkout beyond standard resort fees (which, to be fair, do apply at some properties — more on that in Pro Tips).

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. As a World of Hyatt Credit Card holder, your card activity will naturally keep your account active, so expiry is rarely a concern for cardholders. But if you ever cancel the card, make sure you use your points and certificates before they age out.

Booking a World of Hyatt free night certificate is genuinely one of the easiest processes in all of travel rewards. Here's the complete walkthrough from certificate to check-in.

Log in to your World of Hyatt account at hyatt.com and navigate to your account dashboard. Under the "My Certificates & Awards" section, confirm your Category 1–4 free night certificate is present and note its expiration date. Certificates are typically valid for 12 months from issuance, so don't let it sit unused. If you don't see it and you've crossed the $15,000 annual spend threshold on your World of Hyatt Credit Card, allow a few days for it to post after your statement closes, or call Chase to confirm.

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search function. You can filter by World of Hyatt category — specifically, search for Category 4 properties in any destination you're targeting. Don't shortchange yourself by defaulting to a Category 1 or 2 property out of habit. The certificate works at any Category 1–4 property, so always target the top of the range. Look for properties with high nightly cash rates — this is where your certificate delivers the most value.

Once you've identified a target property, search your dates on hyatt.com and switch the search to "Use Points." Category 4 properties will show award availability for 15,000 points per night. If award availability shows for that date, your certificate will cover it. Hyatt's booking window opens 395 days in advance, so for peak travel dates — holidays, major events, popular travel seasons — you can and should book the maximum window out.

Proceed through the booking process. At the payment step, you'll see an option to "Apply Free Night Award" or select your certificate from your account. Select the Category 1–4 certificate. The system will apply it and your total cash charge drops to $0 for the room rate (plus taxes and any applicable resort fees).

Hyatt award availability at popular properties can be limited during peak periods. Your tactical options:

Hyatt operates on a fixed category system where each property is assigned a category from 1 to 8 based on the brand and location, not the current market rate. This creates a structural pricing inefficiency: a Category 4 property in a high-demand market like Maui or Kyoto charges the same certificate cost as a Category 4 in a mid-tier city. Your free night certificate works at all of them equally. Unlike hotel programs with dynamic pricing where the cost of a free night fluctuates with demand, Hyatt's fixed chart means you can target the highest-value Category 4 properties without paying more. The card's $95 annual fee is one of the lowest in the premium hotel card category, yet the certificate alone delivers $250 to $400 or more in value — a return that makes the math trivially easy for any FI-minded household.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's make this concrete with a real example that represents exactly how this certificate shines.

The Andaz San Diego is a boutique lifestyle hotel in the Gaslamp Quarter — rooftop pool, stylish rooms, walking distance to everything downtown. It's the kind of hotel that signals a real trip, not just a place to sleep. On a standard weekend night, cash rates run $250–$350 per night. During Comic-Con, a Padres playoff weekend, or a major convention, rates push past $400.

Cash cost: $300 (conservative weekend estimate) Certificate cost: 0 points, 1 Category 1–4 free night certificate Your out-of-pocket: $0 for the room rate

You earned this certificate by crossing $15,000 in annual spending on the World of Hyatt Credit Card — a threshold many households reach through regular everyday spending over 12 months. The certificate posts automatically, you search availability on hyatt.com, and you apply it at checkout in about five minutes.

You're not redeeming into a budget experience. The Andaz brand sits at the upper-upscale tier of the Hyatt portfolio. You check in through a host model (no formal front desk), settle into a room with thoughtful design, and wake up knowing that $300 night cost you nothing extra beyond your normal spending.

If you hold World of Hyatt elite status — Discoverist, Explorist, or Globalist — that status applies to certificate bookings exactly like paid stays. Room upgrade requests, early check-in, late check-out: all the same benefits apply.

In every case, your one certificate delivers more value than most points redemptions in any hotel program. And you earned it without touching your points balance.

Your certificate works identically at a $150/night Category 4 property and a $400/night Category 4 property. Always search for the properties with the highest cash rates in your target destination. Use hyatt.com's rate display to compare award availability against current cash pricing — this directly shows you the value you're capturing.

Hyatt's booking window opens 395 days in advance. For properties in high-demand markets — Maui, New York, Chicago during peak season — award inventory gets claimed fast. Set a calendar alert to search exactly 395 days before your target dates and book the moment the window opens.

Your certificate covers one night. If you're staying multiple nights, stack it strategically: apply the certificate to the highest-cost night (often a Saturday) and book the remaining nights with World of Hyatt points transferred instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards at a 1:1 ratio. This hybrid approach maximizes the value of every currency you're using.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of inactivity. As a cardholder, your spending activity resets this clock automatically. But if you ever pause card use, make a small Hyatt purchase — even a $1 on-property charge — to reset the timer and protect your balance.

Hyatt does not waive resort fees on award and certificate bookings at all properties. Before booking, check whether your target property charges a daily resort fee — these can run $25–$50/night and will appear on your final bill. Factor this into your value calculation, especially at resort properties in Hawaii or Las Vegas.

The $15,000 spend threshold should come from natural household spending, not manufactured purchases. In the FI community, we optimize around spending you're doing anyway — insurance premiums, tax payments, groceries, utilities. If you're buying things you don't need to hit the threshold, you're eroding the value of the certificate.

Certificates issued by Hyatt are typically valid for 12 months. Mark the expiration date in your calendar the moment the certificate posts. An expired certificate is $300+ in value that simply disappears — one of the most painful mistakes in travel rewards.

This sweet spot is built for the everyday FI household that's already spending $15,000 or more annually on a single credit card and wants to redirect that activity toward a meaningful travel benefit. You don't need a large points balance. You don't need to understand transfer partners or award chart math. You earn the certificate by spending, you apply it at checkout, and you get a free night at a genuinely nice hotel.

You need: the World of Hyatt Credit Card, $15,000 in annual card spending, and a World of Hyatt account. No minimum points balance required — this is a card perk, not a points redemption.

If your annual spending is significantly below $15,000 on a single card, this particular mechanism won't trigger. In that case, the World of Hyatt Credit Card still earns Hyatt points on spending and delivers a Category 1–4 certificate on each card anniversary — so it retains value, just through a different path. Also, if you're deeply committed to a non-Hyatt hotel program, the benefit is obviously less useful without a library of Hyatt properties in your regular rotation.

## Rated: Easy (4/5 Beginner Friendly) This is one of the most accessible sweet spots in the entire travel rewards ecosystem, and that's by design. The certificate mechanism removes the two biggest friction points in traditional points redemptions: **finding the right number of points** and **navigating complex transfer timing**. You earn the certificate passively through spending, it posts to your account automatically, and the booking process on hyatt.com is as intuitive as booking any other hotel stay. ## What Makes It Easy - **No transfer required** — the certificate lives in your World of Hyatt account, ready to apply at checkout - **Fixed pricing** — Category 4 is Category 4 everywhere in the world; no dynamic pricing surprises - **Simple availability search** — hyatt.com's award search is clean and straightforward ## The One Genuine Challenge: Availability at Popular Properties The only real friction point is award inventory at high-demand Category 4 properties on desirable dates. Hyatt limits how many award rooms it releases per night, and popular properties in destinations like Hawaii or New York fill quickly. **Three ways to beat this:** 1. Search 395 days in advance when fresh inventory releases 2. Build a shortlist of 3–5 Category 4 properties in your target region so you have backup options 3. Stay flexible on dates — midweek nights almost always have more award availability than weekends If you can approach this with even modest date flexibility, you will find great options. The Hyatt portfolio at Category 4 is large and geographically diverse, and there is almost always a compelling property available somewhere you'd actually want to go. For anyone new to travel rewards, this certificate is the perfect first redemption — low complexity, high reward, and a genuinely memorable hotel stay to show your household what this strategy can deliver.

Log in to hyatt.com and check My Certificates and Awards after your card anniversary. Note the expiration date — certificates are typically valid for 12 months. If it does not appear within a few weeks of your anniversary, contact Chase.

Search hyatt.com for Category 4 hotels in your target destinations. Compare the cash rate against the free certificate value. Target properties where cash rates exceed $300 per night — these deliver the highest return on your $95 annual fee.

Hyatt opens its booking window 395 days in advance. For popular Category 4 properties in Maui, New York, or Kyoto, set a calendar reminder and book the day the window opens. Apply your certificate during the booking process on hyatt.com.

Use the free night certificate for the most expensive night of your stay (typically weekends or peak dates), then book remaining nights with World of Hyatt points at 15,000 points per Category 4 night. This combination stretches your overall lodging value significantly.

Category 4 includes well-known properties like the Andaz Maui at Wailea, Hyatt Regency Kyoto, Andaz San Diego, Hyatt Centric locations in major cities, and many Thompson hotels. The full list is available on hyatt.com by filtering the award chart. Category 4 is the sweet spot tier where property quality is high but the award cost remains accessible.

The World of Hyatt credit card automatically issues a Category 1-4 free night certificate each year on your card anniversary. A second certificate is earned after you spend $15,000 on the card in a calendar year. No special action is required beyond holding the card and meeting the spending threshold for the bonus certificate.

Yes. The free night certificate is valid for any available standard room at a Category 1-4 property, including weekends and holidays. There are no blackout dates. However, standard room availability may be limited during peak periods, so booking early is recommended.

The certificate expires 12 months after issuance and cannot be extended or refunded. If you know you will not use it, consider booking a refundable reservation at a Category 4 property to hold the value, then cancel and rebook if your plans change. Do not let it expire unused — the value easily exceeds the annual fee.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Hyatt Category 4 free night certificate is the most accessible sweet spot in travel rewards. You do not need to understand transfer partners, award charts, or complex booking strategies. You hold the World of Hyatt credit card, the certificate arrives on your anniversary, and you redeem it at a hotel where cash rates run $250 to $400 or more per night. The $95 annual fee pays for itself three to four times over with a single use. For FI-minded households that consolidate $15,000 or more in annual spending on one card, the second certificate doubles the value. This is the card perk that turns skeptics into believers — simple math, real savings, no tricks required.

From its humble beginnings in 2008 to today, Bitcoin’s history has been relatively short but very eventful. The original protocol for this popular digital currency was created in 2008 by Satoshi Nakamoto, believed to be a pseudonym for an unknown developer or group of developers.

Nakamoto launched the Bitcoin network just a year later and began mining the currency— an estimated 1 million bitcoins were mined in the early years.

The creator(s) of this first-of-its-kind asset developed the cryptocurrency in response to the Great Recession of 2007-2009, spurred by a distrust of the traditional banking system and concerns about its stability.

Given the recent values of Bitcoin, it’s hard to believe the currency first started trading on exchanges in 2010 at under $0.10. Since then, it’s experienced astronomical growth and some pretty wild price swings.

At its most recent high, one bitcoin was worth over $64,000—a far cry from trading for pennies in its earliest days.

Whether you’re thinking of investing in Bitcoin or you’ve held this cryptocurrency for several years, it’s fun to look back at this groundbreaking asset’s history. Read on for insights on Bitcoin milestones, historical returns, and how its returns compare to those of other assets.

Since being created, Bitcoin has experienced several milestones. Here’s a look back at some of the most significant moments in the short history of this cryptocurrency:

While Bitcoin isn’t exempt from the volatility cryptocurrencies often experience, it’s delivered some impressive returns over the years. Here’s a look at Bitcoin’s annual returns from 2010 to 2022:

And here’s a look at monthly returns, if you feel like getting a deeper dive:

While Bitcoin has experienced some wild monthly price swings and a couple of years where its value has declined, you can see that its declines have been eclipsed by some incredible gains. Now let’s explore how Bitcoin’s value has changed over 10, 5, 3, and 1 years.

Let’s say you bought one bitcoin on August, 3rd 2013, for $1,106.75, its price at the time. If you held that one bitcoin until August 3rd, 2023, it would’ve been worth $29,310.44, and your total ROI for the 10 years would be 2,546.8%.

We’ll also assume you purchased one Bitcoin for this example. A single bitcoin was valued at $965.31 on August, 3rd, 2018, and its value climbed to $29,310.44 by August 2023. Using our calculation above, your total ROI for those five years would be 294.1%.

A single bitcoin was valued at $11,246.20 in August 2020, and its value climbed to $29,310.44 at the end of 2021. Your total ROI for those three years would be 160.6%.

If you purchased a single bitcoin in August 2022, you would’ve paid around $22,626.83. In one year, that value would’ve increased to $29,310.44. Your total returns for that year would be 29.54%.

Instead of buying one bitcoin, let’s say you decided to invest $1,000 into Bitcoin. Here’s a look at how this $1,000 investment would’ve performed if you bought and held your Bitcoin for 10, 5, 3, and 1 years.

While Bitcoin’s earliest investors would have benefitted the most from buying and holding their Bitcoin, those who’ve invested recently also fared well.

If you’re curious how Bitcoin returns compare to those of other asset classes, here’s how its annual and total returns compare to gold, real estate, and the S&P 500.(Spoiler alert: Bitcoin outperformed all three assets by an enormous margin.)

If you compare Bitcoin’s returns to gold’s returns, you’ll notice a stark difference. Bitcoin has an average annual return of 1,576% and a total return of 18,912% from 2010 to 2022, while SPDR Gold Shares had an average annual return of just 5.14% and a total return of 61.67% over the same period.

Let’s see if real estate fared any better compared to Bitcoin. The cryptocurrency delivered a whopping 1,576% average annual return and an 18,912% total return from 2010 to 2021, while the Vanguard Real Estate ETF had an average annual return of 13.49% and a total return of 161.91% over the same period.

So, real estate saw slightly higher returns than gold, but it still didn’t come close to Bitcoin’s returns.

The S&P 500 didn’t fare too much better in its head-to-head with Bitcoin. From 2011 to 2023, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF delivered an average annual return of 15.74% and a total return of 173.14%. While those numbers aren’t too shabby, Bitcoin’s average annual return for the same period was a whopping 819%, and its total return was 9,012%.

We’ve analyzed how Bitcoin compares to gold, real estate, and the stock market, but how does it stack up against some of the best-performing stocks? Here’s how this popular cryptocurrency stacks up against major companies like Amazon, Apple, Berkshire Hathaway, JP Morgan, Microsoft, Visa, and Walmart.

We looked at the average annual and total returns for each asset. This data assumes you bought the asset in 2010 and held it until 2023.

While some investors may be skeptical about cryptocurrency, citing concerns over market volatility and a high risk of loss, Bitcoin’s performance over time paints a rosy picture. With its longevity and astronomically high returns, Bitcoin has been worth the risk for many investors—especially early adopters.

Of course, historical performance doesn’t guarantee future returns. So if you’re considering investing in cryptocurrency, only invest what you can afford to lose.

#8652. $656,000 of Frugal Things I Still Love Doing

“Until he got all rich and fancy so that he no longer understands the common person’s plight.

Stash probably doesn’t even practice any of these money-saving things he preaches any more!”

When I read things like this, I can’t help but laugh. Because on the one hand, when you put a bunch of personal life details online like this, being misunderstood is just part of the package. But on the other hand, if the critics could peek in and see our real lives – not just mine but those of all the Mustachians – they would have to give up their conspiracy theories and accept the fact that this stuff just works.

Because really, not much has changed when it comes to the basics. Like many MMM readers over the past twelve years, my total wealth level has increased pretty regularly.  But also like many of us, I haven’t felt the need to change very much about my spending because I was doing my best to live an enjoyable life in the first place.

How have so many people found such great success? I think we Mustachians have something that’s a bit more rare and special than standard financial advice, which is what makes it work so well:

Standard Advice: Slash your spending and make sacrifices until you reach a certain savings percentage, and beyond that it doesn’t matter, it’s all personal choice. More income? Great, that means you don’t have to sacrifice as much! FatFIRE for everyone!

Mustachianism: Cultivate a love of efficiency, creativity, self awareness, and self improvement. Use this knowledge to improve your life in all ways, including those which help you live better even as your monthly expense rate drops over time.

Well, I’ll give you some examples from my own present-day life. Things I do because I happen to enjoy them, which also happen to save a lot of money. Some of these are normal, some are silly and may end up in some future gossip magazine hit piece, but all of them happen to work for me, so the critics can be damned.

As I list each item, I’ll include an estimate of how much the activity saves me per decade, because you should always think at least in terms of decades. To make that calculation yourself, just use the “rule of 172” – take a monthly expense and multiply it by 172 to estimate how much it would compound into over ten years, if invested.

1) Fixing my own House (and everybody else’s too)

I’m a big believer in self-sufficiency, and working to build up the skills to manage the most important parts of your own life without depending on too many things (or people) that are outside of your control. In other words, one giant recipe for a happy life is simply to Become a Producer of the Things You Most Enjoy Consuming.

And in my case, I happen to love houses. I like living in beautiful, functional spaces and sharing them with friends. But most houses are ugly and poorly designed when you buy them, so I realized that I also love solving problems and redesigning old buildings to become new again. I enjoy this process so much that I spend most of my free time doing it – on both my own properties and the homes of friends.

And I love teaching other people to gain power over their own houses too. It’s amazing how great people feel as they lose their fear and dependence on outside contractors, and gain the ability to fix and maintain things with their own two hands.

Savings: An average of $20,000 per year = $287,000 per decade

You know what’s great? Having so much money that you can buy whatever you want – high quality things which get delivered to your front door the very next day.

You know what’s even better? Not buying some of those new things, and instead finding ways to share, repurpose and buy equally high quality items from other people who don’t need them any more. All while building up your own community and creating new friendships in the process.

Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, and even NextDoor all have Buy Nothing groups for most areas. In the MMM-HQ community, we run a Discord server with about 200 local people, who chat around the clock on a wide range of subjects. They help each other with major projects in one channel called #diyhowto, and give away and sell things on #forsale and #buynothing.

Although our private Discord group is my favorite, I also use Craigslist regularly, and probably save (and earn) a few thousand every year thanks to the habit:

We all know that Mr. Money Mustache’s biggest contribution to personal finance is to insist that bike transportation is the best way to get around. And I still feel this way. As we learned in The True Cost of Commuting, cars cost at least 50 cents per mile to operate, while bikes are much cheaper, mainly due to reduced depreciation and maintenance costs (which are even bigger than the gas savings).

I do still use bikes (or walking) for at least 95% of my local trips these days, but because I live in the center of a small city, my life is pretty local. So this still only adds up to about 2000 miles per year, a savings of “only” $14,000 per decade.

But when you choose active transportation, there’s much more to the picture than just cutting your car expenses. You’re changing everything about your physical and mental health picture for the better, which brings us to the next point of…

Although I’m no competitive athlete, whenever I see an option to make my body work a bit harder, I usually take it. Stairs instead of elevators, running the golf course instead of using a golf cart, moving my own furniture and appliances instead of calling a mover, shoveling snow and raking leaves instead of using a machine.

When I face a decision like this, I simply ask myself the question: “Well, Mustache. Do you want MORE health and fitness, or LESS?” Putting it in that context makes the answer obvious.  Every bit helps, because when it comes to your body, the rule is pretty much use it or lose it.

But how much money does this save? There’s no real way to calculate it exactly, but I like to think of it this way: The US average health care spending is about $13,000 per person per year. My lifetime costs due to illness or medication so far have been just about zero, plus I know I’ve had more energy and greater productivity due to being healthy. Let’s just put it very conservatively and set the estimated savings and benefits at $10k per year which means

5) Saving Energy by Running my home like a Glamping Retreat

Here’s where things get a bit silly, but my level of joy is actually at its greatest.

My personality type is probably a weird combination of an engineer, a carpenter, an artsy hippie, and a mad scientist. Oh, and a devoted homebody too. Because of this, my favorite activity most days is to just run around my house taking care of things and trying new little experiments and improvements.

Sometimes I’ll cut a few big holes on on the South side of the house and install sliding doors and big windows to allow nice sunbeams and passive solar energy to get into my house and give me free heat in the winters. Other times it’s just smaller things to save energy and live more at at one with the seasons of my area:

Even taken all together, these things are pretty small – the average combined gas and electric bill for my area is about $250 per month, while my usage adds up to about $75. So while we’re only saving about $30,000 per decade for what sounds like a lot of work to most people, I consider this to be the biggest win because I enjoy living in “MMM’s Energy Efficiency Playground” so much.

“Hey, we’re having a big back yard pool party next weekend to celebrate Amy’s graduation from kindergarten, can you make it?”

“OH NOOOO!!! We will be off in at Disneyland that whole week! We planned the trip months ago, I wish we could make it!

As I type this in the height of the summer season, I really feel this effect at its fullest: almost all of my friends are off on trips, and my guest suite here at home is almost constantly full. People are traveling a lot, and many of them sound like they wish they could spend a few more of their precious summer weeks and weekends at home.

I’ll let you in on a little secret: you can! The trick is saying, “no thanks” more often to plans that involve you being away, and “yes please” to things that let you stay at home. The benefits are numerous:

Estimated Savings: Even if you replace just two weeks of travel for a family of four, with equivalent time at home you might save $5,000 per year in direct costs and a further $5,000 per year in incidental benefits like the health and local friendships. This would work out to a shocking $143,000 per decade of wealth increase!

Of course, travel is generally a good thing for broadening the life experience of you and your kids. It’s worth spending on, lavishly at times. But the key is to balance it out and be discerning, keeping the most enriching trips and pruning a few off the bottom of the list. And remembering that home time is valuable and healthy too.

And Whoa! We’ve already built up a huge list and I feel like I was just getting started.

Taken all together, we’ve already detailed things that compound to $656,000 every decade, which already more than double the median wealth that most American seniors have as they cruise nervously into their retirement years – after over 40 years of work!

And now that I’ve been writing this blog for over ten years myself, I can safely say that over $656,000 of even my most recent worth increases are directly attributable to these simple habits. The same ones many of us have been enjoying and preaching about all along, both before and after our retirement dates.

If money is in genuinely short supply, you could go a lot further than the examples in this article. And indeed, there’s a lot more laid out in this blog or the MMM Boot Camp email series.

But one of the points of Mustachianism is that you usually don’t have to try all that hard. Just tweaking your lifestyle to be slightly less ridiculous and more efficient than average is usually all it takes.

In the comments: what are your quirks and frugal indulgences? The things you do now to save money, or things you still do even after it’s no longer about the money? I often wonder how widespread this frugality-just-for-fun is. But since we Humans are a naturally curious and problem solving species in our natural state, I suspect there are many more of us out there.

I think his first point “Fixing my own House” is invaluable advice for any homeowner in HCOL areas. I live in a very HCOL city (a conscious decision that currently is worth the tradeoff for me) and bought a modest “fixer upper” for well below my neighborhoods average home price during COVID.

Boy did I quickly hit the “find out” part of that decision. I’d never touched renovations or building or fixing a home / apartment beyond mounting bike racks on my rented apartments walls. I received insane quotes for electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and all the drywall repairs required for that kind of work. I did the math out for many of these projects based on the number of people and days the companies told me it would take and in many cases these companies were pulling in $300 per man-hour.

So I didn’t hire any of them. I spent an entire year learning the plumbing and electrical code for my city / state / country. I bothered the hell out of my city inspectors with questions. Made dozens of trips (sadly mostly via car) to the big box stores – eventually even started accounts with supply houses and lumber yards for better variety and deals.

In the two years I spent renovating the house, I’ve saved myself more than $300,000 (estimating the value of my time at $50/hour).

If anybody on here is considering buying a home, but isn’t willing to learn to do this stuff themselves, I think renting might be the more Mustachian decision if the alternative is paying for somebody else to do this work. I also don’t think there’s anything wrong with that.

Another good one is learning to replace capacitors yourself, with a multimeter you can check them, this is the most common HVAC failure point and an easy DIY job with lots of YouTube vids showing how to do it. Replacuparts on Amazon are cheap and have reviews to help ensure quality.

Thanks for the post MMM! Like those above, I resonated with your article. A lot of these were things I have “always just done” (like hang dry clothes) so a few more that “I just have always done”

(1) My grad school room mate and I loved new clothes but really couldn’t afford them. So we would challenge ourselves to keep our apartment as cold as we could tolerate in Ann Arbor, Michigan and “reward” ourselves in cost savings from our heating bill by buying a new sweater to keep us warm. That $50/month difference meant we were stoked by our new sweater and usually pocketed the savings the other months.

(2) Buy wool clothing. It’s more durable, needs to be washed less, and you can have a smaller wardrobe (which takes up less space, saving you money in storage/heating costs). Even better buy used wool clothing.

(3) Books. I love reading and go through upwards of 50+ books a year. Buying those new at a bookstore would be $30-$50 a month! Instead, I use Libby through my library and constantly have a multitude of books on hold. So yes, I need to wait, but honestly, it’s not that bad if you just had a great book come up that you’ve been waiting for. Slow gratification :)

(4) Shampoo / Conditioner. I’ve experimented a lot with this over the years. Especially for women, there is an expectation to have clean, styled, long hair. There just is. I have finally settled on washing hair 2-3x a week, using tiny amounts of shampoo and conditioner only when necessary means I can save 5 bottles of each a year.

(5) Buying the clearance veggies and cooking them that day. I’m also vegetarian. Both of these things save a TON of money, especially eating out (it’s about 10-15% less to be a vegetarian consistently when ordering out).

My last thought to add to your post is to be adaptable. My partner and I are throwing a large wedding in a month. Weddings are crazy expensive if you let them be. It may not be planned and perfectly coordinated, but we’ve created a wedding we’re proud of – both financially and visually. #8651. Pay Less for Meat – The Big Savings Are in Slow-Cooking Cuts, Not Bone-In Chicken

You can keep eating meat and still pay less for it. Choose slow-cooking cuts like chuck roast over steak, and buy bone-in chicken thighs only when they’re under about 60% of the price of boneless breasts. Cook or freeze markdowns the day you buy them, and stock up when your usual cuts go on sale.

USDA’s Food Price Outlook forecasts 2026 price increases of 8.7% for beef and veal, 1.2% for poultry, and 1% for pork.

By USDA’s Food Buying Guide, a pound of boneless breast cooks down to about 12 ounces of meat. Once the bones and skin come off, a pound of bone-in thighs gives about 7 ounces and a pound of whole chicken about 6. So thighs are the cheaper meat only when priced under about 60% of the breast price, and a whole chicken only under about half.

In USDA’s survey of supermarket ads for the week of Nov. 9, boneless skinless breasts averaged $2.95 a pound, boneless thighs $3.51, and bone-in thighs $1.50. Ounce for ounce, the bone-in thigh meat cost about 14% less than breast meat. At $1.57, whole chickens cost about 8% more than breasts per ounce of meat, unless you eat the skin.

For beef and pork, choose the cuts made for slow cooking. In the same week’s beef ads, boneless chuck roast averaged $7.54 a pound against $13.35 for boneless strip steak, and the pork ads had bone-in shoulder at $2.20 against $3.18 for bone-in center-cut chops. Precut stew meat cost $8.59 a pound, so cube a chuck roast yourself or ask the meat counter to.

The sell-by date tells the store when to pull a package, not when the meat turns unsafe, USDA says. FoodSafety.gov’s storage chart gives ground meat and poultry only a day or two in the fridge, so cook or freeze a markdown the day you buy it.

When a cut you use goes on sale, buy several weeks’ worth, split it into meal-size bags, and freeze it. At 0°F, it can be stored indefinitely, though by the same chart, roasts, steaks, and chops are best within 4 to 12 months and ground meat within 3 to 4. Then serve smaller portions of meat with more beans, grains, and vegetables.

Check this week’s store ad for bone-in thighs under about 60% of the breast price or a chuck roast on sale, and buy enough to freeze.

It’s almost Halloween, and much like everyone else, I have been sucked into the tradition of watching horror movies with my wife before we take our daughter trick-or-treating. One of the movies I’m still thinking about from last week is Backrooms. It is the highest-grossing film A24 has ever released, and most of it takes place in rooms that look like a hospital at 3 a.m.

Yellowed walls. Fluorescent tubes that buzz loud enough to notice. Carpet that has absorbed something you would rather not identify. Corridors that turn left, then left again, until you’re somehow back where you started. If you trained at a big academic center, you have walked these halls, and probably still dream about them.

The film grew out of Kane Parsons’s YouTube series about a dimension of endless, empty rooms. Instead of the creature feature I expected, I got a picture of the doctor who is close to financial independence and can’t bring themselves to leave.

Full disclaimer: only read ahead if you’ve watched the film because there will be spoilers!

Clark is a failed architect running a struggling furniture store in San Jose. He drinks too much, his marriage is over, and he has started sleeping at the store. One night he goes down to check the breaker box, notices a glowing slit in the wall, and falls through it.

On the other side is a copy of the world that is slightly wrong. Rooms that almost look like rooms. Furniture that seems to have melted at the edges. Hallways longer than the building could possibly hold. Later in the film it gets described as a faulty, misremembered version of reality.

That description fits medical training better than anything I’ve heard in a wellness lecture. Residency is a copy of adult life with the proportions off. You have a title and real responsibility for people’s lives, but you’re 31 with a negative net worth, and you haven’t made it to a friend’s wedding without checking your phone in years.

Real life is always one room ahead: after boards, after fellowship, after the loans, after partnership. So you keep walking.

After a few trips in and out, Clark leaves his therapist a message. He’s staying in the Backrooms, and he won’t be coming back. He has found a way out of the failing store, the drinking, the empty house. The place he picked is worse than the one he’s leaving, but it’s familiar, and it doesn’t ask him to deal with anything.

The FIRE crowd has a name for this: one more year. You hit your number, or get close enough to see it, and you sign another contract anyway. The reasons all sound sensible. The market is choppy. The kids start college in four years. The group is short two partners.

Besides, what else would you do on a Wednesday morning?

Plenty of physicians keep working after financial independence because they love the work, and that’s a good outcome. The question worth asking is whether you’re staying because you chose to, or because the hallway is the only place you know how to stand.

Early in the film, Clark shoots a cheap TV commercial for the store dressed as its pirate mascot. It’s a little embarrassing and a little sweet. It is the version of himself he has to perform to keep the business alive.

By the end of the film, the costume becomes a towering, distorted Clark in the pirate outfit, peg leg and all, is waiting for him in the Backrooms. Clark tries to calm it down the way you’d talk to a dog you raised from a puppy. It kills him.

The Backrooms in this film make monsters from what people carry in, their memories and their feelings, and build with it.

Doctors have a costume too. The white coat, the title, the steady voice you use to tell a family the scan came back bad. You need it, and your patients need you to have it. The trouble starts when it stops coming off after the shift. You introduce yourself as Dr. at your kid’s soccer game. The hobbies lapse one at a time. Every close friend works in your department. Your income, your marriage, and your sense of being a decent person all run through one job.

Then the job goes sideways. A lawsuit, a patient death you can’t stop replaying, an RVU target that climbs every year, a private equity buyout that changes everything except your title.

What turns on you in those moments is the professional self you spent fifteen years building, now bigger than the person wearing it.

The second half belongs to Clark’s therapist, Dr. Mary Kline (Renate Reinsve). Worried about her patient, she goes to the store and walks into the Backrooms after him.

She doesn’t walk in clean. Mary is still working through the demolition of her childhood home and her mother’s institutionalization. A professional helper carrying a stack of her own unprocessed losses into someone else’s crisis is a fair description of a lot of people in medicine.

Inside, Clark ties her to a chair in a fake dining room. Three human-shaped figures sit around the table with them. They don’t move or react to anything. Clark shows her they’re made of an edible white substance, and it becomes clear the Backrooms feed on them.

It might sound odd, but I couldn’t watch that scene without thinking about the Maslach Burnout Inventory. It measures three things: emotional exhaustion, a fading sense of accomplishment, and depersonalization.

Doctors are familiar with depersonalization. Patients start to feel like tasks, and after a while you feel like one too. You’re at the table every day, and you look fine from across the room, while the place slowly takes what it needs from you.

The pirate gets rid of Clark comes for Mary next. Her survival is noteworthy.

Cornered in a lopsided replica of the furniture store, she snaps the monster’s peg leg with a hat rack, then hits it in the face with a chunk of concrete from her childhood home. The thing she has been grieving the whole movie turns out to be the thing she fights with.

For a physician, that chunk of concrete is whoever you were before medicine. The kid who played bass in a garage band. The person who built bookshelves, or ran trails, or cooked for twelve friends on a Saturday. Those parts didn’t vanish when you matched. They got buried under a decade of training.

The doctors I’ve seen leave clinical work well, or drop to part-time without falling apart, usually started digging some of that back up long before they needed it. They had a corner of life the job wasn’t allowed into, and they’d been living in it for years by the time they gave notice.

This is where the analogy gets uncomfortable.

Mary’s fight with the pirate sets off a gas trap. Researchers in hazmat suits haul her out to a facility run by Async, a company that used to make MRI machines before it found the Backrooms and made them its main business.

Whether or not the filmmakers meant anything by it, a medical imaging company ending up in charge of the maze is a hard detail to ignore if you work in a hospital.

In the last scene, Mary sits in an interrogation room across from Phil, one of Async’s scientists. She asks whether they’re going to let her go. He tells her the decision isn’t his.

A lot of doctors make it through the burnout, the bad years, the cases that almost broke them, and end up in that room. They’re ready to leave, and they find out the exit belongs to someone else:

None of these are sinister on their own. Each one just moves the decision a little further from you and a little closer to a contract, a lender, or an employer.

For a physician, that’s what financial independence is really for. It’s less about retiring at 45 and more about who gets to answer the question Mary asks.

The film’s final shot is a copy of Mary, deformed and silent, sitting in a rough replica of that interrogation room somewhere deep in the Backrooms. The place has learned her. Whatever happens to the real Mary, a version of her stays behind.

Medicine leaves a copy of you behind too, and that isn’t all bad. The judgment, the pattern recognition, the calm you have in a code are yours for life. The goal isn’t to get out with nothing of the doctor left. It’s to make sure the doctor isn’t the only thing left.

A few things that help, roughly in order of effort:

Clark stayed because the maze was easier than his life. Most doctors who stay too long do it for a version of the same reason. Staying in medicine can be a great choice, as long as you’re the one making it.

The Pro Forma Never Paid Anyone’s Mortgage

If you bought into a multifamily syndication around 2021, you remember the deck. Glossy photos, a tidy IRR, a confident exit year. Then rates climbed, valuations slid, and plenty of investors watched distributions pause while their capital sat locked inside a deal that no longer penciled out.

Private real estate lending puts you in a different seat. The lender gets paid ahead of equity, holds a lien on the property, and collects interest from monthly loan payments rather than waiting on a sale that may never hit its number. You give up the home-run upside. In exchange, nobody calls you about a broken water heater at 2 a.m., a perk I’ve come to value after enough overnight shifts.

In a recent webinar, I joined Dr. Christy Burakovsky and Chris Lopez of Property Llama to discuss how private real estate loans are underwritten, where the actual risks lie, and what investors should ask any fund before wiring a dollar.

We also covered the importance of looking beyond projected returns and understanding the fundamentals behind a lending strategy.

The takeaway? Before investing, know how the loan is structured, what protects your capital, and what happens when a deal doesn’t go according to plan.

#8649. Your Student Loan Offer Is a Maximum – Accept Only What You Need

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. The federal loans in your college aid offer are what you’re eligible to borrow, not what you need. Subtract grants, scholarships, savings, and earnings from your real costs, and borrow only what’s left. Take subsidized loans first, since the government pays their interest while you’re in school. Lower or decline the rest through your school’s aid office.

Schools set the loan amount at their cost of attendance, an estimate of a year’s tuition, fees, housing, food, books, transportation, and personal costs, minus the other aid you receive, up to a federal limit. Your savings, summer pay, and family help don’t lower the total.

The school’s housing and food figures are usually averages that can run higher or lower than what you’ll actually spend. For a dependent student, the federal limit is $5,500 the first year, no more than $3,500 of it subsidized, and $7,500 a year from the third year on.

Unsubsidized loans build interest from the day they’re paid out, at a fixed 6.52% on undergraduate federal loans first paid out this school year.

To figure what you need, start with the school’s cost of attendance and replace its housing and food figures with your own. Subtract grants, scholarships, savings, what you’ll earn, and what your family will pay, then cover that gap with subsidized loans first, unsubsidized next, and private or parent loans only for anything still left.

Say a dependent freshman on track to graduate in four years gets an offer of $3,000 in subsidized loans and $2,500 unsubsidized, and grants and summer earnings leave a $3,000 gap. Paid out half each semester at 6.52%, the unneeded $2,500 would build about $650 in interest before repayment starts six months after graduation. Accepting only the $3,000 subsidized loan keeps the $2,500 and its interest off the books.

To take less, enter a lower amount in your school’s aid portal, or ask the financial aid office to reduce or cancel the loan before the money is paid out.

Money already paid out can still go back. The Education Department treats loan money returned within 120 days of being paid out as canceled, with no interest or loan fee owed on it. Ask the aid office to send it back, or return it through your loan servicer, the company that manages your federal loans and is listed in your StudentAid.gov account.

Choose a warehouse club by which one is near you and stocks what your household buys most, since Costco, Sam’s Club, and BJ’s all charge $60 or $65 a year for a basic membership. Join only if a year’s savings on your own shopping list beat that fee.

With fees that close, compare what each club sells, which coupons and credit cards it takes, and where it has stores.

Costco’s U.S. warehouses take only Visa credit cards, so pay there with one of the best credit cards for Costco. Sam’s Club and BJ’s take all major credit cards, and the BJ’s One Mastercard earns 3% in BJ’s rewards on most purchases there.

BJ’s has about 270 clubs, all in 22 states. Each club’s upgrade, $130 a year at Costco and $120 at the other two, pays up to 2% back on eligible purchases, which covers its extra cost only once you spend $3,000 to $3,250 a year there.

Before you join, compare unit prices at each nearby club and your usual store on 10 to 15 things you buy monthly. Multiply the monthly difference by 12, add any gas savings, and weigh the total against the fee. At a club that charges 20% less, a family of four that spends $150 a month on diapers, coffee, and paper towels saves $360 a year, more than five times a $65 fee. A single shopper buying mostly fresh food saves far less than that.

Join the club whose total beats its fee by the most. A household with no club nearby, or savings below the fee, does better at a discount grocer.

Shop from a list, split big packs with another household, and skip the bulk buys that go bad.

All three refund the year’s fee to an unsatisfied member, so treat your first year as a trial. Keep your receipts, price the same items at your old store, and cancel for a refund if the savings fall short of the fee.

“I’m sick of the scaring, the terror, the fright. I’m tired of being something that goes bump in the night. I’m bored with leering my horrible glances, And my feet hurt from dancing those skeleton dances. I don’t like graveyards, and I need something new. There must be more to life than just yelling, ‘Boo!'”

—Tim Burton, The Nightmare Before Christmas

Dr. Wednesday Addams sat alone in her office at 11 PM, glaring at her retirement calculator the way you’d glare at a pathology report you already suspect is bad.

Twenty years of serious income, the kind that makes the neighbors assume you’re rich, and the screen looked like a crime scene.

Projected retirement age: 79. Probability of success: 23%. Her portfolio had roughly the life expectancy of a jack-o’-lantern left on the porch until Thanksgiving.

She was 58. She wanted out at 61, and blocking the exit stood a tangle of whole life policies her cousin had sold her, a 401(k) ignored for a decade, a pre-tax balance quietly wiring itself into a tax bomb, and a household burning $35,000 a month like a furnace nobody remembered to turn down.

Her story isn’t rare. It isn’t even interesting.

Physicians stumble into the same open graves with the reliability of a zombie shuffling toward the nearest brain, and the tax code waiting at the bottom helps itself to 37 cents of every married dollar above $768,700. Some of these graves are fresh. A few were dug by Congress.

The AMA’s latest national data has 41.9% of physicians reporting at least one symptom of burnout in 2025, down from 48.2% in 2023. Progress, technically. Emergency medicine and hematology-oncology still sit near 50%, coin-flip odds that the physician running tonight’s code is cooked.

Burnout steals your joy first and your retirement date second. You plan to work until 68, the call schedule wins at 61, and the seven years of full income your plan quietly assumed shrink to a few years of part-time pay, or nothing at all.

The itch is arriving earlier, too. In Doximity’s polling, the share of physicians aged 45 to 49 considering early retirement nearly doubled between 2023 and 2026, from 23% to 44%.

Dr. Smart and Dr. Addams both started at 35 earning $300,000. Smart saved 25%, or $75,000 a year. Addams saved 10%.
